uni-bsc-math-linear-programming.title: B.Sc Mathematics · Linear Programming
uni-bsc-math-linear-programming.description: Formulation of LPPs, graphical solution, convex sets and basic feasible solutions, the simplex method, Big-M and two-phase methods, degeneracy and special cases, duality and the dual simplex method, and the transportation and assignment problems, with fully worked tableaux and exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Formulation and graphical solution of LPPs
courses.summary: Mathematical formulation of linear programming problems from product-mix, diet and blending situations; graphical method for two variables; corner-point theorem; special cases (multiple optima, unbounded and infeasible problems); standard form with slack and surplus variables; basic and basic feasible solutions.
outcomes: Learners can formulate an LPP with decision variables, objective and constraints
Learners can solve two-variable LPPs graphically by the corner-point method
Learners can recognise multiple optima, unboundedness and infeasibility
Learners can convert an LPP to standard form using slack and surplus variables
Learners can list basic solutions and identify basic feasible ones

scenes.text: A Saharanpur workshop makes tables and chairs with limited carpentry and painting hours.
How many of each maximise profit? First, write it as an LPP.

steps.title: Ingredients of an LPP
steps.body:
1. **Decision variables** x₁, …, xₙ (quantities to choose)
2. **Objective function** Z = c₁x₁ + … + cₙxₙ to maximise or minimise
3. **Constraints**: linear inequalities/equations from limited resources or requirements
4. **Non-negativity**: xⱼ ≥ 0

Assumptions: proportionality, additivity, divisibility, certainty.

steps.title: Solved: product mix
steps.body:
Table: 3 h carpentry, 1 h painting, profit ₹300. Chair: 1 h carpentry, 1 h painting, profit ₹200. Available: 30 h carpentry, 14 h painting.

Max Z = 300x + 200y
subject to 3x + y ≤ 30, x + y ≤ 14, x, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Solved: diet problem
steps.body:
Food A: 2 units protein, 1 unit iron, ₹20/kg; food B: 1 unit protein, 3 units iron, ₹30/kg. Need ≥ 8 protein and ≥ 9 iron.

Min Z = 20x + 30y
subject to 2x + y ≥ 8, x + 3y ≥ 9, x, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ≥ for resource limits (should be ≤) or ≤ for requirements (should be ≥).
- Forgetting non-negativity constraints.
- Mixing units (hours vs minutes) inside one constraint.

activity.prompt: Which kind of constraint does each statement give?

items.text: The diet must contain at least 50 g protein
Exactly 100 kg of blend must be produced
Demand of at least 20 units must be met

quiz.why: Linear programming requires both the objective and constraints to be linear in the decision variables.

quiz.why: LP allows continuous values; requiring integers gives an integer programming problem instead.

quiz.q: 'At least 8 units of protein' gives a constraint of type:
quiz.why: A minimum requirement is written as (protein supplied) ≥ 8.

scenes.text: The constraints cut out a polygon of feasible plans.
The best plan always sits at a corner of that polygon.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Draw each constraint as a line; shade the side satisfying it.
2. The common region is the **feasible region** (a convex polygon).
3. **Corner-point theorem**: if an optimum exists, it occurs at a vertex.
4. Evaluate Z at each vertex (or slide the iso-profit line Z = k outward).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing a vertex formed by two constraint lines.
- Shading the wrong side: test the origin in each inequality.

steps.title: Special cases
steps.body:
- **Multiple optima**: objective line parallel to a binding edge (e.g. Max x + y with x + y ≤ 5).
- **Unbounded**: region extends so Z can grow indefinitely (Max x + y with x − y ≤ 1, x, y ≥ 0).
- **Infeasible**: no point satisfies all constraints (x + y ≤ 2 and x + y ≥ 5).
- An unbounded region does not always mean an unbounded solution (the diet minimum above is finite).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring 'unbounded' for any open region in a minimisation.
- Missing alternative optima when two vertices give equal Z.

quiz.why: Evaluating at the vertex (3, 2) gives 20·3 + 30·2 = ₹120, the lowest of the corner values.

lessons.title: Standard form and basic feasible solutions

scenes.text: With three or more variables we cannot draw the region.
Vertices become basic feasible solutions of a system of equations.

steps.title: Standard form
steps.body:
Max Z = cᵀx subject to Ax = b, x ≥ 0, b ≥ 0.

- ≤ constraint: add a **slack** s ≥ 0: 3x + y + s₁ = 30.
- ≥ constraint: subtract a **surplus** s ≥ 0: x + y − s₂ = 4.
- Min Z ⇔ Max (−Z). Unrestricted x = x′ − x″ with x′, x″ ≥ 0.

steps.title: Basic solutions
steps.body: With m equations and n variables (n > m), set n − m variables (non-basic) to 0 and solve for the m basic ones. At most ⁿCₘ basic solutions. A basic solution with all variables ≥ 0 is a **basic feasible solution (BFS)**; BFSs correspond exactly to vertices of the feasible region. If a basic variable is 0, the BFS is **degenerate**.

steps.title: Solved: furniture problem
steps.body:
3x + y + s₁ = 30, x + y + s₂ = 14 (m = 2, n = 4 ⇒ up to 6 basic solutions).

- x = y = 0: s₁ = 30, s₂ = 14 (BFS, vertex (0, 0))
- s₁ = s₂ = 0: x = 8, y = 6 (BFS, vertex (8, 6))
- y = s₁ = 0: x = 10, s₂ = 4 (BFS)
- x = s₂ = 0: y = 14, s₁ = 16 (BFS)
- y = s₂ = 0: x = 14, s₁ = −12 (**not feasible**)
- x = s₁ = 0: y = 30, s₂ = −16 (**not feasible**)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding a slack to a ≥ constraint.
- Leaving b negative in standard form — multiply that row by −1 first.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Convex sets and the simplex method
courses.summary: Convex sets, extreme points, convex hull and the fundamental theorem of linear programming; the simplex algorithm with the initial tableau, optimality and feasibility (ratio) conditions, pivoting, and reading the final tableau, including alternative optima and unboundedness.
outcomes: Learners can test convexity and identify extreme points
Learners can state the fundamental theorem of LP
Learners can set up an initial simplex tableau with slack variables
Learners can perform the ratio test and pivot correctly
Learners can read optimal values, alternative optima and unboundedness from a tableau

lessons.title: Convex sets and the fundamental theorem

scenes.text: Join any two points inside an egg by a straight line — the line stays inside.
That is convexity, and it is why LP optima sit at corners.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- S ⊆ ℝⁿ is **convex** if x, y ∈ S, 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1 ⇒ λx + (1 − λ)y ∈ S.
- **Extreme point**: a point of S that is not a convex combination of two other distinct points of S.
- **Convex hull**: the smallest convex set containing a given set.
- Hyperplanes, half-spaces and their intersections (polyhedra) are convex.

steps.title: Fundamental theorem of LP
steps.body:
1. The feasible set {x: Ax = b, x ≥ 0} is convex.
2. If it is non-empty, it has at least one BFS (extreme point).
3. If an optimal solution exists, an optimal BFS exists.

Proof idea for 1: if Ax = Ay = b, then A(λx + (1 − λ)y) = b, and non-negativity is preserved.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- {(x, y): x² + y² ≤ 1}: convex; every boundary point is extreme.
- {(x, y): xy ≥ 1, x > 0}: convex (region above a hyperbola branch).
- {(x, y): x² + y² ≥ 1}: **not convex** — (−1, 0) and (1, 0) are in it, but their midpoint (0, 0) is not.
- Square [0, 1]²: convex with 4 extreme points (corners).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every boundary point of a polygon is extreme (only vertices are).
- Thinking the union of convex sets is convex.

activity.prompt: Convex or not convex?

items.text: The union of two disjoint discs
The feasible region of an LPP

quiz.q: The intersection of convex sets is:
quiz.why: If two points lie in every set, then so does the segment between them, so the intersection is convex.

quiz.q: Extreme points of a triangle are:
quiz.why: Any other boundary point lies on a segment between two vertices, so only the vertices are extreme.

quiz.q: The fundamental theorem says an optimum, if it exists, is attained at:
quiz.why: An optimal BFS always exists when the LPP has an optimum, which is why simplex checks only vertices.

scenes.text: A climber on a polyhedral hill moves from corner to corner, always uphill.
When no neighbouring corner is higher, she is at the top — the optimum.

steps.title: Algorithm (maximisation, all ≤ with b ≥ 0)
steps.body:
1. Add slacks; start at x = 0 with the slacks basic.
2. Compute Zⱼ − Cⱼ for each column. If all ≥ 0, the current BFS is **optimal**.
3. **Entering variable**: column with the most negative Zⱼ − Cⱼ.
4. **Ratio test**: for positive entries aᵢⱼ in that column, compute bᵢ/aᵢⱼ; the smallest gives the **leaving variable**. If no positive entry, the LPP is **unbounded**.
5. **Pivot**: divide the pivot row by the pivot element; eliminate the entering column from other rows.
6. Repeat from step 2.

steps.title: Reading the tableau
steps.body:
- Basic variables take the values in the solution column; non-basic are 0.
- Z value appears in the Z-row of the solution column.
- In the optimal tableau, Zⱼ − Cⱼ under the slacks are the **shadow prices** (dual values).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including zero or negative entries in the ratio test.
- Choosing the largest ratio instead of the smallest (leads to infeasibility).
- Forgetting to update the Z-row during pivoting.

activity.prompt: Order one iteration of the simplex method.
items: Check Zⱼ − Cⱼ for optimality
Select the entering variable (most negative Zⱼ − Cⱼ)
Do the ratio test on positive column entries
Select the leaving variable (minimum ratio)
Divide the pivot row by the pivot element
Eliminate the entering column from all other rows, including Z

quiz.why: A negative Zⱼ − Cⱼ means increasing that variable would raise Z; if none is negative, no improvement is possible.

quiz.q: If the entering column has no positive entries, the LPP is:
quiz.why: The entering variable can increase indefinitely without any basic variable hitting zero, so Z grows without bound.

quiz.q: The leaving variable is chosen by the:
quiz.why: The minimum ratio is the first basic variable to reach zero, keeping the next solution feasible.

scenes.text: A glass company makes two products using capacity in three plants.
Two simplex iterations find the best mix.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: Max Z = 3x₁ + 5x₂ subject to x₁ ≤ 4, 2x₂ ≤ 12, 3x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 18, x ≥ 0. Add slacks s₁, s₂, s₃.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Arithmetic slips with fractions — check Z by substituting: 3·2 + 5·6 = 36 ✔.
- Forgetting that s₁ = 2 means unused capacity, so its shadow price is 0.

activity.prompt: In the initial tableau, what is the minimum ratio when x₂ enters?

quiz.why: The Zⱼ − Cⱼ entry under s₃ is 1, so one extra hour in plant 3 would raise Z by 1.

quiz.q: Why is the shadow price of s₁ zero?
quiz.why: s₁ = 2 is basic, so plant 1 is not binding and extra capacity there adds nothing.

quiz.q: After iteration 1, Z equals:
quiz.why: With x₂ = 6 and x₁ = 0, Z = 5 × 6 = 30, shown in the Z-row.

scenes.text: The final tableau says more than the answer.
A zero in the wrong place reveals other equally good plans.

steps.title: Diagnostics
steps.body:
- **Alternative optima**: in the optimal tableau, a non-basic variable has Zⱼ − Cⱼ = 0. Pivoting it in gives another optimal BFS; all convex combinations are optimal.
- **Unbounded**: entering column has no positive entries.
- **Minimisation**: either maximise −Z, or choose the most positive Zⱼ − Cⱼ to enter and stop when all are ≤ 0.

steps.title: Solved: alternative optimum
steps.body: Max Z = 2x₁ + 4x₂, x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 5, x₁ + x₂ ≤ 4. The objective is parallel to the first constraint. Simplex ends with x₂ = 2.5, s₂ = 1.5, Z = 10, and Zⱼ − Cⱼ = 0 under non-basic x₁ ⇒ alternative optimum at (3, 1), Z = 10.

steps.title: Solved: unbounded
steps.body: Max Z = x₁ + x₂, x₁ − x₂ ≤ 1. Initial: x₁ enters, s₁ leaves. Next tableau: x₂ has Zⱼ − Cⱼ = −2 but its column entry is −1 (no positive entry) ⇒ **unbounded**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring zero Zⱼ − Cⱼ entries for non-basic variables.
- Using maximisation rules unchanged on a minimisation tableau.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Artificial variables: Big-M, two-phase and degeneracy
courses.summary: Why artificial variables are needed for ≥ and = constraints, the Big-M (penalty) method, the two-phase method, detecting infeasibility, degeneracy, ties in the ratio test, cycling and Bland's rule.
outcomes: Learners can set up an initial tableau with artificial variables
Learners can solve LPPs by the Big-M method
Learners can carry out Phase I and Phase II of the two-phase method
Learners can detect infeasibility from a final tableau
Learners can recognise degeneracy and apply an anti-cycling rule

lessons.title: Why artificial variables? The Big-M method

scenes.text: With ≥ constraints the origin is not feasible, so simplex has no place to start.
Add temporary 'artificial' variables, penalise them heavily, and let simplex push them out.

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body:
- ≤: add slack (basic at start).
- ≥: subtract surplus, then add an **artificial** variable A ≥ 0.
- =: add an artificial variable.
- **Big-M**: in Max Z, give each artificial the cost −M (in Min Z, +M), M a very large positive number. Simplex then drives artificials to zero if a feasible solution exists.

steps.title: Solved: Min Z = 4x₁ + x₂
steps.body:
Constraints: 3x₁ + x₂ = 3, 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≥ 6, x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 4.

Standard form: 3x₁ + x₂ + A₁ = 3; 4x₁ + 3x₂ − s₁ + A₂ = 6; x₁ + 2x₂ + s₂ = 4; Min Z = 4x₁ + x₂ + MA₁ + MA₂.

Initial basis A₁, A₂, s₂. After the iterations (x₁ enters, A₁ leaves; x₂ enters, A₂ leaves; s₁ enters, s₂ leaves) the optimum is

**x₁ = 2/5, x₂ = 9/5, Z = 17/5**.

steps.title: Check without tableaux
steps.body: On 3x₁ + x₂ = 3, x₂ = 3 − 3x₁ and Z = x₁ + 3. The other constraints give 0.4 ≤ x₁ ≤ 0.6, so Z is least at x₁ = 0.4: Z = 3.4 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to make the Z-row consistent: subtract M × (artificial rows) so that basic artificials have zero Zⱼ − Cⱼ.
- Giving artificials the wrong sign of M for maximisation.

activity.prompt: What must be added to each constraint to start the simplex?

quiz.q: In a minimisation Big-M problem, artificial variables get cost:
quiz.why: A huge positive cost penalises any solution that keeps an artificial variable positive.

quiz.q: An = constraint needs:
quiz.why: There is no slack or surplus to start the basis, so an artificial variable supplies one.

quiz.q: If an artificial variable remains positive in the optimal tableau, the LPP is:
quiz.why: A positive artificial means the original constraints cannot all be satisfied.

story.title: First find any corner, then the best one

scenes.text: Phase I ignores profit and simply looks for a feasible starting corner.
Phase II then optimises the real objective from there.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
**Phase I**: minimise W = sum of artificial variables, subject to the constraints.
- If W_min > 0 ⇒ the original LPP is **infeasible**.
- If W_min = 0 ⇒ a BFS of the original problem has been found.

**Phase II**: drop artificial columns (and any artificial still basic at zero level, carefully), restore the original objective and continue simplex.

steps.title: Solved: small example
steps.body:
Min Z = 2x + 3y, x + y ≥ 4, x + 3y ≥ 6.

- Phase I: W = A₁ + A₂. Pivots bring x and y into the basis, ending at x = 3, y = 1 with W = 0.
- Phase II: Z = 2(3) + 3(1) = 9; reduced costs of the surpluses are ≥ 0, so **x = 3, y = 1, Z = 9** is optimal (agrees with the graphical answer).

steps.title: Big-M vs two-phase
steps.body: Two-phase avoids choosing a numerical M, so it is preferred for computer work (no round-off from huge numbers). Both give the same optimum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Carrying the Phase I objective into Phase II.
- Concluding optimality in Phase I — it only gives feasibility.

activity.prompt: Order the two-phase method.
items: Add slack, surplus and artificial variables
Phase I: minimise the sum of artificials
Check W_min: if positive, stop — infeasible
Remove artificial columns
Phase II: restore the original objective
Continue simplex to optimality

quiz.q: Phase I minimises:
quiz.why: Driving the artificials to zero produces a genuine basic feasible solution of the original problem.

quiz.q: W_min = 3 at the end of Phase I means:
quiz.why: The artificials cannot all be removed, so the original constraints have no common solution.

quiz.q: A practical advantage of the two-phase method over Big-M is:
options: no need to choose a large M
quiz.why: Avoiding a huge numerical M reduces round-off error in computation.

scenes.text: Sometimes a pivot changes the basis but not the solution.
In rare cases simplex can cycle forever — Bland's rule prevents it.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Degenerate BFS**: some basic variable is 0.
- Arises from a **tie** in the minimum ratio test.
- A degenerate pivot may leave Z unchanged; in theory simplex can **cycle**.
- **Bland's rule**: choose the entering variable with the smallest index among those with negative Zⱼ − Cⱼ, and break ratio ties by smallest index — guarantees termination.

steps.title: Solved: a tie
steps.body: Max Z = 3x₁ + 9x₂, x₁ + 4x₂ ≤ 8, x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 4. x₂ enters; ratios 8/4 = 2 and 4/2 = 2 tie ⇒ the next BFS is degenerate (one basic variable becomes 0). Continuing gives x₁ = 0, x₂ = 2, Z = 18.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a zero-valued basic variable as non-basic.
- Concluding 'no progress ⇒ optimal' after a degenerate pivot; check Zⱼ − Cⱼ.

activity.prompt: In the tie example, what is the optimal value of Z?

quiz.q: Degeneracy in the simplex method is signalled by:
options: a tie in the minimum ratio
quiz.why: When two rows tie, after pivoting the other tied basic variable becomes zero.

quiz.q: Bland's rule is used to:
quiz.why: Choosing the smallest-index candidates guarantees the method never revisits a basis.

quiz.q: A degenerate pivot changes:
options: the basis but possibly not Z
quiz.why: The entering variable comes in at level 0, so the basis changes while the solution and Z may stay the same.

lessons.title: Practice: choosing and checking the method

scenes.text: Exam questions often say 'solve by Big-M' or 'by two-phase' — but some just say 'solve'.
Know which constraints force artificials, and always verify the answer.

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body:
1. Make all b ≥ 0 (multiply rows by −1 if needed, flipping inequalities).
2. Only ≤ constraints? Plain simplex.
3. Any ≥ or =? Big-M or two-phase.
4. At the end, substitute the solution into every original constraint and the objective.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Duality and the dual simplex method

scenes.text: The glass company could make products — or rent out its plant hours to a rival.
The rental prices that make both options equally good solve the dual problem.

steps.title: Symmetric form
steps.body:
Primal: Max Z = cᵀx, Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0
Dual: Min W = bᵀy, Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0

Rules: one dual variable per primal constraint; one dual constraint per primal variable; objective coefficients and right-hand sides swap; A is transposed.

steps.title: Unsymmetric cases
steps.body:
- Primal = constraint ⇒ dual variable **unrestricted** in sign.
- Primal unrestricted variable ⇒ dual constraint is an **equation**.
- For Max primal, convert any ≥ constraint to ≤ by multiplying by −1 first.
- The dual of the dual is the primal.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Primal: Max Z = 3x₁ + 5x₂, x₁ ≤ 4, 2x₂ ≤ 12, 3x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 18.

Dual: **Min W = 4y₁ + 12y₂ + 18y₃**
subject to y₁ + 3y₃ ≥ 3, 2y₂ + 2y₃ ≥ 5, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to transpose A (rows become columns).
- Making a dual variable non-negative when its primal constraint is an equation.

activity.prompt: Match primal features to dual features.

quiz.q: A primal equality constraint corresponds to a dual variable that is:

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
- **Weak duality**: for feasible x (primal Max) and y (dual Min), cᵀx ≤ bᵀy. Proof: cᵀx ≤ (Aᵀy)ᵀx = yᵀAx ≤ yᵀb.
- **Strong duality**: if either has a finite optimum, so does the other, and Z* = W*.
- If the primal is unbounded, the dual is infeasible (and vice versa).

steps.title: Complementary slackness
steps.body:
At optimality:

- yᵢ × (slack of primal constraint i) = 0
- xⱼ × (surplus of dual constraint j) = 0

So a non-binding primal constraint has zero shadow price, and a positive primal variable makes its dual constraint tight.

steps.title: Solved: find the dual solution
steps.body:
Primal optimum: x₁ = 2, x₂ = 6 (from Unit 2). Constraint 1: 2 < 4 slack ⇒ **y₁ = 0**. x₁, x₂ > 0 ⇒ both dual constraints tight:

- y₁ + 3y₃ = 3 ⇒ y₃ = 1
- 2y₂ + 2y₃ = 5 ⇒ y₂ = 3/2
- W = 0 + 12(3/2) + 18(1) = **36** = Z* ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

scenes.text: Sometimes the starting tableau already satisfies optimality but has negative right-hand sides.

steps.title: When and how
steps.body:
Use when all Zⱼ − Cⱼ satisfy the optimality condition but some bᵢ < 0 (typical for Min problems with ≥ constraints, written as ≤ by multiplying by −1).

1. **Leaving row**: most negative bᵢ. If all bᵢ ≥ 0, stop — optimal and feasible.
2. **Entering column**: among negative entries aᵢⱼ in that row, take the minimum of |(Zⱼ − Cⱼ)/aᵢⱼ|. If no negative entry ⇒ infeasible.
3. Pivot as usual and repeat.

steps.title: Solved: Min Z = 2x₁ + x₂
steps.body:
Constraints 3x₁ + x₂ ≥ 3, 4x₁ + 3x₂ ≥ 6, x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 3. Rewrite the first two as −3x₁ − x₂ + s₁ = −3, −4x₁ − 3x₂ + s₂ = −6.

- Row s₂ (b = −6) leaves; ratios |2/−4| = 0.5, |1/−3| = 0.33 ⇒ x₂ enters.
- Next, row s₁ is negative and leaves; x₁ enters.
- Final: **x₁ = 3/5, x₂ = 6/5, Z = 12/5**.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: 3(0.6) + 1.2 = 3 ✔, 4(0.6) + 3(1.2) = 6 ✔, 0.6 + 2.4 = 3 ✔ (all tight). Other vertices: (1.5, 0) gives Z = 3, (3, 0) gives 6, so 2.4 is the minimum ✔

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body:
- Dual value yᵢ = increase in optimal Z per unit increase in bᵢ (**shadow price**), valid while the current basis remains optimal (the **range of feasibility**).
- Buy extra resource i if its cost is below yᵢ.
- **Reduced cost** of a non-basic variable: how much its profit must rise before it enters the optimal plan.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Transportation, assignment, revision & exam
courses.summary: The transportation problem as an LPP, balanced and unbalanced cases, initial basic feasible solutions by the north-west corner, least-cost and Vogel's methods, the MODI (u–v) optimality test with loop improvement, degeneracy, the assignment problem by the Hungarian method, and a full-syllabus revision and exam.

scenes.text: A cement company ships from three plants to three construction sites.
Which plant should supply which site to keep freight cost lowest?

steps.title: Formulation
steps.body:
m sources with supplies aᵢ, n destinations with demands bⱼ, unit costs cᵢⱼ, shipments xᵢⱼ ≥ 0.

Min Z = ΣΣ cᵢⱼxᵢⱼ, Σⱼ xᵢⱼ = aᵢ, Σᵢ xᵢⱼ = bⱼ.

- **Balanced** if Σaᵢ = Σbⱼ; otherwise add a dummy row/column with zero cost.
- A BFS has **m + n − 1** basic (allocated) cells; fewer means degeneracy.

steps.title: Better starting methods
steps.body:
- **Least-cost**: allocate as much as possible to the cheapest remaining cell.
- **Vogel's approximation (VAM)**: for each row/column compute the penalty (difference of the two smallest costs); allocate in the cheapest cell of the line with the largest penalty. VAM usually starts at or near the optimum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to balance the problem before starting.
- Having fewer than m + n − 1 allocations without adding a zero (ε) allocation.

activity.prompt: A transportation problem has 4 sources and 5 destinations. How many basic cells does a non-degenerate BFS have?

quiz.why: Excess supply of 20 is sent to a dummy destination at zero cost.

quiz.q: NWC ignores:
quiz.why: The north-west corner rule allocates purely by position, so it often gives a costly start.

quiz.q: VAM allocates first in the row or column with:
quiz.why: A large penalty means a big loss if the cheapest cell there is not used, so it is filled first.

scenes.text: The NWC plan costs ₹480. Is there a cheaper route?
MODI prices each empty cell; a negative price means shifting goods along a loop saves money.

steps.title: MODI (u–v) method
steps.body:
1. For basic cells, set uᵢ + vⱼ = cᵢⱼ (start with u₁ = 0).
2. For each empty cell, Δᵢⱼ = cᵢⱼ − uᵢ − vⱼ.
3. All Δᵢⱼ ≥ 0 ⇒ optimal (a zero Δ means an alternative optimum).
4. Otherwise enter the most negative cell; form a closed loop of basic cells with alternating + and −; shift θ = minimum allocation on the − corners.

steps.title: Iteration 2 and optimum
steps.body:
Now Δ₃₂ = −1. Loop (3,2)+ (3,3)− (2,3)+ (2,2)−; θ = 15 (a tie ⇒ keep x₃₃ = 0 as a basic, degenerate cell).

Cost = 470 − 15 = **₹455**: x₁₂ = 20, x₂₃ = 30, x₃₁ = 10, x₃₂ = 15.

New u, v give Δ₁₁ = 0, Δ₁₃ = 3, Δ₂₁ = 1, Δ₂₂ = 1 — all ≥ 0 ⇒ **optimal ₹455** (Δ₁₁ = 0 signals an alternative optimum).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Building a loop through empty cells (corners must be basic except the entering cell).
- Losing a basic cell in a tie and ending with fewer than m + n − 1 cells.

quiz.why: Taking the smallest allocation on a − corner keeps all shipments non-negative.

scenes.text: Three technicians, three repair jobs, and a table of times.
The Hungarian method finds the best one-to-one assignment with simple row and column subtractions.

steps.title: Method (minimisation, n × n)
steps.body:
1. Subtract each row's minimum from that row.
2. Subtract each column's minimum from that column.
3. Cover all zeros with the minimum number of lines. If lines = n, make the assignment on zeros.
4. Otherwise subtract the smallest uncovered value from uncovered entries, add it at intersections, and repeat step 3.

Maximisation: subtract every entry from the largest first. Unbalanced: add a dummy row/column of zeros.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping column reduction.
- Assigning two jobs to the same person when choosing zeros.

quiz.why: Subtracting the smallest uncovered value creates new zeros while keeping the optimal assignment unchanged.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- Corner-point theorem; BFS ↔ vertex; at most ⁿCₘ basic solutions
- Simplex (Max): enter most negative Zⱼ − Cⱼ; leave by minimum positive ratio
- Big-M (Min: +M), two-phase (Phase I min ΣA)
- Dual: transpose, swap b and c, Max ↔ Min; = ↔ unrestricted
- Weak/strong duality; complementary slackness
- Dual simplex: leave most negative b; enter min |(Zⱼ − Cⱼ)/aᵢⱼ| for aᵢⱼ < 0
- Transport: m + n − 1 cells; MODI uᵢ + vⱼ = cᵢⱼ, Δ = c − u − v
- Hungarian: row, column reduction, cover, adjust

scenes.text: Two tugboats pull a ship at Mumbai port with ropes at an angle.
The ship moves as if pulled by a single resultant force.

steps.title: Parallelogram law
steps.body:
Forces P and Q at angle α from a point have resultant R with

- R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos α
- tan θ = Q sin α/(P + Q cos α), θ measured from P

Special cases: α = 0 ⇒ R = P + Q; α = 180° ⇒ R = |P − Q|; α = 90° ⇒ R = √(P² + Q²). Equal forces: R = 2P cos(α/2), bisecting the angle.

steps.title: Resolution into components
steps.body:
For forces Fᵢ at angles θᵢ to the x-axis:

X = ΣFᵢ cos θᵢ, Y = ΣFᵢ sin θᵢ, R = √(X² + Y²), tan φ = Y/X (watch the quadrant).

steps.title: Solved: parallelogram law
steps.body:
- P = 3 N, Q = 4 N at 90°: R = **5 N**, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ **53.13°** from P.
- P = Q = 10 N at 60°: R = 2·10·cos 30° = **17.32 N**, along the bisector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the cosine rule with −2PQ cos α (that is for the triangle side opposite α, not the parallelogram diagonal).
- Taking tan⁻¹(Y/X) without checking the signs of X and Y.

quiz.why: R = 2P cos 60° = P.

quiz.why: X < 0 and Y > 0 puts R in the second quadrant: 180° − 53.13° ≈ 126.87°.

lessons.title: Triangle of forces and Lami's theorem

scenes.text: A 100 N lamp hangs from two wires fixed to the ceiling at different angles.
Three forces in equilibrium — Lami's theorem gives both tensions in one line.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
- **Triangle of forces**: if three forces at a point can be represented in magnitude and direction by the sides of a triangle taken in order, they are in equilibrium (and conversely).
- **Lami's theorem**: if three concurrent forces P, Q, R are in equilibrium,

P/sin α = Q/sin β = R/sin γ,

where α is the angle between Q and R, β between R and P, γ between P and Q.

steps.title: Solved: the lamp
steps.body:
Wires at 30° and 60° to the horizontal; weight W = 100 N.

- Angle between the 30° wire (T₁) and the vertical weight: 90° + 30° = 120°; between T₂ and W: 150°; between T₁ and T₂: 90°.
- Lami: T₁/sin 150° = T₂/sin 120° = 100/sin 90°
- **T₁ = 50 N**, **T₂ = 86.6 N** (the steeper wire carries more).

steps.title: Check by resolving
steps.body: Horizontal: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60° ⇒ 43.3 = 43.3 ✔. Vertical: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 25 + 75 = 100 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pairing each force with the wrong angle — use the angle between the OTHER two forces.
- Using Lami for more than three forces or for non-concurrent forces.

activity.prompt: A 200 N weight hangs from two strings each making 45° with the vertical. Find the tension in each string (1 decimal).

quiz.q: In Lami's theorem P/sin α, α is the angle between:
quiz.why: Each force is paired with the sine of the angle between the other two forces.

quiz.q: A 60 N weight hangs from a string pulled sideways by a horizontal force of 80 N. The string tension is:

scenes.text: A 30 kg child sits 2 m from the pivot. Where must her 40 kg brother sit?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Moment** of F about O = F × perpendicular distance (N·m); anticlockwise positive by convention. Vector form M = r × F.
- **Varignon's theorem**: the moment of the resultant about any point equals the algebraic sum of the moments of the components.
- **Like parallel forces** P, Q at A, B: resultant P + Q at C with P·AC = Q·CB. **Unlike**: P − Q, outside AB on the side of the larger force.
- **Couple**: two equal, opposite, parallel forces; moment P·d is the same about every point. A couple can be balanced only by another couple.

steps.title: Solved: like parallel forces
steps.body: P = 20 N at A, Q = 30 N at B, AB = 1 m. R = 50 N at C with 20·AC = 30·(1 − AC) ⇒ **AC = 0.6 m**.

steps.title: Solved: a couple
steps.body: A steering wheel of diameter 0.4 m is turned by 25 N with each hand in opposite directions: moment = 25 × 0.4 = **10 N·m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the slant distance instead of the perpendicular distance.
- Placing the resultant of unlike forces between them.

quiz.why: R = 50 − 30 = 20 N, located outside the segment on the side of the larger force (here 1.5 m from the 50 N force).

Three equations — ΣX = 0, ΣY = 0, ΣM = 0 — find the support forces.

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
A rigid body under coplanar forces is in equilibrium iff

- ΣX = 0, ΣY = 0 (no translation)
- ΣM_O = 0 about any point O (no rotation)

Tip: take moments about a point where unknown forces act to eliminate them. Three non-parallel forces in equilibrium must be concurrent.

steps.title: Solved: simply supported beam
steps.body:
Uniform beam AB, 6 m, weight 200 N, supports at A and B, load 400 N at 2 m from A.

- Moments about A: 6R_B = 200·3 + 400·2 = 1400 ⇒ **R_B ≈ 233.3 N**

courses.title: Unit 2 · Friction, centre of gravity and virtual work
courses.summary: Laws of friction, angle and cone of friction, equilibrium on rough inclined planes, the ladder problem, centres of gravity of rods, laminae and solids including composite bodies, and the principle of virtual work with applications.
outcomes: Learners can apply the laws of limiting friction and the angle of friction

lessons.title: Laws of friction and the rough inclined plane

story.title: Pushing a crate up a ramp

scenes.text: A warehouse worker pushes a 10 kg crate up a 30° loading ramp.
Friction always opposes the motion — so pushing up is harder than letting it slide down.

steps.title: Laws of friction
steps.body:
- Friction opposes the tendency to move, and adjusts up to a limiting value.
- Limiting friction F = μR, R = normal reaction; μ is the coefficient of friction (dimensionless).
- Independent of contact area (within limits); kinetic friction is slightly less than limiting friction.
- **Angle of friction** λ: tan λ = μ — the angle between R and the total reaction at limiting equilibrium.
- On a rough incline, a body rests without other forces iff tan θ ≤ μ (**angle of repose** = λ).

steps.title: Solved: pushing up the ramp
steps.body:
m = 10 kg, θ = 30°, μ = 0.3, g = 9.8 m/s². Force P parallel to the plane, just moving up:

- R = mg cos 30° = 98 × 0.866 = 84.87 N
- P = mg sin 30° + μR = 49 + 25.46 = **74.46 N**
- To prevent sliding down: mg sin 30° − μR = 23.54 N

steps.title: Solved: least force
steps.body: The least force to drag a body of weight W on a rough horizontal plane acts at angle λ above the horizontal, with magnitude **W sin λ**. For W = 100 N, μ = 0.75 (λ = 36.87°): P_min = 60 N (versus 75 N horizontally).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Always writing F = μR — that is only at limiting equilibrium.
- Reversing the direction of friction when the motion direction changes.

activity.prompt: A block just begins to slide down an incline when μ = 1/√3. Find the angle of the incline.

quiz.q: The angle of friction λ satisfies:
quiz.why: The total reaction makes angle λ with the normal, where tan λ = F/R = μ at limiting equilibrium.

quiz.q: Friction below the limiting value equals:
options: just what is needed for equilibrium
quiz.why: Static friction is self-adjusting and only reaches μR at the point of slipping.

scenes.text: A painter leans a ladder against a smooth wall on a rough floor.
Too shallow an angle and the foot slides out — how steep must it be?

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body:
Uniform ladder, length 2a, weight W, angle θ with the floor. Smooth wall: reaction S (horizontal). Rough floor: R (vertical), F (towards wall).

- ΣY: R = W; ΣX: F = S
- Moments about the foot: S·2a sin θ = W·a cos θ ⇒ S = (W/2) cot θ
- No slipping: F ≤ μR ⇒ (1/2)cot θ ≤ μ ⇒ **tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ)**

steps.title: Solved: with a person
steps.body: Ladder 2a, weight W, man of weight 3W at the top? Moments about the foot: S·2a sin θ = W a cos θ + 3W·2a cos θ ⇒ S = (7W/2) cot θ; R = 4W; need (7/2)cot θ ≤ 4μ. For μ = 0.5: tan θ ≥ 1.75 ⇒ θ ≥ 60.3°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a smooth wall gives no vertical force.
- Using the length a instead of 2a for the moment arm of S.

activity.prompt: Uniform ladder, smooth wall, rough floor with μ = 0.25. Find the minimum tan θ (θ with the floor) for no slipping.

quiz.q: For a smooth wall, the wall's reaction is:
quiz.why: A smooth surface can push only along its normal, which for a vertical wall is horizontal.

quiz.q: Increasing μ at the floor allows the ladder to stand:

quiz.q: In the basic ladder problem, R (floor) equals:
quiz.why: The only vertical forces are the weight W and the floor reaction R, so R = W.

scenes.text: A shop sign of odd shape must hang level from a single hook.
Hang it directly above its centre of gravity.

steps.title: Definition and formulae
steps.body:
x̄ = Σmᵢxᵢ/Σmᵢ (discrete), x̄ = ∫x dm/∫dm (continuous); similarly ȳ, z̄. For uniform bodies the CG is the centroid.

| Body (radius r, height h) | CG from centre / base |
|---|---|
| Semicircular arc | 2r/π from centre |
| Semicircular lamina | 4r/(3π) from centre |
| Solid hemisphere | 3r/8 from centre |
| Hemispherical shell | r/2 from centre |
| Solid cone | h/4 from base |
| Triangular lamina | h/3 from base (meet of medians) |

steps.title: Solved: semicircular lamina by integration
steps.body: Strips at height y, width 2√(r² − y²): ȳ = ∫₀ʳ y·2√(r² − y²)dy / (πr²/2) = (2r³/3)/(πr²/2) = **4r/(3π)**.

steps.title: Solved: composite lamina
steps.body:
Rectangle 4 × 2 (area 8, centroid (2, 1)) with a 2 × 2 square on top of its left part (area 4, centroid (1, 3)).

- x̄ = (8·2 + 4·1)/12 = 20/12 ≈ **1.667**
- ȳ = (8·1 + 4·3)/12 = 20/12 ≈ **1.667**

steps.title: Solved: removed part
steps.body: A disc of radius 2 with a disc of radius 1 cut out, centre of hole 1 from the main centre: x̄ = (4π·0 − π·1)/(4π − π) = **−1/3** (away from the hole).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding (not subtracting) the area of a hole.
- Confusing lamina and arc formulae for the semicircle.

activity.prompt: Masses 2 kg at x = 0, 3 kg at x = 4 and 5 kg at x = 6 (m). Find x̄.

quiz.q: CG of a solid hemisphere of radius r is at distance from the centre:
quiz.why: Integrating discs of radius √(r² − z²) gives z̄ = 3r/8 for the solid hemisphere.

quiz.q: CG of a solid cone of height 12 cm from its base:
quiz.why: The CG of a solid cone lies h/4 = 3 cm above the base.

quiz.q: When a part is removed, its moment is:
quiz.why: The remaining body is the whole minus the hole, so both the hole's area and its moment are subtracted.

scenes.text: Instead of resolving forces at every joint, imagine shifting the whole framework very slightly.
In equilibrium, the total work done by the active forces in that imagined shift is zero.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
A system with workless constraints (smooth contacts, light inextensible strings, rigid joints) is in equilibrium iff the total work done by the applied forces in every small displacement consistent with the constraints is zero: **Σ Fᵢ·δrᵢ = 0**.

Reactions at smooth surfaces and internal forces at joints do no work and drop out.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Choose a single coordinate (an angle θ).
2. Express positions of weights (depths below a fixed level) and lengths of strings/rods in terms of θ.
3. Give θ a variation δθ; write W·δ(depth) for weights, −T·δ(length) for a string tension, +T·δ(length) for a strut thrust.
4. Set the sum to zero.

steps.title: Solved: rhombus of rods
steps.body:
Four equal uniform rods, each of length a and weight W, are freely jointed as a rhombus ABCD, hung from A. A light rod BD keeps ∠BAD = 2θ.

- Depths of centres: AB, AD at (a/2)cos θ; BC, CD at (3a/2)cos θ. Total weight-depth: 4Wa cos θ.
- BD = 2a sin θ, with thrust T.
- Virtual work: W·δ(4a cos θ) + T·δ(2a sin θ) = 0 ⇒ −4Wa sin θ + 2Ta cos θ = 0
- **T = 2W tan θ** (thrust).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring heights upward but treating weights as doing positive work when rising.
- Forgetting which forces do no work (smooth reactions, internal joint forces).

activity.prompt: In the rhombus problem with W = 10 N and θ = 45°, find the thrust in BD.

quiz.q: Forces that do no virtual work include:
quiz.why: A smooth reaction is perpendicular to the allowed motion, so it does no work in a displacement consistent with the constraint.

quiz.q: The principle of virtual work is especially useful because it:
quiz.why: Reactions at smooth contacts and joints vanish from the equation, leaving only the forces of interest.

quiz.q: For a weight W whose depth below a fixed level increases by δh, its virtual work is:
quiz.why: Gravity acts downward, so moving down by δh means the weight does positive work W δh.

questions.why: From virtual work with depth 4a cos θ and BD = 2a sin θ.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Kinematics: rectilinear and curvilinear motion
courses.summary: Displacement, velocity and acceleration in a straight line with variable acceleration, Newton's laws for a particle, velocity and acceleration in Cartesian, radial–transverse (polar) and tangential–normal (intrinsic) components, and motion in a resisting medium.
outcomes: Learners can find velocity, acceleration and distance from x(t), and v from a(x) using v dv/dx
Learners can derive and use radial and transverse components of velocity and acceleration
Learners can use tangential and normal components with radius of curvature
Learners can solve motion with resistance proportional to velocity

scenes.text: A lift's position follows a cubic in time: up, back down, then up again.
Distance travelled is not the same as displacement when the motion reverses.

steps.title: Relations
steps.body:
- v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt = d²x/dt² = v dv/dx.
- a = f(t): integrate twice in t. a = f(x): use v dv/dx = f(x) ⇒ v²/2 = ∫f(x)dx + C. a = f(v): dt = dv/f(v) or dx = v dv/f(v).
- Distance = ∫|v| dt — split the interval where v changes sign.

steps.title: Solved: x = t³ − 6t² + 9t (m, s)
steps.body:
- v = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) ⇒ momentarily at rest at t = 1 s, 3 s
- a = 6t − 12 ⇒ a = 0 at t = 2 s
- x(0) = 0, x(1) = 4, x(3) = 0, x(4) = 4
- Displacement in [0, 4] = 4 m; distance = 4 + 4 + 4 = **12 m**

steps.title: Solved: a = f(x)
steps.body: A particle has a = 2x (m/s²) and v = 0 at x = 1. v dv/dx = 2x ⇒ v² = 2x² − 2 ⇒ at x = 3: v = √16 = **4 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking |x(4) − x(0)| as distance when the particle turns back.
- Using d v/dt when a is given as a function of x — use v dv/dx.

activity.prompt: For x = t³ − 6t² + 9t, find the velocity at t = 2 s.

quiz.q: a can be written as:
quiz.why: By the chain rule dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx.

scenes.text: A ground station measures a satellite's distance r and bearing θ.
Polar components of velocity and acceleration come straight from r(t) and θ(t).

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
With unit vectors e_r, e_θ (de_r/dt = θ̇ e_θ, de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r):

- v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ
- a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (2ṙθ̇ + rθ̈) e_θ
- Transverse acceleration = (1/r) d(r²θ̇)/dt

If the transverse acceleration is zero, r²θ̇ = h is constant (areal velocity h/2).

steps.title: Solved: uniform circular motion
steps.body: r = R constant, θ̇ = ω constant: v = Rω e_θ, a = −Rω² e_r (centripetal, towards the centre). R = 0.5 m, ω = 4 rad/s ⇒ a = 8 m/s².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a_r = r̈ (forgetting −rθ̇²).
- Dropping the factor 2 in the Coriolis-type term 2ṙθ̇.

activity.prompt: r = t², θ = 2t. Find the transverse acceleration 2ṙθ̇ + rθ̈ at t = 1.

quiz.q: The radial acceleration is:
quiz.why: Differentiating ṙe_r + rθ̇e_θ produces r̈ in the radial direction and −rθ̇² from the turning of e_θ.

quiz.q: If r²θ̇ is constant, the transverse acceleration is:
quiz.why: The transverse acceleration equals (1/r) d(r²θ̇)/dt, which vanishes when r²θ̇ is constant.

quiz.q: For uniform circular motion, the acceleration is directed:
quiz.why: With r and θ̇ constant, a = −rθ̇² e_r, pointing to the centre.

scenes.text: A car speeds up while going round a bend on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway.
Its acceleration has a part along the road (speeding up) and a part towards the centre of the bend.

steps.title: Intrinsic components
steps.body:
With s = arc length, ψ = angle of the tangent, ρ = ds/dψ the radius of curvature:

- v = v T (along the tangent)
- a = (dv/dt) T + (v²/ρ) N, where dv/dt = v dv/ds
- Curvature of y = f(x): 1/ρ = |y″|/(1 + y′²)^{3/2}

steps.title: Solved: car on a bend
steps.body:
Radius 100 m, speed 20 m/s, increasing at 3 m/s².

- a_n = 400/100 = 4 m/s²
- a_t = 3 m/s²
- |a| = **5 m/s²**

steps.title: Solved: curvature of a parabola
steps.body: y = x² at x = 0: y′ = 0, y″ = 2 ⇒ ρ = 1/2. A particle passing the vertex at 3 m/s has a_n = 9/(1/2) = **18 m/s²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a_n as zero when speed is constant — direction still changes.
- Using the radius of the road as ρ for a non-circular path.

activity.prompt: A train moves at 30 m/s round a curve of radius 450 m at constant speed. Find its acceleration.

quiz.q: At constant speed on a curve, the tangential acceleration is:
quiz.why: Tangential acceleration is dv/dt, which is zero when the speed does not change.

quiz.q: Normal acceleration formula:
quiz.why: Changing direction along a curve of radius ρ at speed v requires v²/ρ towards the centre of curvature.

quiz.q: Radius of curvature of a straight line:
quiz.why: A straight line has zero curvature, so its radius of curvature is infinite.

scenes.text: A steel ball dropped into thick oil soon falls at a steady speed.
That is terminal velocity: weight balanced by resistance.

steps.title: Linear resistance
steps.body:
Falling body, resistance mkv: dv/dt = g − kv.

- v(t) = (g/k)(1 − e^{−kt}) from rest
- **Terminal velocity** V = g/k
- Horizontal motion with only resistance: v = u e^{−kt}, distance → u/k.

steps.title: Quadratic resistance
steps.body: For resistance mkv²: V = √(g/k), and v = V tanh(gt/V) from rest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the mass factor when resistance is given as a force, not per unit mass.
- Expecting the body to actually reach V in finite time (it only approaches it).

activity.prompt: A body falls with resistance kv per unit mass, k = 0.5 s⁻¹, g = 9.8 m/s². Find the terminal velocity.

quiz.q: Terminal velocity with linear resistance kv per unit mass is:
quiz.why: Setting dv/dt = g − kv = 0 gives v = g/k.

quiz.q: With quadratic resistance kv², terminal velocity is:
quiz.why: g − kv² = 0 gives v = √(g/k).

quiz.q: A particle sliding with only linear resistance from speed u travels a total distance:
quiz.why: x = (u/k)(1 − e^{−kt}) approaches u/k as t → ∞.

Centripetal acceleration for v = 10 m/s, r = 20 m:
Transverse velocity in polar form:
questions.why: v_θ = rθ̇.

questions.why: v² = 9(4 − x²) gives v = 6 at x = 0.

Car at 15 m/s on radius 75 m, speeding up at 4 m/s². |a| =

courses.title: Unit 4 · Simple harmonic motion and projectiles
courses.summary: Simple harmonic motion: equation, amplitude, period, velocity and energy; springs and the simple pendulum; projectile motion on a horizontal plane (time of flight, greatest height, range, trajectory) and on an inclined plane.
outcomes: Learners can solve ẍ = −ω²x and use v² = ω²(a² − x²)
Learners can find periods of spring–mass systems and simple pendulums
Learners can compute time of flight, height and range of a projectile
Learners can derive the trajectory equation and maximum range
Learners can find the range on an inclined plane

scenes.text: A child on a swing goes back and forth, fastest at the bottom, pausing at the ends.
Small oscillations like this are simple harmonic: acceleration proportional to displacement, towards the centre.

steps.title: Equation and solution
steps.body:
- SHM: ẍ = −ω²x (acceleration towards O, proportional to distance).
- Solution: x = a cos(ωt + ε); a = amplitude, ε = phase.
- Period T = 2π/ω, frequency f = 1/T.
- v² = ω²(a² − x²) (from v dv/dx = −ω²x); v_max = aω at O, a_max = aω² at the ends.
- Energy per unit mass: v²/2 + ω²x²/2 = ω²a²/2 (constant).

steps.title: Solved: from two speeds
steps.body:
Speeds 3 and 4 m/s at distances 4 and 3 m from the centre.

- ω²(a² − 16) = 9, ω²(a² − 9) = 16
- Subtract: 7ω² = 7 ⇒ ω = 1 ⇒ a² = 25 ⇒ **a = 5 m**, **T = 2π s**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing ω (rad/s) with f (Hz): ω = 2πf.
- Thinking the period depends on amplitude — in SHM it does not.

activity.prompt: A particle in SHM has amplitude 0.2 m and ω = 5 rad/s. Find its maximum speed.

quiz.q: In SHM, the speed is greatest at:
quiz.why: v² = ω²(a² − x²) is largest at x = 0, the centre.

quiz.q: If ω doubles, the period:
quiz.why: T = 2π/ω, so doubling ω halves T.

quiz.q: Acceleration at the extreme position has magnitude:
quiz.why: |ẍ| = ω²|x| is maximum at |x| = a, giving aω².

scenes.text: A clock's pendulum must swing with a period of exactly 2 s to tick seconds.
How long must it be? About a metre.

steps.title: Spring–mass
steps.body: Hooke's law F = −kx (k in N/m). m ẍ = −kx ⇒ ω = √(k/m), **T = 2π√(m/k)**. For a vertical spring the equilibrium shifts by mg/k but the period is unchanged.

steps.title: Simple pendulum
steps.body: Bob of mass m on a light string of length l: ml θ̈ = −mg sin θ ≈ −mgθ for small θ ⇒ ω = √(g/l), **T = 2π√(l/g)** (independent of mass and, for small swings, amplitude).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
- Spring: m = 0.5 kg, k = 200 N/m ⇒ ω = 20 rad/s, T = **0.314 s**
- Pendulum: l = 1 m, g = 9.8 ⇒ T = 2π√(0.102) ≈ **2.007 s**
- Seconds pendulum (T = 2 s): l = g/π² ≈ **0.993 m**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin θ ≈ θ for large swings.
- Inverting the ratio: it is √(m/k), not √(k/m), in the period.

activity.prompt: A 2 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 50 N/m. Find the period (3 decimals).

quiz.q: Period of a pendulum depends on:
quiz.why: T = 2π√(l/g) for small oscillations, so only length and g matter.

quiz.q: Quadrupling the length of a pendulum makes the period:
A stiffer spring (larger k) gives:
quiz.why: T = 2π√(m/k) decreases as k increases.

scenes.text: A fielder throws from the boundary at 20 m/s, 30° above the horizontal.
Ignoring air resistance, the ball traces a parabola.

steps.title: Formulae (u at angle α, g down)
steps.body:
- x = ut cos α, y = ut sin α − gt²/2
- **Trajectory**: y = x tan α − g x²/(2u² cos² α) — a parabola
- Time of flight T = 2u sin α/g
- Greatest height H = u² sin² α/(2g)
- Range R = u² sin 2α/g; maximum u²/g at α = 45°; angles α and 90° − α give the same range.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin α instead of sin 2α in the range.
- Forgetting the second (complementary) angle.

activity.prompt: A ball is projected at 30 m/s at 45°. Find its range (g = 9.8 m/s², 2 decimals).

quiz.q: At the highest point, the velocity of a projectile is:
quiz.why: The vertical component is zero at the top, but the horizontal component u cos α never changes.

quiz.q: Angles 20° and 70° with the same u give:
quiz.why: sin 40° = sin 140°, so complementary angles give equal ranges.

quiz.q: Time of flight for u = 9.8 m/s, α = 90°:

scenes.text: A water jet from a fire hose is aimed up a 30° slope.
How far up the slope does it land, and at what aim is that distance greatest?

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
Plane at angle β, projection at angle α to the horizontal (α > β), in the vertical plane through the line of greatest slope:

- Time of flight T = 2u sin(α − β)/(g cos β)
- Range up the plane R = 2u² sin(α − β) cos α/(g cos² β)
- Maximum range up the plane R_max = u²/(g(1 + sin β)), when α = π/4 + β/2 (the direction bisects the angle between the plane and the vertical).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring α from the plane instead of the horizontal (formulae change).
- For range down the plane, β changes sign: R_max = u²/(g(1 − sin β)).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Work W = ∫F·dr (J); constant force: Fs cos θ.
- KE = mv²/2; gravitational PE = mgh; spring PE = kx²/2.
- **Work–energy principle**: work done by all forces = change in KE.
- Conservative forces: KE + PE = constant.
- Power P = dW/dt = F·v (W); 1 kW = 1000 W.

steps.title: Solved: power of a car
steps.body: Car of 1000 kg at a steady 20 m/s against resistance 500 N on level road: driving force = 500 N ⇒ P = 500 × 20 = **10 kW**. Up a slope of sin θ = 1/50: extra force mg sin θ = 196 N ⇒ P = 696 × 20 ≈ 13.9 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
- Impulse J = ∫F dt = change in momentum (N·s).
- Conservation of momentum in an impact: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
- **Newton's experimental law**: v₂ − v₁ = e(u₁ − u₂), 0 ≤ e ≤ 1 (e = 1 perfectly elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic).
- KE loss = [m₁m₂/(2(m₁ + m₂))](1 − e²)(u₁ − u₂)².

steps.body:
m₁ = 2 kg at 5 m/s hits m₂ = 3 kg at rest, e = 0.5.

- Momentum: 2v₁ + 3v₂ = 10
- Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 2.5
- ⇒ 5v₁ = 2.5 ⇒ **v₁ = 0.5 m/s**, **v₂ = 3 m/s**
- KE before 25 J, after 0.25 + 13.5 = 13.75 J ⇒ loss **11.25 J** (formula: (6/10)(0.75)(25) = 11.25 ✔)

Force always towards a fixed point O, magnitude P per unit mass.

**Kepler's laws**: (1) planets move in ellipses with the Sun at a focus; (2) radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times; (3) T² = (4π²/μ)a³, i.e. T² ∝ a³.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Metric spaces: definition and examples
courses.summary: The axioms of a metric, standard metrics on ℝ and ℝⁿ, the discrete metric, sequence spaces and function spaces, Cauchy–Schwarz and Minkowski inequalities, bounded metrics, diameter and distance between sets.
outcomes: Learners can verify the metric axioms for a given function
Learners can compute d₁, d₂ and d∞ distances in ℝⁿ

lessons.title: The metric axioms and metrics on ℝⁿ

scenes.text: In a grid city like Chandigarh's sectors, a taxi cannot cut diagonally across blocks.
A crow flies straight. Both measure 'distance' — they are different metrics on the same plane.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **metric** on a non-empty set X is d: X × X → ℝ with, for all x, y, z ∈ X:

- (M1) d(x, y) ≥ 0, and d(x, y) = 0 ⇔ x = y
- (M2) d(x, y) = d(y, x) (symmetry)
- (M3) d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) (triangle inequality)

(X, d) is a **metric space**.

steps.title: Standard metrics on ℝⁿ
steps.body:
For x = (x₁, …, xₙ), y = (y₁, …, yₙ):

- d₁(x, y) = Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ| (taxicab)
- d₂(x, y) = √Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ)² (Euclidean)
- d∞(x, y) = max|xᵢ − yᵢ| (sup / Chebyshev)

They satisfy d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ n·d∞. On ℝ the usual metric is |x − y|.

steps.title: Solved: a non-metric
steps.body: d(x, y) = (x − y)² on ℝ. M1, M2 hold, but with x = 0, y = 1, z = 2: d(0, 2) = 4 > d(0, 1) + d(1, 2) = 2. **Not a metric.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only d(x, x) = 0 and forgetting d(x, y) = 0 ⇒ x = y.
- Testing the triangle inequality on one friendly triple and declaring it proved.
- Assuming every 'distance-like' formula is a metric — squares usually break M3.

activity.prompt: Find the Euclidean distance d₂ between (2, −1, 3) and (−1, 3, 3) in ℝ³.

quiz.why: d∞ takes the largest coordinate difference, max(3, 7) = 7.

quiz.q: Which axiom clearly fails for d(x, y) = |x − 2y| on ℝ?
quiz.why: d(1, 0) = 1 but d(0, 1) = 2, so d(x, y) ≠ d(y, x) and symmetry fails (and d(2, 1) = 0 with 2 ≠ 1 breaks M1 too).

quiz.q: For any x, y in ℝⁿ, which is always true?
quiz.why: The largest |xᵢ − yᵢ| squared is at most the sum of all squared differences, so d∞ ≤ d₂.

The largest gap and the area between curves are two different metrics on C[0, 1].

steps.title: Discrete metric
steps.body: On any set X: d(x, y) = 0 if x = y, 1 if x ≠ y. M3 holds because if x ≠ z then at least one of x ≠ y, y ≠ z, so the right side is ≥ 1. Every subset is open in this metric.

steps.title: Sequence spaces
Function spaces C[a, b]
steps.body:
- **Sup (uniform) metric**: d∞(f, g) = sup_{x∈[a,b]} |f(x) − g(x)|
- **Integral metric**: d₁(f, g) = ∫ₐᵇ |f(x) − g(x)| dx

For d₁, M1 needs continuity: a continuous non-negative function with zero integral is identically zero.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x, g(x) = x² on [0, 1]
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d₁ on Riemann-integrable (not continuous) functions — two different functions can then have distance 0.
- Forgetting the absolute value when f − g changes sign.

activity.prompt: In C[0, 1] with the sup metric, find d∞(f, g) for f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x².

quiz.q: d₁(f, g) on C[0, 1] for f = 1, g = 0 is:
Which sequence lies in ℓ² but not in ℓ¹?
quiz.why: Σ1/n² converges while Σ1/n diverges, so (1/n) is square-summable but not summable.

scenes.text: Everyone 'knows' a side of a triangle is shorter than the other two — but in ℝⁿ that needs proof.
Cauchy–Schwarz is the key lemma; Minkowski is the triangle inequality itself.

steps.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
steps.body:
(Σaᵢbᵢ)² ≤ (Σaᵢ²)(Σbᵢ²).

**Proof**: for all real t, Σ(aᵢ + tbᵢ)² ≥ 0, i.e. At² + 2Bt + C ≥ 0 with A = Σbᵢ², B = Σaᵢbᵢ, C = Σaᵢ². A quadratic that never goes negative has discriminant ≤ 0: 4B² − 4AC ≤ 0 ∎

steps.title: Minkowski (p = 2)
steps.body:
√Σ(aᵢ + bᵢ)² ≤ √Σaᵢ² + √Σbᵢ².

**Proof**: Σ(aᵢ + bᵢ)² = Σaᵢ² + 2Σaᵢbᵢ + Σbᵢ² ≤ Σaᵢ² + 2√Σaᵢ²√Σbᵢ² + Σbᵢ² = (√Σaᵢ² + √Σbᵢ²)². Put aᵢ = xᵢ − yᵢ, bᵢ = yᵢ − zᵢ to get d₂(x, z) ≤ d₂(x, y) + d₂(y, z) ∎

steps.title: Solved: a bounded metric
steps.body:
If d is a metric, so is ρ = d/(1 + d), and ρ < 1.

Key step: t ↦ t/(1 + t) is increasing, and a/(1 + a + b) + b/(1 + a + b) ≤ a/(1 + a) + b/(1 + b). Hence ρ(x, z) ≤ ρ(x, y) + ρ(y, z).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the case A = Σbᵢ² = 0 in the discriminant argument (then the inequality is trivial).
- Confusing equality in Cauchy–Schwarz with a = b; equality holds when a, b are proportional.

activity.prompt: Order the proof that d₂ satisfies the triangle inequality.
items: Consider the quadratic Σ(aᵢ + tbᵢ)² ≥ 0 for all t
Its discriminant is ≤ 0, giving Cauchy–Schwarz
Expand Σ(aᵢ + bᵢ)² and bound the cross term by Cauchy–Schwarz
Recognise the right side as (√Σaᵢ² + √Σbᵢ²)² — Minkowski
Substitute aᵢ = xᵢ − yᵢ and bᵢ = yᵢ − zᵢ

quiz.why: The quadratic touches zero exactly when aᵢ + tbᵢ = 0 for all i for some t, i.e. the vectors are proportional.

quiz.q: ρ = d/(1 + d) is always:
quiz.why: Since d ≥ 0, d/(1 + d) < 1, so ρ is a bounded metric.

lessons.title: Diameter, bounded sets and distance between sets

scenes.text: A surveyor asks for the greatest distance between any two points of a plot.
That is the diameter of the set — finite exactly when the set is bounded.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- diam(A) = sup{d(x, y): x, y ∈ A}. A is **bounded** if diam(A) < ∞.
- d(x, A) = inf{d(x, a): a ∈ A}.
- d(A, B) = inf{d(a, b): a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.
- d(x, A) = 0 does not imply x ∈ A (x may be a limit point).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- In ℝ, diam(0, 1) = 1 (sup, not attained).
- d(0, (0, 1]) = 0 although 0 ∉ (0, 1].
- A = x-axis, B = graph of y = 1/x (x > 0) in ℝ²: d(A, B) = 0 though A ∩ B = ∅.
- In the discrete metric, diam(X) = 1 if X has 2 or more points.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating d(A, B) = 0 as meaning A and B intersect.
- Thinking boundedness is a property of the set alone — it depends on the metric (ℝ is bounded under d/(1 + d)).

courses.title: Unit 2 · Open sets, closed sets and the topology of a metric space
courses.summary: Open and closed balls, open sets and their unions and intersections, limit points, closure, closed sets, interior, boundary, dense sets, separability, subspaces and equivalent metrics.
outcomes: Learners can prove that open balls are open sets
Learners can decide whether a set is open, closed, both or neither
Learners can compute interior, closure, derived set and boundary
Learners can identify dense subsets and separable spaces
Learners can relate open sets in a subspace to open sets in the whole space

scenes.text: A point inside a soap bubble can wiggle a little and stay inside.
A set is open when every point has such wiggle room — a small ball around it inside the set.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Open ball B(x, r) = {y: d(x, y) < r}; closed ball B[x, r] = {y: d(x, y) ≤ r}; sphere S(x, r) = {y: d(x, y) = r}.
- G ⊆ X is **open** if for every x ∈ G there is r > 0 with B(x, r) ⊆ G.

steps.title: Theorem: an open ball is open
steps.body: Let y ∈ B(x, r) and put s = r − d(x, y) > 0. If z ∈ B(y, s), then d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) < d(x, y) + s = r, so z ∈ B(x, r). Hence B(y, s) ⊆ B(x, r) ∎

steps.title: Properties of open sets
steps.body:
- ∅ and X are open.
- Any union of open sets is open.
- A **finite** intersection of open sets is open (take the minimum radius).
- Infinite intersections may fail: ∩(−1/n, 1/n) = {0}, not open in ℝ.

steps.title: Solved: balls in different metrics
steps.body:
- In ℝ²: B((0,0), 1) is a round disc for d₂, a diamond |x| + |y| < 1 for d₁, a square max(|x|, |y|) < 1 for d∞.
- Discrete metric: B(x, 1/2) = {x}, B(x, 2) = X.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a radius that does not depend on the point (r must work for that y).
- Believing ℤ is open in ℝ — no ball around 1 stays inside ℤ.

activity.prompt: Is the set open in ℝ (usual metric)?

quiz.why: Only points at distance less than 1 belong, and every other point is at distance exactly 1, so B(x, 1) = {x}.
Only 0 lies in every interval, showing an infinite intersection of open sets need not be open.
