lessons.title: Limit points, closure and closed sets

scenes.text: The numbers 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, … crowd ever closer to 0 without reaching it.
Adding such limit points 'closes' a set.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- x is a **limit point** of A if every ball B(x, r) contains a point of A other than x. The set of limit points is the derived set A′.
- **Closure** Ā = A ∪ A′; x ∈ Ā ⇔ d(x, A) = 0 ⇔ some sequence in A converges to x.
- A is **closed** if A′ ⊆ A, equivalently Ā = A, equivalently X ∖ A is open.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets are closed.
- Ā is the smallest closed set containing A.
- Closed balls are closed sets (but B[x, r] may be larger than the closure of B(x, r), e.g. in a discrete space).

steps.title: Solved: A = {1/n: n ∈ ℕ}
Solved: ℚ in ℝ
steps.body: Every real is a limit of rationals, so ℚ′ = ℝ and the closure of ℚ is ℝ. ℚ is neither open nor closed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'not open' means 'closed' — sets can be both (∅, X) or neither ([0, 1)).
- Calling isolated points limit points.

activity.prompt: Match each subset of ℝ to its closure.

quiz.q: The derived set of ℤ in ℝ is:
quiz.why: Every integer has a ball of radius 1/2 containing no other integer, and non-integers also have such balls, so ℤ has no limit points.

quiz.q: A set is closed iff its complement is:
quiz.why: This is the standard characterisation: closed sets are exactly the complements of open sets.

quiz.q: Which set is both open and closed in ℝ?
quiz.why: ℝ (and ∅) are always both open and closed; since ℝ is connected, these are its only clopen sets.

lessons.title: Interior, boundary, dense sets and separability

scenes.text: An island has inland points, sea points, and the shoreline in between.
Interior, exterior and boundary split every metric space the same way.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Interior** A° = {x: some B(x, r) ⊆ A}, the largest open subset of A. A is open ⇔ A = A°.
- **Boundary** ∂A = Ā ∖ A° = Ā ∩ (X ∖ A)‾.
- (A°)ᶜ = closure of Aᶜ.
- A is **dense** in X if Ā = X. X is **separable** if it has a countable dense subset.

steps.title: Solved: ℚ in ℝ
steps.body:
- ℚ° = ∅ (every interval contains irrationals)
- closure = ℝ ⇒ ∂ℚ = ℝ
- ℝ is **separable** (ℚ is countable and dense); ℝⁿ is separable via ℚⁿ.

steps.title: A non-separable space
steps.body: ℓ^∞ is not separable: the uncountably many 0–1 sequences are pairwise at sup-distance 1, so no countable set can approximate all of them within 1/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ∂A = A ∖ A° (should use the closure).
- Assuming the interior of a non-empty set is non-empty.

activity.prompt: Match each set in ℝ to its boundary.

quiz.q: Interior of [2, 5] in ℝ:
quiz.why: Endpoints have no ball inside the set, but every point strictly between does.

quiz.q: Interior of the irrationals in ℝ is:
quiz.why: Every interval contains rationals, so no ball fits inside the set of irrationals.

quiz.q: A space is separable if it has:
quiz.why: Separability means some countable subset has closure equal to the whole space.

scenes.text: Is [0, 1/2) open? Not in ℝ — but inside the space [0, 1] it is!
Openness depends on the ambient space.

steps.title: Subspaces
steps.body:
For Y ⊆ X, the restricted metric d_Y makes (Y, d_Y) a **subspace**.

- Balls: B_Y(y, r) = B(y, r) ∩ Y.
- G is open in Y ⇔ G = U ∩ Y for some U open in X. Same for closed sets.

steps.title: Solved: relative openness
steps.body: In Y = [0, 1]: [0, 1/2) = (−1, 1/2) ∩ Y is **open in Y** though not open in ℝ. In Y = ℤ ⊆ ℝ every subset is open (ℤ inherits the discrete topology).

steps.title: Equivalent metrics
steps.body:
d and ρ on X are (topologically) **equivalent** if they have the same open sets. They are **strongly equivalent** if a·d ≤ ρ ≤ b·d for constants a, b > 0.

- d₁, d₂, d∞ on ℝⁿ are strongly equivalent (d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ n·d∞).
- d and d/(1 + d) are equivalent but not strongly equivalent on ℝ (one is bounded).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'open' without specifying the space.
- Assuming equivalent metrics give the same bounded sets — they need not.

activity.prompt: Open in the subspace Y = [0, 1]?

quiz.q: In the subspace ℤ of ℝ, {3} is:
quiz.why: {3} = (2.5, 3.5) ∩ ℤ is open in ℤ, and it is also closed.

quiz.q: d₁ and d∞ on ℝⁿ are:
quiz.why: d∞ ≤ d₁ ≤ n·d∞ gives constants on both sides, so they are strongly equivalent.

quiz.q: Equivalent metrics always share:
quiz.why: Topological equivalence is defined by having identical open sets; boundedness and ball shapes can differ.

questions.q: Any union of open sets is:
questions.why: Each point of the union lies in some open member, which supplies a ball.

questions.q: Closure of (0, 1) in ℝ:
questions.why: Adding the limit points 0 and 1 gives [0, 1].

questions.q: Which set is neither open nor closed in ℝ?
questions.why: 0 has no ball inside it, and 1 is a limit point not in it.

questions.q: In a discrete metric space every subset is:
questions.why: Singletons are open balls, so all sets are open, hence all complements are too.

questions.q: Boundary of the open unit disc in ℝ²:
questions.why: Closure minus interior is the circle x² + y² = 1.

questions.q: A finite intersection of open sets is open because:
options: the minimum of finitely many positive radii is positive
questions.why: With finitely many radii, the smallest one still works for every set.

questions.q: Derived set of (0, 1) ∪ {2}:
questions.why: 2 is isolated, so it is not a limit point; the limit points are [0, 1].

questions.q: ℝ is separable because:
questions.why: Separability needs a countable dense subset, and ℚ is one.

questions.q: Interior of ℚ in ℝ:
questions.why: No interval is made up only of rationals.

questions.q: (1/2, 1] is open in:
questions.why: (1/2, 2) ∩ [0, 1] = (1/2, 1], so it is relatively open in [0, 1].

questions.q: In a discrete space with ≥ 2 points, the closure of B(x, 1) versus B[x, 1]:
questions.why: B(x, 1) = {x} is closed so its closure is {x}, while B[x, 1] is the whole space.

questions.q: ℓ^∞ is:
questions.why: The uncountable family of 0–1 sequences is 1-separated, ruling out a countable dense set.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Sequences, completeness, Cantor's and Baire's theorems
courses.summary: Convergent and Cauchy sequences in metric spaces, uniqueness of limits, complete metric spaces and standard examples, completeness of ℝⁿ, ℓ^p and C[a, b], Cantor's intersection theorem, nowhere dense sets and the Baire category theorem.
outcomes: Learners can prove convergence and the Cauchy property from the definitions
Learners can decide whether a given space is complete
Learners can prove that C[a, b] with the sup metric is complete
Learners can state and apply Cantor's intersection theorem
Learners can state the Baire category theorem and use it to show ℝ is uncountable

scenes.text: 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … get closer to each other with every digit.
In ℚ they never reach a limit — Cauchy, yet not convergent.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- xₙ → x if ∀ε > 0 ∃N: n ≥ N ⇒ d(xₙ, x) < ε.
- (xₙ) is **Cauchy** if ∀ε > 0 ∃N: m, n ≥ N ⇒ d(xₘ, xₙ) < ε.
- Limits are unique: d(x, y) ≤ d(x, xₙ) + d(xₙ, y) → 0.
- Convergent ⇒ Cauchy ⇒ bounded. Cauchy with a convergent subsequence ⇒ convergent.

steps.title: Solved: convergent ⇒ Cauchy
steps.body: If xₙ → x, pick N with d(xₙ, x) < ε/2 for n ≥ N. Then d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ d(xₘ, x) + d(x, xₙ) < ε ∎

steps.title: Solved: a Cauchy sequence that does not converge
steps.body: In X = (0, 1] with the usual metric, xₙ = 1/n is Cauchy (|1/m − 1/n| < 1/N) but its only candidate limit, 0, is not in X.

steps.title: Solved: discrete metric
steps.body: In a discrete space, (xₙ) is Cauchy ⇔ it is eventually constant (take ε = 1/2). Such a sequence converges, so every discrete space is complete.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only d(xₙ, xₙ₊₁) → 0: the partial sums of the harmonic series have consecutive gaps → 0 but are not Cauchy.
- Forgetting that convergence depends on the metric and the space.

activity.prompt: For xₙ = 1/n → 0 in ℝ, what is the smallest N such that |xₙ| < 0.01 for all n ≥ N?

quiz.q: Every convergent sequence in a metric space is:
quiz.why: The triangle inequality through the limit shows terms get close to one another, so a convergent sequence is Cauchy.

quiz.q: Sₙ = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n has Sₙ₊₁ − Sₙ → 0. Is (Sₙ) Cauchy?
quiz.why: S₂ₙ − Sₙ ≥ n·(1/2n) = 1/2 for all n, so the terms never cluster and the sequence is not Cauchy.

quiz.q: A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence:
quiz.why: Once the subsequence is near x and all terms are near each other, every term is near x.

scenes.text: ℚ has holes where √2 and π should be.
A complete space has no holes: every Cauchy sequence lands on a point of the space.

steps.title: Definition and facts
steps.body:
- (X, d) is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence converges in X.
- A subspace of a complete space is complete ⇔ it is closed.
- Complete: ℝ, ℝⁿ (any of d₁, d₂, d∞), ℓ^p, ℓ^∞, C[a, b] with sup metric, discrete spaces.
- Not complete: ℚ, (0, 1), C[a, b] with the integral metric d₁.

steps.title: Theorem: (C[a, b], d∞) is complete
steps.body:
Let (fₙ) be Cauchy in d∞.

1. For each x, |fₙ(x) − fₘ(x)| ≤ d∞(fₙ, fₘ), so (fₙ(x)) is Cauchy in ℝ; define f(x) = lim fₙ(x).
2. Given ε, choose N with d∞(fₙ, fₘ) < ε for m, n ≥ N; let m → ∞: |fₙ(x) − f(x)| ≤ ε for all x. So fₙ → f uniformly.
3. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so f ∈ C[a, b] ∎

steps.title: Solved: d₁ on C[0, 1] is not complete
steps.body: Let fₙ rise linearly from 0 at x = 1/2 to 1 at x = 1/2 + 1/n, equal 0 before and 1 after. ∫|fₙ − fₘ| ≤ 1/(2 min(m, n)) → 0, so (fₙ) is Cauchy, but the d₁-limit would be the step function, which is not continuous.

steps.title: Solved: (0, 1) versus ℝ
steps.body: (0, 1) is not complete (1/n has no limit inside) though it is homeomorphic to ℝ via tan(π(x − 1/2)). Completeness is a metric property, not a topological one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking closed ⇒ complete in any space (true only inside a complete space).
- Confusing pointwise and uniform convergence in step 2 of the C[a, b] proof.

activity.prompt: Complete or not complete?

quiz.q: A subset of ℝ is complete iff it is:
quiz.why: ℝ is complete, and a subspace of a complete space is complete exactly when it is closed.

quiz.q: Completeness is preserved by:
quiz.why: Isometries preserve distances, hence Cauchy sequences and limits; homeomorphisms need not, as (0, 1) ≅ ℝ shows.

quiz.q: ℚ is not complete because:
options: it is not closed in ℚ
a rational sequence can converge to √2 ∉ ℚ
quiz.why: Decimal truncations of √2 are Cauchy in ℚ but their limit is irrational.

scenes.text: Nested Russian dolls get smaller and smaller.
In a complete space, nested closed sets with shrinking diameter trap exactly one point.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: X is complete ⇔ for every decreasing sequence F₁ ⊇ F₂ ⊇ … of non-empty closed sets with diam Fₙ → 0, ∩Fₙ consists of exactly one point.

steps.title: Proof (⇒)
steps.body:
1. Pick xₙ ∈ Fₙ. For m ≥ n, xₘ ∈ Fₙ, so d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ diam Fₙ → 0: (xₙ) is Cauchy.
2. By completeness xₙ → x. For each n the tail lies in the closed set Fₙ, so x ∈ Fₙ. Thus x ∈ ∩Fₙ.
3. If y is also in ∩Fₙ, d(x, y) ≤ diam Fₙ → 0, so y = x ∎

steps.title: Why each hypothesis matters
steps.body:
- Not closed: Fₙ = (0, 1/n) in ℝ — empty intersection.
- Diameter not → 0: Fₙ = [n, ∞) — closed, nested, empty intersection.
- Not complete: in ℚ, Fₙ = ℚ ∩ [√2 − 1/n, √2 + 1/n] — empty intersection.

steps.title: Bisection method
steps.body: Repeated halving of [a, b] where f changes sign gives nested closed intervals with length (b − a)/2ⁿ → 0; Cantor's theorem guarantees a single root point in the limit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to show the limit lies in every Fₙ (needs closedness).
- Claiming uniqueness without diam → 0.

activity.prompt: Bisection on [1, 2]: after how many halvings is the interval length first below 0.001?

quiz.q: Fₙ = [n, ∞) in ℝ has ∩Fₙ =
quiz.why: No real number exceeds every n, so the intersection is empty — the diameters are infinite.

quiz.q: Which hypothesis fails for Fₙ = (0, 1/n)?
quiz.why: The sets are open intervals, not closed, and the would-be point 0 is excluded.

quiz.q: Cantor's theorem characterises:
quiz.why: The nested-closed-sets property holds exactly in complete metric spaces.

story.title: You can't build a plane from lines

scenes.text: Countably many lines in the plane, however many, leave most of the plane uncovered.
Baire's theorem turns this intuition into a powerful tool.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A is **nowhere dense** if the interior of Ā is empty (e.g. ℤ, a line in ℝ², the Cantor set).
- A is of **first category** (meagre) if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets; otherwise **second category**.

steps.title: Theorem
steps.body:
A complete metric space is of second category in itself. Equivalently: if X = ∪Fₙ with each Fₙ closed, some Fₙ has non-empty interior; and a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.

Proof idea: if each Fₙ were nowhere dense, choose nested closed balls Bₙ avoiding F₁, …, Fₙ with radii → 0; Cantor's theorem gives a point outside every Fₙ — contradiction.

steps.title: Solved: ℝ is uncountable
steps.body: If ℝ = {r₁, r₂, …}, then ℝ = ∪{rₙ}, a countable union of closed singletons with empty interior — contradicting Baire's theorem.

steps.title: Solved: ℚ is not complete (again)
steps.body: ℚ = ∪{qₙ} is a countable union of nowhere dense singletons, so ℚ is of first category in itself. By Baire, ℚ cannot be complete under any metric equivalent to the usual one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing 'nowhere dense' with 'not dense': ℚ ∩ [0, 1] is not dense in ℝ yet not nowhere dense either.
- Applying Baire to incomplete spaces.

activity.prompt: Nowhere dense in ℝ (usual metric)?

quiz.q: A set is nowhere dense if:
options: the interior of its closure is empty
quiz.why: Nowhere dense means even after closing it, the set contains no ball.

quiz.q: Baire's theorem applies to:
quiz.why: The proof uses Cantor's intersection theorem, which needs completeness.

quiz.q: ℚ in its usual metric is of:
quiz.why: ℚ is a countable union of singletons, each nowhere dense, so it is meagre in itself.

questions.q: A Cauchy sequence in ℝ always:
questions.why: ℝ is complete.

questions.q: Which space is not complete?
questions.why: Rational approximations of √2 have no rational limit.

questions.q: Limits in a metric space are unique because of:
questions.why: d(x, y) ≤ d(x, xₙ) + d(xₙ, y) → 0.

questions.q: In a discrete space a Cauchy sequence is:
questions.why: With ε = 1/2, terms beyond N must be equal.

questions.q: A closed subset of a complete space is:
questions.why: Limits of Cauchy sequences exist in X and stay in the closed set.

questions.q: (C[0, 1], d∞) convergence means:
questions.why: Sup-metric convergence is exactly uniform convergence.

questions.q: Fₙ = [0, 1/n] in ℝ: ∩Fₙ =
questions.why: Nested closed intervals with length → 0 in complete ℝ meet in exactly 0.

questions.q: (0, 1) and ℝ are homeomorphic but only ℝ is complete. This shows completeness is:
questions.why: A homeomorphism need not preserve Cauchy sequences.

questions.q: Baire's theorem shows ℝ is:
questions.why: A countable union of singletons cannot be a complete space with no isolated points.

questions.q: A countable intersection of dense open sets in a complete space is:
questions.why: This is the dense-open-sets form of Baire's theorem.

questions.q: Bisection on an interval of length 1 needs how many steps to get length < 0.01?
Which hypothesis is missing so that ℚ ∩ [√2 − 1/n, √2 + 1/n] has empty intersection?
questions.why: The sets are closed in ℚ, nested and shrinking; the failure comes from ℚ being incomplete.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Continuity, uniform continuity and the contraction principle
courses.summary: Continuity of maps between metric spaces via ε–δ, sequences and open sets; uniform continuity and Lipschitz maps; homeomorphisms and isometries; contraction mappings and the Banach fixed point theorem with applications.
outcomes: Learners can prove continuity using ε–δ, sequential and open-set characterisations
Learners can distinguish continuity from uniform continuity with examples
Learners can identify isometries and homeomorphisms
Learners can state and prove the Banach contraction principle
Learners can find fixed points by iteration and estimate the error

scenes.text: Turning a thermostat dial a tiny bit should change the temperature only a tiny bit.
Continuity says exactly that — and in metric spaces it can be phrased three ways.

steps.title: Theorem
steps.body:
For f: (X, d) → (Y, ρ), the following are equivalent:

1. **ε–δ**: ∀x₀, ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0: d(x, x₀) < δ ⇒ ρ(f(x), f(x₀)) < ε.
2. **Sequential**: xₙ → x₀ ⇒ f(xₙ) → f(x₀).
3. **Topological**: f⁻¹(G) is open in X for every open G ⊆ Y (equivalently, preimages of closed sets are closed).

steps.title: Proof of (1) ⇒ (3)
steps.body: Let G be open in Y and x₀ ∈ f⁻¹(G). Since f(x₀) ∈ G, some B(f(x₀), ε) ⊆ G. Choose δ from (1); then B(x₀, δ) ⊆ f⁻¹(B(f(x₀), ε)) ⊆ f⁻¹(G). So f⁻¹(G) is open ∎

steps.title: Solved: using preimages
steps.body:
- {(x, y): x² + y² < 1} is open in ℝ² since it is f⁻¹((−∞, 1)) for continuous f(x, y) = x² + y².
- {x: sin x ≥ 0} is closed in ℝ (preimage of the closed set [0, ∞)).

steps.title: Solved: discontinuity by sequences
steps.body: f(x) = 1 for x ∈ ℚ, 0 otherwise (Dirichlet). For any x₀, take rationals and irrationals converging to x₀: f-values tend to 1 and 0, so f is continuous nowhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking images of open sets are open (f(x) = x² maps (−1, 1) onto [0, 1)).
- Letting δ depend on ε only when proving uniform continuity — for ordinary continuity it may depend on x₀ too.

activity.prompt: Match each characterisation of continuity to its statement.

quiz.q: Every function from a discrete space to any metric space is:
quiz.why: Every subset of a discrete space is open, so every preimage is open.

quiz.q: Under a continuous map, the image of an open set is:
quiz.why: Continuity controls preimages, not images; x² sends (−1, 1) to [0, 1), which is not open.

quiz.q: The Dirichlet function is continuous at:
quiz.why: Near any point both rationals and irrationals occur, giving function values 1 and 0, so no limit exists anywhere.

scenes.text: For f(x) = 2x a tolerance of ε needs δ = ε/2 — anywhere on the line.
For x² you need tighter δ the further out you go. That is the difference.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- f is **uniformly continuous** if ∀ε ∃δ: d(x, y) < δ ⇒ ρ(f(x), f(y)) < ε for **all** x, y.
- f is **Lipschitz** with constant K if ρ(f(x), f(y)) ≤ K·d(x, y).
- Lipschitz ⇒ uniformly continuous (δ = ε/K) ⇒ continuous.
- Uniformly continuous maps send Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences.

steps.title: Solved: x² on ℝ is not uniformly continuous
steps.body: Take xₙ = n + 1/n, yₙ = n. |xₙ − yₙ| = 1/n → 0 but |xₙ² − yₙ²| = 2 + 1/n² > 2. So for ε = 2 no δ works.

steps.title: Solved: √x on [0, ∞) is uniformly continuous but not Lipschitz
steps.body:
- |√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|, so δ = ε² works.
- Not Lipschitz near 0: (√x − 0)/x = 1/√x → ∞.

steps.title: Solved: 1/x on (0, 1)
steps.body: xₙ = 1/n is Cauchy but f(xₙ) = n is not, so 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking bounded derivative is needed for uniform continuity (√x is a counterexample).
- Forgetting that on compact sets, continuity already implies uniform continuity (Unit 5).

activity.prompt: Uniformly continuous on the given domain?

quiz.q: A Lipschitz constant for sin x on ℝ is:
quiz.why: By the mean value theorem |sin x − sin y| = |cos c||x − y| ≤ |x − y|.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 5x, a δ that works for every x with ε given is:
quiz.why: |5x − 5y| = 5|x − y| < ε whenever |x − y| < ε/5.

quiz.q: Uniformly continuous maps preserve:
quiz.why: Uniform control of distances means d(xₘ, xₙ) small forces ρ(f(xₘ), f(xₙ)) small.

scenes.text: Topologists joke that a coffee mug and a doughnut are the same shape.
A homeomorphism stretches without tearing; an isometry does not even stretch.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Homeomorphism**: a bijection f with f and f⁻¹ continuous. Preserves open sets, closures, convergence, compactness, connectedness.
- **Isometry**: ρ(f(x), f(y)) = d(x, y). Injective and uniformly continuous; preserves completeness and boundedness too.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- f(x) = x/(1 + |x|) is a homeomorphism ℝ → (−1, 1).
- tan: (−π/2, π/2) → ℝ is a homeomorphism; boundedness is not preserved.
- Rotations and translations of ℝ² are isometries for d₂ (not, in general, for d₁).

steps.title: Solved: a continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism
steps.body: f: [0, 2π) → circle S¹, f(t) = (cos t, sin t). Continuous and bijective, but f⁻¹ is discontinuous at (1, 0): points just below the x-axis map back near 2π, not near 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a continuous bijection automatically has continuous inverse.
- Expecting homeomorphisms to preserve completeness.

activity.prompt: Preserved by every homeomorphism, or only by isometries?

quiz.q: An isometry is always:
quiz.why: If f(x) = f(y), then d(x, y) = ρ(f(x), f(y)) = 0, so x = y.

quiz.q: ℝ and (−1, 1) are:
quiz.why: x/(1 + |x|) is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, but distances are not preserved.

quiz.q: f(t) = (cos t, sin t) from [0, 2π) to S¹ fails to be a homeomorphism because:
options: S¹ is not a metric space
quiz.why: Near (1, 0), the inverse jumps between values near 0 and near 2π.

scenes.text: Drop a map of your city anywhere on the floor of a room in that city.
Exactly one point on the map lies directly above the place it represents — a fixed point.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
Let (X, d) be complete and T: X → X a **contraction**: d(Tx, Ty) ≤ α·d(x, y) with 0 ≤ α < 1. Then T has a **unique fixed point** x*, and for any x₀ the iterates xₙ = Tⁿx₀ converge to x*, with

d(xₙ, x*) ≤ αⁿ/(1 − α) · d(x₁, x₀).

steps.title: Proof
steps.body:
1. d(xₙ₊₁, xₙ) ≤ αⁿd(x₁, x₀).
2. For m > n: d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ (αⁿ + … + α^{m−1})d(x₁, x₀) ≤ αⁿ/(1 − α)·d(x₁, x₀) → 0, so (xₙ) is Cauchy.
3. Completeness: xₙ → x*. T is continuous, so Tx* = lim Txₙ = lim xₙ₊₁ = x*.
4. Uniqueness: if Ty = y, d(x*, y) = d(Tx*, Ty) ≤ αd(x*, y) ⇒ d(x*, y) = 0 ∎

steps.title: Solved: why each hypothesis matters
steps.body:
- α = 1 fails: T(x) = x + 1 has |Tx − Ty| = |x − y| and no fixed point.
- Incomplete space fails: T(x) = x/2 on (0, 1] is a contraction with no fixed point in (0, 1].
- d(Tx, Ty) < d(x, y) alone is not enough on ℝ: T(x) = x + 1/(1 + eˣ)… is a standard counterexample; on compact spaces it does suffice.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Picard's existence theorem for y′ = f(x, y), iterative solution of linear systems (Jacobi), Newton-type methods and the PageRank iteration all rest on contraction arguments.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only that T maps X into a smaller set — you must verify the Lipschitz constant α < 1.
- Forgetting to check that T maps X into X.

activity.prompt: T(x) = x/3 + 4 on ℝ is a contraction. Find its fixed point.

quiz.q: The contraction constant of T(x) = 0.8x + 3 on ℝ is:
T(x) = x/2 on (0, 1] has no fixed point because:
quiz.why: Iterates tend to 0, which is missing from (0, 1]; Banach's theorem needs completeness.

quiz.q: For α = 1/2 and d(x₁, x₀) = 1, the error bound after 5 iterations is:

questions.q: f is continuous iff preimages of ___ sets are open.
questions.why: This is the topological characterisation of continuity.

questions.q: A Lipschitz function is always:
questions.why: δ = ε/K works for every pair of points.

questions.q: Fixed point of T(x) = x/4 + 3:
questions.why: x = x/4 + 3 gives 3x/4 = 3, so x = 4.

questions.q: x² is uniformly continuous on:
questions.why: On a closed bounded interval |x² − y²| ≤ 6|x − y|, so it is Lipschitz.

questions.q: {(x, y): xy > 1} in ℝ² is open because:
options: it is f⁻¹((1, ∞)) for continuous f = xy
questions.why: Preimages of open sets under continuous maps are open.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Compactness and connectedness
courses.summary: Open covers and compactness, the Heine–Borel theorem, sequential compactness and total boundedness, continuous images of compact sets, the extreme value theorem and uniform continuity on compact sets, connected sets, connected subsets of ℝ, the intermediate value theorem and path-connectedness.
outcomes: Learners can test compactness using open covers and sequences
Learners can apply Heine–Borel in ℝⁿ and explain why it fails in general
Learners can prove that continuous images of compact sets are compact
Learners can prove that continuous functions on compact sets are bounded, attain extrema and are uniformly continuous
Learners can identify connected sets and use connectedness to prove the intermediate value theorem

scenes.text: However you place umbrellas to shelter a closed stretch of road, a finite number of them already does the job.
For an open-ended stretch, you may need infinitely many — that is non-compactness.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- An **open cover** of K is a family of open sets whose union contains K.
- K is **compact** if every open cover has a finite subcover.
- Compact ⇒ closed and bounded (in any metric space).

steps.title: Heine–Borel theorem
steps.body:
In ℝⁿ (usual metric), K is compact ⇔ K is closed and bounded.

The ⇐ direction fails in general: in ℓ² the closed unit ball is closed and bounded, but the unit vectors eₙ satisfy d(eₘ, eₙ) = √2, so no subsequence converges; the ball is not compact. Also an infinite discrete space is closed and bounded but not compact.

steps.title: Solved: (0, 1) is not compact
steps.body: Gₙ = (1/n, 1), n ≥ 2, cover (0, 1). Any finite subfamily has union (1/N, 1), which misses 1/(2N). No finite subcover.

steps.title: Solved: a convergent sequence with its limit
steps.body: K = {0} ∪ {1/n}. Given any open cover, some G₀ contains 0, hence all 1/n with n > N. Add one set for each of 1, 1/2, …, 1/N: a finite subcover. K is compact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing that ONE cover has a finite subcover — compactness needs EVERY cover.
- Applying Heine–Borel outside ℝⁿ.

activity.prompt: Compact or not compact?

quiz.q: In ℝⁿ, compact sets are exactly those that are:
quiz.why: This is the Heine–Borel theorem.

quiz.q: An infinite set with the discrete metric is:
quiz.why: The singletons form an open cover with no finite subcover.

quiz.q: Every compact subset of a metric space is:
quiz.why: Compact sets are always closed and bounded, though the converse can fail outside ℝⁿ.

scenes.text: Bees confined to a closed jar must crowd near some spot.
In a compact space every sequence has a convergent subsequence.

steps.title: Equivalent conditions
steps.body:
For a metric space X, the following are equivalent:

1. X is compact.
2. X is **sequentially compact**: every sequence has a convergent subsequence.
3. X has the **Bolzano–Weierstrass property**: every infinite subset has a limit point.
4. X is **complete and totally bounded** (for every ε, finitely many ε-balls cover X).

steps.title: Solved: [0, 1] is totally bounded
steps.body: For ε > 0, choose n > 1/ε; the balls of radius ε centred at 0, 1/n, 2/n, …, 1 cover [0, 1]. Being closed in ℝ, it is complete, hence compact.

steps.title: Solved: bounded but not totally bounded
steps.body: ℝ with the metric min(1, |x − y|) is bounded, but for ε = 1/2 a finite number of balls of radius 1/2 (length-1 intervals) cannot cover ℝ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing bounded with totally bounded (they agree only in ℝⁿ).
- Forgetting completeness in condition 4.

activity.prompt: What is the minimum number of closed intervals of length 0.2 needed to cover [0, 1]?

quiz.q: xₙ = (−1)ⁿ in ℝ has:
quiz.why: The even-indexed terms are all 1, a constant and therefore convergent subsequence, as Bolzano–Weierstrass predicts for a bounded sequence.

quiz.q: Compact metric space ⇔ complete and:
quiz.why: Total boundedness together with completeness is equivalent to compactness for metric spaces.

quiz.q: (0, 1) is totally bounded but not compact because it is not:
quiz.why: Finitely many ε-balls do cover (0, 1), but 1/n is a Cauchy sequence without a limit in the set.

scenes.text: Temperature varies continuously over a day from midnight to midnight.
Because [0, 24] is compact, some instant is the hottest of the day.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
Let X be compact and f: X → Y continuous.

1. f(X) is compact. Proof: if {Gα} covers f(X), then {f⁻¹(Gα)} is an open cover of X; take a finite subcover and map it forward.
2. (Extreme value) If Y = ℝ, f is bounded and attains its sup and inf.
3. (Heine) f is **uniformly continuous**.
4. A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a metric space is a homeomorphism.

steps.title: Solved: extreme values
steps.body: f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 2]. f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = 1. Values: f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(2) = 2. **Max 2, min −2** — attained, as the theorem promises.

steps.title: Solved: compactness is essential
steps.body:
- f(x) = x on (0, 1): sup 1 not attained.
- f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1]: unbounded.
- f(x) = 1/x on [1, ∞): inf 0 not attained.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the extreme value theorem on open intervals.
- Thinking continuous images of closed sets are closed (eˣ maps ℝ onto (0, ∞)).

activity.prompt: Find the maximum value of f(x) = 4x − x² on [0, 3].

quiz.why: Pulling back an open cover and using a finite subcover of the domain shows the image is compact.

quiz.q: Which function on [0, 1] must attain a maximum?
quiz.why: [0, 1] is compact, so the extreme value theorem applies to every continuous real function on it.

quiz.q: x² is uniformly continuous on [−10, 10] because:
quiz.why: Heine's theorem: continuity on a compact set implies uniform continuity.

lessons.title: Connectedness and the intermediate value theorem

scenes.text: A hiker going from one bank to the other along a continuous path must touch the water.
Connectedness makes 'you cannot jump over' precise.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- X is **disconnected** if X = A ∪ B with A, B non-empty, disjoint and open. Otherwise **connected**.
- Equivalent: the only clopen subsets are ∅ and X; or every continuous f: X → {0, 1} is constant.
- **Path-connected**: any two points are joined by a continuous path γ: [0, 1] → X. Path-connected ⇒ connected.

steps.title: Key theorems
steps.body:
- A subset of ℝ is connected ⇔ it is an **interval**.
- Continuous images of connected sets are connected.
- **IVT**: if f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous and c lies between f(a) and f(b), then f(x) = c for some x. (Image of the interval is an interval.)
- Union of connected sets with a common point is connected; closure of a connected set is connected.

steps.title: Solved: ℚ is totally disconnected
steps.body: For any irrational r, ℚ = (ℚ ∩ (−∞, r)) ∪ (ℚ ∩ (r, ∞)), two disjoint non-empty relatively open sets.

steps.title: Solved: IVT application
steps.body: f(x) = x³ + x − 1: f(0) = −1 < 0, f(1) = 1 > 0 ⇒ a root in (0, 1). Since f′ > 0, it is unique.

steps.title: Connected but not path-connected
steps.body: The topologist's sine curve {(x, sin(1/x)): 0 < x ≤ 1} ∪ ({0} × [−1, 1]) is connected (closure of a connected set) but no path joins (0, 0) to (1, sin 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sets that are disjoint but not open in the splitting.
- Assuming connected implies path-connected.

questions.why: Compact sets must be bounded.

questions.why: Intervals are connected.

questions.why: Extreme value theorem.

questions.why: This is the standard characterisation.

questions.why: Any two rationals are separated by an irrational cut.

questions.q: Closed unit ball of ℓ² is not compact because:
options: the unit vectors eₙ have no convergent subsequence
questions.why: d(eₘ, eₙ) = √2 for m ≠ n.

questions.why: It maps closed (compact) sets to compact, hence closed, sets, so the inverse is continuous.

questions.why: It is the closure of a connected set, but no path reaches the vertical segment.

uni-bsc-math-numerical-methods.title: Numerical Methods with Python Labs (B.Sc Mathematics)
uni-bsc-math-numerical-methods.description: Errors, root finding (bisection, Newton–Raphson, secant, fixed point), linear systems (Gauss elimination, LU, Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel), interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and numerical solution of ODEs (Euler, Runge–Kutta), each with Python code labs. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc (Hons) Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Errors and roots of non-linear equations
courses.summary: Floating-point representation and error types, then the bisection, Newton–Raphson, secant and fixed-point iteration methods with convergence orders, each implemented in Python.
outcomes: Distinguish absolute, relative, round-off and truncation errors
Apply and code the bisection method with a stopping tolerance
Derive and code Newton–Raphson and state its quadratic convergence
Apply the secant and fixed-point methods and check the convergence condition
Compare methods by order of convergence and robustness

scenes.text: A student types 0.1 + 0.2 into Python and gets 0.30000000000000004.
Binary floating point cannot store 0.1 exactly. Numerical methods are about controlling such errors.

steps.title: Error measures
steps.body: If x is the true value and x* an approximation: absolute error |x − x*|, relative error |x − x*|/|x|, percentage error = 100 × relative error. Example: π ≈ 3.14 gives absolute error ≈ 0.00159 and relative error ≈ 0.000507 (0.0507%).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Round-off error: from finite digits (IEEE 754 double has about 15–16 significant decimal digits, machine epsilon ≈ 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶). Truncation error: from cutting an infinite process short (e.g. stopping a Taylor series). Inherent/data error: from measured inputs.

steps.title: Worked example: loss of significance
steps.body: Computing √(x² + 1) − x for x = 10⁸ directly gives 0 in double precision, although the true value ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁹. Rationalising: 1/(√(x² + 1) + x) ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁹ is accurate. Subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys significant digits.

steps.title: Worked example: truncation error
steps.body: Approximating e by 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! = 2.666667 gives absolute error 2.718282 − 2.666667 = 0.051615. Adding 1/4! = 0.041667 gives 2.708333, error 0.009948. The error is roughly the first omitted term.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Testing floats with ==; use abs(a − b) < tol. Reporting more digits than the method's accuracy justifies.

activity.prompt: Print the relative error of 22/7 as an approximation of math.pi, formatted in scientific notation with 2 decimals (e.g. 1.23e-04).
activity.starter:
import math
approx = 22/7
# compute relative error and print it
activity.solution:
import math
approx = 22/7
rel = abs(math.pi - approx) / math.pi
print(f"{rel:.2e}")
activity.hint: Relative error = |true − approx| / |true|; use an f-string with :.2e.

quiz.why: Truncation error is the part discarded when, for example, a series or iteration is stopped after finitely many terms.

quiz.q: Machine epsilon for IEEE double is about:
quiz.why: Doubles have a 52-bit fraction, giving ε = 2⁻⁵² ≈ 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶.

Subtracting two nearly equal numbers causes:
quiz.why: The leading digits cancel, leaving only the less reliable trailing digits.

scenes.text: In a number-guessing game, halving the range each time always finds the answer.
Bisection applies this to a continuous f with a sign change on [a, b].

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Requires f continuous on [a, b] with f(a)f(b) < 0 (intermediate value theorem). Repeat: c = (a + b)/2; if f(a)f(c) < 0 set b = c, else set a = c; stop when (b − a)/2 < tol. After n steps the error is at most (b − a)/2ⁿ⁺¹.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body: Always converges (robust), linear convergence with ratio 1/2, about 3.3 iterations per decimal digit. Needs a bracketing interval; cannot find double roots like x² = 0 where no sign change occurs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not checking f(a)f(b) < 0 first. Using f(a)·f(c) with large values can overflow — compare signs instead.

activity.prompt: Implement bisection for f(x) = x³ − x − 2 on [1, 2] with tolerance 1e-6 and print the root to 4 decimal places.

a, b = 1.0, 2.0

quiz.why: The error after n steps is at most (b − a)/2ⁿ⁺¹ = 1/2048.

quiz.why: The intermediate value theorem needs continuity and a sign change to guarantee a root in the bracket.

quiz.q: Order of convergence of bisection:
quiz.why: The error bound halves at each step, a linear rate with constant 1/2.

quiz.why: f(1.5) < 0 so the new interval is [1.5, 2], whose midpoint is 1.75.

scenes.text: Standing on a curve, slide down its tangent line to where it hits the x-axis — that is your next guess.
Near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body: Taylor: 0 = f(x_n + h) ≈ f(x_n) + h f′(x_n) ⇒ h = −f(x_n)/f′(x_n). Iteration x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n). Near a simple root, e_{n+1} ≈ (f″(α)/(2f′(α))) e_n² — quadratic convergence.

steps.title: Worked example: x³ − x − 2
steps.body: f′ = 3x² − 1. x₀ = 1.5: f = −0.125, f′ = 5.75, x₁ = 1.5 + 0.125/5.75 = 1.521739. x₂ = 1.521380. Compare with bisection's 20 iterations for similar accuracy.

steps.title: Failure modes
steps.body: f′(x_n) = 0 (division by zero), cycling (x³ − 2x + 2 from x₀ = 0 alternates 0, 1, 0, 1 …), divergence from a poor start, and only linear convergence at multiple roots (use x_{n+1} = x_n − m f/f′ for multiplicity m).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the wrong derivative. Stopping on |f(x_n)| small only — also check |x_{n+1} − x_n|.

activity.prompt: Use Newton–Raphson with x0 = 3 to find √10 (solve x² − 10 = 0). Iterate until successive values differ by less than 1e-10 and print the result to 6 decimals.

    pass
activity.solution:

    x_new = x - (x*x - 10) / (2*x)
    if abs(x_new - x) < 1e-10:
        x = x_new
        break
    x = x_new
print(f"{x:.6f}")

scenes.text: When f′ is hard to compute, replace the tangent by a secant through the last two points.
Or rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate — if |g′| < 1 near the root.

steps.title: Secant method
steps.body: x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)(x_n − x_{n−1})/(f(x_n) − f(x_{n−1})). Order ≈ 1.618 (golden ratio), one function evaluation per step.

steps.title: Fixed-point iteration
steps.body: Rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate x_{n+1} = g(x_n). If |g′(x)| ≤ k < 1 near the root, the iteration converges linearly with rate about |g′(α)|.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Choosing a rearrangement with |g′| > 1. Secant can fail when f(x_n) = f(x_{n−1}).

quiz.why: Then g is a contraction near α, so the errors shrink by about |g′(α)| each step.

quiz.why: Newton's update uses f(x_n)/f′(x_n) explicitly.

courses.summary: Direct methods (Gauss elimination with partial pivoting, Gauss–Jordan, LU decomposition) and iterative methods (Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel) for Ax = b, with diagonal dominance, operation counts and ill-conditioning, implemented in Python.
outcomes: Solve Ax = b by Gauss elimination with back substitution and partial pivoting

lessons.title: Lab: Gauss elimination with partial pivoting

scenes.text: Kirchhoff's laws on a three-loop circuit give three linear equations in three currents.
Gauss elimination turns the system into a triangle that can be solved from the bottom up.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Forward elimination: for k = 1..n−1, for each row i > k subtract mᵢₖ = aᵢₖ/aₖₖ times row k, making the system upper triangular. Back substitution: xₙ = bₙ/aₙₙ, then xᵢ = (bᵢ − Σ_{j>i} aᵢⱼxⱼ)/aᵢᵢ. Cost ≈ 2n³/3 operations.

steps.title: Partial pivoting
steps.body: Before eliminating column k, swap in the row with the largest |aᵢₖ| (i ≥ k). This avoids division by zero and limits growth of round-off errors. Example: 0.0001x + y = 1, x + y = 2 without pivoting in 3-digit arithmetic gives x = 0 (wrong); with pivoting x ≈ 1.000, y ≈ 1.000.

steps.title: Gauss–Jordan
steps.body: Eliminate above and below each pivot to reach the identity; useful for computing A⁻¹ by reducing [A | I] to [I | A⁻¹]. Cost ≈ n³, more than Gauss elimination.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Updating the right-hand side b inconsistently with the rows. Forgetting to swap b entries when pivoting.

activity.prompt: Complete Gauss elimination with partial pivoting and back substitution for the 3 × 3 system in the worked example. Print the solution as three numbers with 2 decimals separated by spaces.
activity.starter:
A = [[2.0, 1.0, -1.0], [-3.0, -1.0, 2.0], [-2.0, 1.0, 2.0]]
b = [8.0, -11.0, -3.0]
n = 3
# forward elimination with partial pivoting

# back substitution
x = [0.0]*n

print(" ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in x))
activity.solution:
A = [[2.0, 1.0, -1.0], [-3.0, -1.0, 2.0], [-2.0, 1.0, 2.0]]
b = [8.0, -11.0, -3.0]
n = 3
for k in range(n-1):
    p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda i: abs(A[i][k]))
    A[k], A[p] = A[p], A[k]
    b[k], b[p] = b[p], b[k]
    for i in range(k+1, n):
        m = A[i][k] / A[k][k]
        for j in range(k, n):
            A[i][j] -= m * A[k][j]
        b[i] -= m * b[k]
x = [0.0]*n
for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
    s = sum(A[i][j]*x[j] for j in range(i+1, n))
    x[i] = (b[i] - s) / A[i][i]
print(" ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in x))
activity.hint: Swap both the rows of A and the entries of b when pivoting; then eliminate below the pivot.

quiz.why: Eliminating below each pivot costs about Σ 2(n − k)² ≈ 2n³/3 operations.

quiz.q: Back substitution starts from:

Factorising A = LU once makes each new solve cheap: O(n²) instead of O(n³).

steps.title: Doolittle factorisation
steps.body: A = LU with L unit lower triangular (1s on the diagonal) and U upper triangular. The multipliers of Gauss elimination are exactly the sub-diagonal entries of L. Crout's method puts the 1s on U's diagonal instead; Cholesky A = LLᵀ applies to symmetric positive definite A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting the negatives of the multipliers in L. LU without pivoting fails if a zero pivot appears; then use PA = LU with a permutation matrix P.

activity.prompt: For A = [[1,1,1],[4,3,−1],[3,5,3]] (worked example), find det A from the diagonal of U.

quiz.why: Doolittle's convention makes L unit lower triangular.

quiz.q: Cost of each new solve with a known LU:

steps.title: Jacobi
steps.body: Solve equation i for xᵢ: xᵢ^{(k+1)} = (bᵢ − Σ_{j≠i} aᵢⱼ xⱼ^{(k)})/aᵢᵢ, using only old values.

steps.title: Gauss–Seidel
steps.body: Same, but use new values as soon as they are available: xᵢ^{(k+1)} = (bᵢ − Σ_{j<i} aᵢⱼ xⱼ^{(k+1)} − Σ_{j>i} aᵢⱼ xⱼ^{(k)})/aᵢᵢ. Usually converges about twice as fast as Jacobi.

steps.title: Convergence test
steps.body: Both converge for any starting vector if A is strictly diagonally dominant: |aᵢᵢ| > Σ_{j≠i} |aᵢⱼ| for every row. Gauss–Seidel also converges for symmetric positive definite A. Reorder equations to achieve dominance where possible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying iterations to a non-dominant ordering and wondering why they diverge. In Jacobi, accidentally overwriting x in place (that turns it into Gauss–Seidel).

steps.title: Existence and uniqueness
steps.body: Given n + 1 points (xᵢ, yᵢ) with distinct xᵢ, there is exactly one polynomial of degree ≤ n through them (a Vandermonde determinant argument).

steps.title: Lagrange form
steps.body: P(x) = Σ yᵢ Lᵢ(x), where Lᵢ(x) = Π_{j≠i} (x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ). Each Lᵢ equals 1 at xᵢ and 0 at the other nodes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including the j = i factor in Lᵢ (division by zero). High-degree interpolation on equally spaced nodes can oscillate wildly near the ends (Runge's phenomenon).

story.title: Adding a point without starting over

scenes.text: With Lagrange's form, adding a new data point means recomputing everything.
Newton's form just adds one more term on top.

steps.title: Divided differences
steps.body: f[xᵢ] = yᵢ, f[xᵢ, xᵢ₊₁] = (f[xᵢ₊₁] − f[xᵢ])/(xᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ), and in general f[x₀,…,x_k] = (f[x₁,…,x_k] − f[x₀,…,x_{k−1}])/(x_k − x₀). They are symmetric in their arguments.

steps.title: Newton's form
steps.body: P(x) = f[x₀] + f[x₀,x₁](x − x₀) + f[x₀,x₁,x₂](x − x₀)(x − x₁) + … Adding a point appends one term.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Data (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 7). First differences: (3 − 1)/1 = 2, (7 − 3)/1 = 4. Second: (4 − 2)/(2 − 0) = 1. P(x) = 1 + 2x + 1·x(x − 1) = x² + x + 1, matching Lagrange.

steps.title: Worked example: adding a point
steps.body: Add (3, 13). New first difference (13 − 7)/1 = 6, second (6 − 4)/2 = 1, third (1 − 1)/3 = 0. The extra term is 0 · x(x − 1)(x − 2): the data come from a quadratic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing by adjacent spacing instead of x_k − x₀ for higher-order differences. Mixing the order of nodes between the table and the formula.

lessons.title: Finite differences: Newton forward and backward

scenes.text: Population data recorded every 10 years is equally spaced — perfect for difference tables.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body: Δf(x) = f(x + h) − f(x), ∇f(x) = f(x) − f(x − h), Ef(x) = f(x + h). Relations: Δ = E − 1, ∇ = 1 − E⁻¹. For a polynomial of degree n, Δⁿf is constant = n! aₙ hⁿ and Δⁿ⁺¹f = 0.

steps.title: Newton's forward formula
steps.body: With x = x₀ + ph: P(x) = y₀ + pΔy₀ + p(p − 1)/2! Δ²y₀ + p(p − 1)(p − 2)/3! Δ³y₀ + … Backward (near the end, x = xₙ + ph): P(x) = yₙ + p∇yₙ + p(p + 1)/2! ∇²yₙ + …

steps.title: Error term
steps.body: f(x) − P(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)! · Π (x − xᵢ) for some ξ in the span of the nodes. Example: linear interpolation of sin x between 0 and π/6 at π/12 has error ≤ (1/2)·|(π/12)(−π/12)|·1 ≈ 0.034.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the forward formula with the wrong sign of p, or using it near the end of a table where the backward formula is more accurate.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Start with coef = ys. For level k = 1..n−1, update from the bottom: coef[i] = (coef[i] − coef[i − 1])/(xs[i] − xs[i − k]) for i = n−1 down to k. Then coef holds f[x₀], f[x₀,x₁], … Evaluate with nested multiplication (Horner-like): p = coef[n−1]; for i from n−2 down to 0, p = p·(x − xs[i]) + coef[i].

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Forward: f′(x) ≈ [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, error O(h). Backward: [f(x) − f(x − h)]/h, O(h). Central: [f(x + h) − f(x − h)]/(2h), O(h²). Second derivative: [f(x + h) − 2f(x) + f(x − h)]/h², O(h²). All follow from Taylor expansions.

steps.title: Worked example: f = eˣ at 0, h = 0.1
The h trade-off
steps.body: Truncation error falls as h shrinks, but round-off error grows like ε/h. For the forward difference in double precision the best h is around √ε ≈ 10⁻⁸; for the central difference around ε^{1/3} ≈ 10⁻⁵.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Choosing h = 10⁻¹⁵ 'for accuracy' — round-off then dominates. Dividing the central difference by h instead of 2h.

steps.title: Composite trapezoidal rule
steps.body: With h = (b − a)/n and yᵢ = f(a + ih): T = (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Error = −(b − a)h² f″(ξ)/12, so O(h²); exact for linear functions.

steps.title: Richardson extrapolation
steps.body: Since T(h) = I + ch² + …, combining (4T(h/2) − T(h))/3 cancels the h² term. This is the first step of Romberg integration and reproduces Simpson's rule.

activity.prompt: Implement the composite trapezoidal rule and print ∫₀¹ eˣ dx with n = 100 to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math

def trap(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    # (h/2)[y0 + 2*(y1 + ... + y_{n-1}) + yn]
    return 0.0

print(f"{trap(math.exp, 0, 1, 100):.4f}")
activity.solution:
import math

def trap(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        s += 2 * f(a + i*h)
    return h / 2 * s

print(f"{trap(math.exp, 0, 1, 100):.4f}")

steps.title: Simpson's 1/3 rule
steps.body: n even, h = (b − a)/n: S = (h/3)[y₀ + 4(y₁ + y₃ + …) + 2(y₂ + y₄ + …) + yₙ]. Error = −(b − a)h⁴ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/180, O(h⁴); exact for cubics.

steps.title: Simpson's 3/8 rule
steps.body: For n a multiple of 3: (3h/8)[y₀ + 3y₁ + 3y₂ + 2y₃ + 3y₄ + … + yₙ]. Also O(h⁴). Example: ∫₀³ x³ dx with h = 1: (3/8)(0 + 3 + 24 + 27) = 20.25 = 81/4 exactly.

steps.body: Using an odd n with the 1/3 rule. Swapping the 4 and 2 weights — odd-index interior points get 4.

activity.prompt: Implement composite Simpson's 1/3 rule and print 4·∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) with n = 10 to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    # weights 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 4, 1 times h/3
    return 0.0

print(f"{4 * simpson(lambda x: 1/(1 + x*x), 0, 1, 10):.4f}")
activity.solution:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        s += (4 if i % 2 == 1 else 2) * f(a + i*h)
    return h / 3 * s

print(f"{4 * simpson(lambda x: 1/(1 + x*x), 0, 1, 10):.4f}")
activity.hint: Odd-index interior points get weight 4, even-index interior points weight 2.

That is Euler's method: tiny straight steps along the slope y′ = f(x, y).

steps.title: Taylor series method
steps.body: y(x₀ + h) = y₀ + hy′₀ + (h²/2)y″₀ + (h³/6)y‴₀ + …, with derivatives found by differentiating the ODE. Example y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1: y′(0) = 1, y″ = 1 + y′ ⇒ 2, y‴ = y″ ⇒ 2. y(0.1) ≈ 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 + 0.000333 = 1.110333 (exact 1.110342).

steps.title: Euler's method
steps.body: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n). Local error O(h²), global error O(h) — first order.

steps.title: Stability
steps.body: For the test equation y′ = −λy (λ > 0), Euler gives y_{n+1} = (1 − λh)y_n, which stays bounded only if |1 − λh| ≤ 1, i.e. h ≤ 2/λ. For λ = 10, h must be ≤ 0.2 or the numerical solution blows up although the true solution decays.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Evaluating f at the new point in explicit Euler. Assuming a smaller h always fixes everything — the global error falls only linearly with h.

activity.prompt: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 for y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1, and print y(0.2) to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
def f(x, y):
    return x + y

x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    # Euler step
    pass
print(f"{y:.4f}")
activity.solution:
def f(x, y):
    return x + y

x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    y = y + h * f(x, y)
    x = x + h
print(f"{y:.4f}")
activity.hint: Update y with the slope at the old point, then advance x.

quiz.q: Global error of Euler's method is:
quiz.why: Local errors of O(h²) accumulate over about 1/h steps, giving O(h) overall.

quiz.q: Euler y₁ for y′ = y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.2:
For y′ = −50y, Euler is stable for h ≤
quiz.why: The stability condition is h ≤ 2/λ = 2/50 = 0.04.

quiz.q: Taylor method second-order term for y′ = x + y at (0,1):
quiz.why: y″(0) = 2, so the term (h²/2)·y″ = h².

scenes.text: Euler uses only the slope at the start of the step. Heun peeks at the end of the step and averages.
This predictor–corrector idea makes the method second order.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Predictor: y* = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n). Corrector: y_{n+1} = y_n + (h/2)[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, y*)]. Global error O(h²). It is a two-stage Runge–Kutta method.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using y* as the final answer (that is just Euler). Forgetting the factor h/2.

activity.prompt: Using Heun's method with h = 0.1 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1, find y(0.1) (4 decimals).

quiz.q: Heun's method has global order:
quiz.why: Averaging the start and predicted end slopes cancels the first-order error term.

quiz.q: Heun y₁ for y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1:
In Heun, the predictor is:
quiz.why: y* = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n) is exactly Euler's step.

quiz.q: Heun's corrector resembles which quadrature rule?
quiz.why: It averages f at both ends of the step, like the trapezoidal rule applied to ∫ f dx.

scenes.text: Satellite orbits, epidemic models and circuit simulations commonly use RK4 or its adaptive cousins.
Four slope samples per step give fourth-order accuracy.

steps.title: Classical RK4
steps.body: k₁ = h f(x_n, y_n); k₂ = h f(x_n + h/2, y_n + k₁/2); k₃ = h f(x_n + h/2, y_n + k₂/2); k₄ = h f(x_n + h, y_n + k₃). y_{n+1} = y_n + (k₁ + 2k₂ + 2k₃ + k₄)/6. Global error O(h⁴).

steps.title: Worked example: y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1
Systems and higher order
steps.body: Write y″ = g(x, y, y′) as a system u₁ = y, u₂ = y′: u₁′ = u₂, u₂′ = g(x, u₁, u₂), and apply RK4 to the vector (u₁, u₂).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using k₁ instead of k₁/2 inside k₂. Forgetting the weights 1, 2, 2, 1 and the division by 6.

activity.prompt: Implement RK4 for y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1 with h = 0.1 and print y(0.2) to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
def f(x, y):
    return x + y

x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    # compute k1..k4 and update y, x
    pass
print(f"{y:.4f}")
activity.solution:
def f(x, y):
    return x + y

x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    k1 = h * f(x, y)
    k2 = h * f(x + h/2, y + k1/2)
    k3 = h * f(x + h/2, y + k2/2)
    k4 = h * f(x + h, y + k3)
    y += (k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4) / 6
    x += h
print(f"{y:.4f}")
activity.hint: Each k uses the previous k at half (or full) weight.

quiz.q: RK4 weights are:
quiz.why: The classical scheme combines the four slopes as (k₁ + 2k₂ + 2k₃ + k₄)/6.

quiz.q: RK4 global error order:
quiz.why: Classical RK4 matches the Taylor series through the h⁴ term.

quiz.q: k₂ in the worked example:
Function evaluations per RK4 step:
quiz.why: k₁ to k₄ each need one evaluation of f.

lessons.title: Lab: Practical exam checklist and formula sheet

scenes.text: A numerical methods practical usually asks you to code one method, run it on given data and answer viva questions.
Here is a checklist covering every method in the course.

steps.title: Formula sheet
steps.body: Bisection error ≤ (b − a)/2ⁿ⁺¹. Newton x − f/f′ (order 2). Secant order 1.618. Fixed point needs |g′| < 1. Gauss elimination ≈ 2n³/3. Jacobi/Gauss–Seidel: diagonal dominance. Lagrange Lᵢ = Π(x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ). Newton forward with p = (x − x₀)/h. Trapezoidal O(h²), Simpson 1/3 O(h⁴), 2-point Gauss exact to degree 3. Euler O(h), Heun O(h²), RK4 O(h⁴).

steps.title: Standard practical list
steps.body: (1) Bisection, (2) Newton–Raphson, (3) Secant/Regula falsi, (4) Gauss elimination / LU, (5) Gauss–Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel, (6) Lagrange interpolation, (7) Newton divided differences, (8) Trapezoidal and Simpson's rules, (9) Euler and modified Euler, (10) RK4. For each: state the algorithm, write the code, show a sample output, and compare with the exact value.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body: Why does bisection always converge? When does Newton fail? Why is Simpson exact for cubics? What does diagonal dominance guarantee? Why is RK4 preferred over Euler? What is the difference between local and global truncation error?

activity.prompt: Order the steps of writing up a numerical methods practical.
items: State the aim and the method's formula
Write the algorithm in steps
Implement and run the program on the given data
Tabulate iterations or intermediate values
Compare with the exact or reference value and comment on error

quiz.q: Newton x₁ for x³ − 4x − 9 with x₀ = 3:
Which method has order 4?
quiz.why: Classical Runge–Kutta has global error O(h⁴).

quiz.q: Which integration rule is exact for cubics?
quiz.why: Simpson's error term involves f⁽⁴⁾, which vanishes for cubics.

RK4 k₁ for y′ = y, y(0) = 2, h = 0.1:
questions.why: k₁ = h f(x₀, y₀) = 0.1·2.

Exact solution of y′ = x + y, y(0) = 1:
questions.why: Linear ODE: y = Ceˣ − x − 1 with C = 2 from y(0) = 1.

questions.why: O(h⁴) error falls by 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: Heun y₁ for y′ = −y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1:
y″ + y = 0 is solved by RK4 after rewriting as:
questions.why: Set u₁ = y and u₂ = y′.

questions.q: Euler for y′ = −10y is unstable if h >
questions.why: Stability needs h ≤ 2/λ = 0.2.

questions.q: Local truncation error of Euler per step:
questions.why: The omitted Taylor term is (h²/2)y″.

Number of f-evaluations per step: Euler, Heun, RK4:

uni-bsc-math-partial-differential-equati.title: B.Sc Mathematics · Partial Differential Equations
uni-bsc-math-partial-differential-equati.description: Formation of PDEs, Lagrange's linear equation, Charpit's method and standard forms, classification and canonical forms of second-order equations, linear PDEs with constant coefficients, and the wave, heat and Laplace equations by d'Alembert's method and separation of variables. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Formation of PDEs and Lagrange's linear equation
courses.summary: Order, degree and classification of PDEs, formation by eliminating arbitrary constants and arbitrary functions, Lagrange's linear equation Pp + Qq = R, the method of grouping and the method of multipliers, and integral surfaces through a given curve.
outcomes: Learners can classify a PDE as linear, semi-linear, quasi-linear or non-linear
Learners can form PDEs by eliminating arbitrary constants or functions
Learners can write and solve Lagrange's auxiliary equations by grouping
Learners can solve Lagrange's equation by the method of multipliers
Learners can find the integral surface through a given curve

scenes.text: The temperature in a metal plate depends on both x and y — and on time t.
Equations linking its partial derivatives are partial differential equations.

steps.title: Notation and definitions
steps.body:
For z = z(x, y): p = ∂z/∂x, q = ∂z/∂y, r = ∂²z/∂x², s = ∂²z/∂x∂y, t = ∂²z/∂y².

- **Order**: highest derivative present. **Degree**: power of the highest-order derivative (after clearing radicals/fractions).
- **Linear**: z and its derivatives appear to first power with coefficients depending only on x, y.
- **Semi-linear**: P(x, y)p + Q(x, y)q = R(x, y, z).
- **Quasi-linear**: P(x, y, z)p + Q(x, y, z)q = R(x, y, z).
- **Non-linear**: anything else, e.g. p² + q² = 1.

steps.title: Solved: classifying
steps.body:
- xp + yq = z: first order, linear
- p + q = z²: semi-linear
- zp + q = 0: quasi-linear
- pq = z: non-linear
- r + t = 0 (Laplace): second order, linear

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling zp + q = 0 linear: the coefficient of p contains z.
- Reading the degree before rationalising, e.g. p = √(1 + q) has degree 2 after squaring? No — squaring gives p² = 1 + q, so degree 2 in p.

activity.prompt: Classify each first-order PDE.

quiz.q: The order of r + 3s + t = x is:
quiz.why: r, s and t are second derivatives, and nothing higher appears, so the equation is of order 2.

quiz.q: zp + yq = x is:
quiz.why: It is first-degree in p and q, but the coefficient of p contains z, which makes it quasi-linear.

quiz.q: q is the symbol for:
quiz.why: By convention p = ∂z/∂x and q = ∂z/∂y.

scenes.text: All spheres of radius 5 centred on the xy-plane form a two-parameter family.
Eliminating the parameters gives a single PDE every member satisfies.

steps.title: Two methods
steps.body:
- **Eliminating arbitrary constants**: from f(x, y, z, a, b) = 0 differentiate partially w.r.t. x and y and eliminate a, b. If the number of constants equals the number of independent variables, a first-order PDE results.
- **Eliminating an arbitrary function**: from z = f(u) or φ(u, v) = 0 differentiate and eliminate f′ (or use the Jacobian).

steps.title: Solved: constants
steps.body:
z = (x − a)² + (y − b)².

- p = 2(x − a), q = 2(y − b)
- (x − a)² = p²/4, (y − b)² = q²/4
- **4z = p² + q²**

z = ax + by + ab ⇒ p = a, q = b ⇒ **z = px + qy + pq** (Clairaut form).

steps.title: Solved: arbitrary functions
steps.body:
z = f(x² + y²).

- p = 2x f′, q = 2y f′
- Divide: p/q = x/y ⇒ **yp − xq = 0**

z = f(x + ct) + g(x − ct) (two functions) gives the second-order wave equation z_tt = c²z_xx.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain rule factor of the inner function.
- Trying to get a first-order PDE from two arbitrary functions — it needs second order.

activity.prompt: Match each family to its PDE.

quiz.q: Eliminating a, b from z = ax + by gives:
quiz.why: p = a and q = b, so substituting back gives z = px + qy.

quiz.q: z = f(x − y) satisfies:
quiz.why: p = f′ and q = −f′, so p + q = 0.

quiz.q: Eliminating two arbitrary functions typically yields a PDE of order:
quiz.why: Each arbitrary function needs one differentiation to remove, so two functions lead to second-order derivatives.

scenes.text: A solution surface is woven from curves along which the PDE becomes an ODE.
Lagrange's auxiliary equations trace those curves.

steps.title: Lagrange's theorem
steps.body:
For Pp + Qq = R (P, Q, R functions of x, y, z), form the **auxiliary (subsidiary) equations**

dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.

If u(x, y, z) = a and v(x, y, z) = b are two independent solutions, the general solution is **φ(u, v) = 0** (or u = f(v)), φ arbitrary.

steps.title: Solved: xp + yq = z
steps.body:
dx/x = dy/y = dz/z.

- From the first pair: ln y = ln x + c ⇒ y/x = a
- From the first and third: z/x = b
- **φ(y/x, z/x) = 0**

steps.title: Solved: yzp + zxq = xy
steps.body:
dx/(yz) = dy/(zx) = dz/(xy).

- First pair ×z: x dx = y dy ⇒ x² − y² = a
- First and third ×y: x dx = z dz ⇒ x² − z² = b
- **φ(x² − y², x² − z²) = 0**

steps.title: Solved: p + q = 1
steps.body: dx/1 = dy/1 = dz/1 ⇒ x − y = a, z − x = b ⇒ **z = x + f(x − y)**. Check: p = 1 + f′, q = −f′, p + q = 1 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Producing two dependent integrals (e.g. y/x and x/y).
- Cancelling a variable that is itself one of the unknowns along the curve without care.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to solve Pp + Qq = R.
items: Write the PDE in the form Pp + Qq = R
Form the auxiliary equations dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R
Integrate one pair to get u(x, y, z) = a
Integrate another pair (or a combination) to get v = b
Check u and v are independent
Write the general solution φ(u, v) = 0

quiz.q: Auxiliary equations for x²p + y²q = z² are:
quiz.why: In Lagrange's method the denominators are P, Q and R themselves, here x², y² and z².

quiz.q: For x²p + y²q = z², one integral is:
quiz.why: dx/x² = dy/y² integrates to −1/x = −1/y + c, i.e. 1/x − 1/y = a.

quiz.q: The general solution of p = 0 is:
quiz.why: ∂z/∂x = 0 means z does not change with x, so z is an arbitrary function of y alone.

lessons.title: Method of multipliers and integral surfaces

scenes.text: Sometimes no pair of auxiliary equations separates nicely.
Multiply by well-chosen l, m, n so that the denominator vanishes — and the numerator becomes exact.

steps.title: The method
steps.body:
For any multipliers l, m, n:

dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R = (l dx + m dy + n dz)/(lP + mQ + nR).

If lP + mQ + nR = 0, then l dx + m dy + n dz = 0, and if this is exact it integrates to u = a.

steps.title: Solved: (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y
steps.body:
- Multipliers 1, 1, 1: denominator (y − z) + (z − x) + (x − y) = 0 ⇒ dx + dy + dz = 0 ⇒ **x + y + z = a**
- Multipliers x, y, z: x(y − z) + y(z − x) + z(x − y) = 0 ⇒ x dx + y dy + z dz = 0 ⇒ **x² + y² + z² = b**
- Solution: φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0 (surfaces of revolution about the line x = y = z).

steps.title: Solved: surface through a curve
steps.body:
Find the integral surface of xp + yq = z through the curve x + y = 1, z = 1.

- General: y/x = a, z/x = b.
- On the curve: z = 1 ⇒ x = 1/b; y = a/b; x + y = 1 ⇒ (1 + a)/b = 1 ⇒ b = 1 + a.
- Substitute: z/x = 1 + y/x ⇒ **z = x + y** (a plane).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing multipliers that make the denominator zero but leave a non-exact numerator.
- In the curve problem, forgetting to eliminate x, y, z using all the curve's equations.

activity.prompt: The integral surface of xp + yq = z through the curve x + y = 1, z = 1 is z = x + y. Find z at (2, 3).

quiz.q: For x(y² − z²)p + y(z² − x²)q = z(x² − y²), multipliers 1/x, 1/y, 1/z give:
quiz.why: The denominator becomes (y² − z²) + (z² − x²) + (x² − y²) = 0, so dx/x + dy/y + dz/z = 0, i.e. ln(xyz) = c.

quiz.q: Multipliers are chosen so that lP + mQ + nR equals:
quiz.why: A zero denominator forces the numerator l dx + m dy + n dz to vanish, which gives an integrable relation.

quiz.q: With multipliers x, y, z giving x dx + y dy + z dz = 0, the integral is:
quiz.why: Integrating gives (x² + y² + z²)/2 = c, i.e. a sphere centred at the origin.

questions.q: p stands for:
questions.why: Standard notation p = ∂z/∂x.

questions.q: xp + yq = z is of order:
questions.why: Only first derivatives appear.

questions.q: Eliminating a, b from z = ax + by + a² + b² gives:
questions.why: p = a, q = b, so substitute back.

questions.q: z = f(x + y) satisfies:
questions.why: p = f′ and q = f′.

questions.q: Auxiliary equations for Pp + Qq = R:
options: P dx = Q dy = R dz
questions.why: This is Lagrange's system.

questions.q: General solution of xp + yq = z:
questions.why: Integrals y/x = a and z/x = b.

questions.q: For yzp + zxq = xy, one integral is:
questions.why: x dx = y dy integrates to x² − y² = a.

questions.q: Multipliers 1, 1, 1 work when:
questions.why: Then dx + dy + dz = 0, giving x + y + z = a.

questions.q: Solution of p + q = 1:
questions.why: Integrals x − y = a and z − x = b.

questions.q: z = f(x² − y²) satisfies:
questions.why: p = 2xf′, q = −2yf′, so yp + xq = 0.

questions.q: Integral surface of p + q = 1 through z = 0 on the line y = 0 is:
questions.why: z = x + f(x − y); on y = 0, 0 = x + f(x) ⇒ f(u) = −u, so z = x − (x − y) = y.

questions.q: zp + zq = 1 is:
questions.why: Coefficients of p and q contain z.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Non-linear first-order PDEs: standard forms and Charpit's method
courses.summary: Complete, general and singular integrals; the four standard forms f(p, q) = 0, f(z, p, q) = 0, separable f(x, p) = g(y, q) and Clairaut's form; Charpit's general method with its auxiliary equations.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish complete, general and singular integrals
Learners can solve equations of standard forms I–III
Learners can find complete and singular integrals of Clairaut's equation
Learners can write Charpit's auxiliary equations and solve problems with them

lessons.title: Kinds of integrals; forms f(p, q) = 0 and f(z, p, q) = 0

scenes.text: The eikonal equation p² + q² = 1 describes wavefronts of light moving at unit speed.
Its complete integral is a family of planes — one for each direction of travel.

steps.title: Types of integrals of f(x, y, z, p, q) = 0
steps.body:
- **Complete integral**: F(x, y, z, a, b) = 0 with two arbitrary constants.
- **General integral**: put b = φ(a) and eliminate a between F = 0 and ∂F/∂a = 0.
- **Singular integral**: eliminate a, b from F = 0, ∂F/∂a = 0, ∂F/∂b = 0 (the envelope of the family), if it satisfies the PDE.

steps.title: Form I: f(p, q) = 0
steps.body: Try z = ax + by + c with f(a, b) = 0. Solve for b = g(a): complete integral z = ax + g(a)y + c.

steps.title: Form II: f(z, p, q) = 0
steps.body: Put u = x + ay, z = z(u): p = dz/du, q = a·dz/du. The PDE becomes an ODE in z(u).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In Form II forgetting the factor a in q = a dz/du.
- Reporting a 'singular integral' without checking that it satisfies the PDE.

activity.prompt: Which standard form does each equation belong to?
buckets: Form III f(x, p) = g(y, q)

quiz.q: A complete integral contains:
options: as many arbitrary constants as independent variables
quiz.why: For z(x, y) it has two arbitrary constants, matching the two independent variables.

quiz.q: For p + q = pq, with p = a the value of q is:
quiz.why: a + b = ab gives b(a − 1) = a, so b = a/(a − 1).

quiz.q: In Form II, the substitution is:
quiz.why: Taking u = x + ay reduces f(z, p, q) = 0 to an ODE for z(u).

scenes.text: When x appears only with p and y only with q, each side must equal the same constant.
Clairaut's form gives a family of planes and, often, an envelope surface.

steps.title: Form III: f(x, p) = g(y, q)
steps.body: Set f(x, p) = a = g(y, q). Solve p = F(x, a), q = G(y, a). Then dz = p dx + q dy ⇒ z = ∫F dx + ∫G dy + b.

steps.title: Solved: p − x² = q + y²
steps.body:
Both sides = a: p = x² + a, q = a − y².

**z = x³/3 + ax + ay − y³/3 + b**

steps.title: Form IV: Clairaut z = px + qy + f(p, q)
steps.body: Complete integral: **z = ax + by + f(a, b)**. Singular integral: eliminate a, b using x + f_a = 0, y + f_b = 0.

steps.title: Solved: z = px + qy + pq
steps.body:
- Complete: z = ax + by + ab
- ∂/∂a: x + b = 0; ∂/∂b: y + a = 0 ⇒ a = −y, b = −x
- Singular: z = −xy − xy + xy = **−xy**. Check: p = −y, q = −x; px + qy + pq = −xy − xy + xy = −xy ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In Form III, using different constants for the two sides.
- Forgetting to verify the singular integral.

activity.prompt: The singular integral of z = px + qy + p² + q² is z = −(x² + y²)/4. Evaluate it at (2, 2).

quiz.q: Complete integral of z = px + qy + p²q²:
quiz.why: In Clairaut's form you simply replace p and q by constants a and b.

quiz.q: For p = 2qx (separable form), write p/x = 2q. Then q = ?
quiz.why: Setting p/x = 2q = a gives q = a/2 (and p = ax).

quiz.q: The singular integral is geometrically the:
quiz.why: Eliminating a, b with ∂F/∂a = ∂F/∂b = 0 gives the envelope of the two-parameter family.

scenes.text: px + qy = pq fits none of the four standard forms.
Charpit's method finds a second relation between p and q, then integrates dz = p dx + q dy.

steps.title: Charpit's auxiliary equations
steps.body:
For f(x, y, z, p, q) = 0:

dp/(f_x + p f_z) = dq/(f_y + q f_z) = dz/(−p f_p − q f_q) = dx/(−f_p) = dy/(−f_q).

Find any simple integral involving p or q, solve it with f = 0 for p and q, then integrate dz = p dx + q dy.

steps.title: Solved: px + qy = pq
steps.body:
f = px + qy − pq: f_x = p, f_y = q, f_z = 0, f_p = x − q, f_q = y − p.

- dp/p = dq/q ⇒ **p = aq**
- Substitute: aqx + qy = aq² ⇒ q = (ax + y)/a, p = ax + y
- dz = (ax + y)dx + ((ax + y)/a)dy = (1/a)(ax + y)d(ax + y)
- **z = (ax + y)²/(2a) + b**

steps.title: Decision guide
steps.body:
1. Linear in p, q? ⇒ Lagrange.
2. Only p, q? ⇒ Form I.
3. z, p, q only? ⇒ Form II (u = x + ay).
4. x with p, y with q separately? ⇒ Form III.
5. z = px + qy + f(p, q)? ⇒ Clairaut.
6. None ⇒ Charpit.

steps.title: Solved: p²z² + q² = 1 (reducible)
steps.body: Put Z = z²/2 so ∂Z/∂x = zp: equation becomes P² + q²… careful — only p carries z. Write P = zp = ∂Z/∂x; then P² + q² = 1 is Form I in (P, q) for Z(x, y)? Not quite: q = ∂z/∂y, not ∂Z/∂y. Use instead Form II: u = x + ay: z²(z′)² + a²(z′)² = 1 ⇒ √(z² + a²) dz = du, integrate: (z/2)√(z² + a²) + (a²/2)ln(z + √(z² + a²)) = x + ay + b.

steps.title: Solved: p = 2qx
steps.body: Form III: p/x = 2q = a ⇒ p = ax, q = a/2 ⇒ **z = ax²/2 + ay/2 + b**.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Second-order linear PDEs: classification and constant coefficients
courses.summary: Classification of Ar + Bs + Ct + … = 0 into hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic types, reduction to canonical forms, homogeneous linear PDEs with constant coefficients (complementary function for distinct and repeated roots) and particular integrals for exponential, trigonometric and polynomial right-hand sides.
outcomes: Learners can classify second-order PDEs using B² − 4AC
Learners can reduce hyperbolic equations to canonical form
Learners can find the complementary function of homogeneous constant-coefficient PDEs
Learners can find particular integrals for eˣ⁺ʸ-type, sine/cosine and polynomial terms
Learners can write the complete solution z = CF + PI

scenes.text: A plucked string, a cooling rod and a soap film obey three different second-order PDEs.
The sign of B² − 4AC sorts them: hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
For A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + (lower-order terms) = 0 at a point:

- B² − 4AC > 0: **hyperbolic** (wave equation u_tt = c²u_xx)
- B² − 4AC = 0: **parabolic** (heat equation u_t = k u_xx)
- B² − 4AC < 0: **elliptic** (Laplace u_xx + u_yy = 0)

If A, B, C depend on x, y, the type can change from region to region.

steps.title: Canonical form (hyperbolic case)
steps.body: Solve the characteristic equation A(dy)² − B dx dy + C(dx)² = 0, i.e. A λ² − Bλ + C = 0 with λ = dy/dx. Its two families of characteristic curves ξ = const, η = const turn the equation into u_ξη = (lower-order terms).

steps.title: Solved: classifying
steps.body:
- u_xx − 4u_xy + 4u_yy = 0: 16 − 16 = 0 ⇒ **parabolic**
- u_xx + u_xy + u_yy = 0: 1 − 4 < 0 ⇒ **elliptic**
- Tricomi y u_xx + u_yy = 0: B² − 4AC = −4y ⇒ elliptic for y > 0, parabolic on y = 0, hyperbolic for y < 0.

steps.title: Solved: wave equation to canonical form
steps.body: u_xx − u_yy = 0: λ² − 1 = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = ±1 ⇒ ξ = x + y, η = x − y. Then u_xx = u_ξξ + 2u_ξη + u_ηη, u_yy = u_ξξ − 2u_ξη + u_ηη ⇒ 4u_ξη = 0 ⇒ **u_ξη = 0**, so u = f(x + y) + g(x − y).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using B² − AC (that is for the form A u_xx + 2B u_xy + C u_yy).
- Forgetting that variable coefficients can change the type.

lessons.title: Homogeneous equations with constant coefficients: CF

scenes.text: Writing D = ∂/∂x and D′ = ∂/∂y turns PDEs into polynomials.
Factorising the polynomial gives the solution almost immediately.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For (a₀Dⁿ + a₁Dⁿ⁻¹D′ + … + aₙD′ⁿ)z = 0, put D = m, D′ = 1 to get the **auxiliary equation** a₀mⁿ + a₁mⁿ⁻¹ + … + aₙ = 0.

- Distinct roots m₁, m₂, …: CF = f₁(y + m₁x) + f₂(y + m₂x) + …
- Root m repeated twice: f₁(y + mx) + x f₂(y + mx); thrice: add x² f₃(y + mx).

steps.title: Solved: repeated root
steps.body:
(D² − 2DD′ + D′²)z = 0: (m − 1)² = 0 ⇒ m = 1 twice.

**z = f₁(y + x) + x f₂(y + x)**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing f(x + my) instead of f(y + mx) with this convention.
- Forgetting the factor x for repeated roots.

quiz.why: (m + 2)² = 0 gives m = −2 twice, so the second function picks up a factor x.

steps.title: Standard rules for F(D, D′)z = φ(x, y)
steps.body:
- φ = e^{ax+by}: PI = e^{ax+by}/F(a, b), if F(a, b) ≠ 0.
- φ = sin(ax + by) or cos(ax + by) (F homogeneous of degree 2): replace D² → −a², DD′ → −ab, D′² → −b².
- φ = xᵐyⁿ: PI = [F(D, D′)]⁻¹xᵐyⁿ, expand in powers of D/D′ or D′/D.
- General φ: for a factor (D − mD′), PI = ∫φ(x, c − mx)dx, then put c = y + mx.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Wave and heat equations
courses.summary: Derivation of the one-dimensional wave equation, d'Alembert's solution, separation of variables for the vibrating string with fixed ends, normal modes and Fourier sine series, the one-dimensional heat equation, steady-state temperature and transient solutions.
outcomes: Learners can derive the wave equation u_tt = c²u_xx for a stretched string

lessons.title: The wave equation and d'Alembert's solution

scenes.text: A sitar string is pulled and released; ripples run both ways along it.
d'Alembert showed the motion is exactly two waves travelling in opposite directions.

steps.title: Derivation (sketch)
steps.body:
A string with tension T and mass per unit length ρ, small transverse displacement u(x, t). On an element dx, the net vertical force is T(sin θ₂ − sin θ₁) ≈ T(u_x(x + dx) − u_x(x)) ≈ T u_xx dx. Newton: ρ dx · u_tt = T u_xx dx ⇒

**u_tt = c² u_xx, c = √(T/ρ)** (wave speed, m/s).

steps.title: d'Alembert's formula
steps.body:
With ξ = x + ct, η = x − ct the equation becomes u_ξη = 0, so u = F(x + ct) + G(x − ct). For u(x, 0) = f(x), u_t(x, 0) = g(x) on −∞ < x < ∞:

u(x, t) = [f(x + ct) + f(x − ct)]/2 + (1/(2c))∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct} g(s) ds.

steps.title: Solved: released from rest
steps.body: f(x) = sin x, g = 0: u = [sin(x + ct) + sin(x − ct)]/2 = **sin x cos ct**.

steps.title: Solved: struck string
steps.body: f = 0, g(x) = cos x: u = (1/(2c))[sin(x + ct) − sin(x − ct)] = **(1/c) cos x sin ct**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/2 in front of f-terms or the 1/(2c) in front of the integral.
- Using d'Alembert on a finite string without extending f, g as odd periodic functions.

lessons.title: Vibrating string by separation of variables

scenes.text: A guitar string sounds a fundamental note plus fainter overtones.
Separation of variables reveals them as the normal modes sin(nπx/L).

steps.title: Problem and separation
steps.body:
u_tt = c²u_xx, 0 < x < L; u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0; u(x, 0) = f(x), u_t(x, 0) = g(x).

Put u = X(x)T(t): X″/X = T″/(c²T) = −λ. Boundary conditions force λ = (nπ/L)², Xₙ = sin(nπx/L).

steps.title: Solution
steps.body:
u(x, t) = Σ [Aₙ cos(nπct/L) + Bₙ sin(nπct/L)] sin(nπx/L), with

- Aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx
- Bₙ = (2/(nπc))∫₀ᴸ g(x) sin(nπx/L) dx

Natural frequencies fₙ = nc/(2L) Hz; the fundamental is f₁ = c/(2L).

steps.title: Solved: one mode
steps.body: f(x) = 3 sin(πx/L), g = 0: only A₁ = 3 ⇒ **u = 3 sin(πx/L) cos(πct/L)**.

steps.title: Solved: two modes
steps.body: f(x) = sin(πx/L) + 0.5 sin(3πx/L), g = 0 ⇒ u = sin(πx/L)cos(πct/L) + 0.5 sin(3πx/L)cos(3πct/L).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing λ ≤ 0: it only gives the trivial solution with fixed ends.
- Forgetting the factor nπc/L when computing Bₙ from g.

lessons.title: The heat equation in a rod

scenes.text: A blacksmith dips both ends of a hot rod in ice water.
Each Fourier mode of the temperature decays exponentially — fast for high modes.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body: u_t = k u_xx, k = K/(ρ s) is the thermal diffusivity (m²/s), from Fourier's law and energy balance. Parabolic type.

steps.title: Ends at zero temperature
steps.body:
u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0, u(x, 0) = f(x). Separation u = X T gives T′/(kT) = X″/X = −(nπ/L)²:

u(x, t) = Σ Bₙ sin(nπx/L) e^{−k n²π² t/L²}, Bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.

steps.title: Solved: one mode
steps.body: f(x) = 5 sin(πx/L) ⇒ **u = 5 sin(πx/L) e^{−kπ²t/L²}**. With L = 1 m, k = 10⁻⁴ m²/s, the amplitude halves when kπ²t = ln 2 ⇒ t ≈ 0.693/(9.87 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ **702 s**.

steps.title: Solved: steady state and transient
steps.body: Ends held at 20 °C and 80 °C, L = 10 cm. Steady state u_xx = 0 ⇒ **u_s = 20 + 6x** (°C, x in cm). The full solution is u = u_s + v, where v solves the zero-end problem with v(x, 0) = f(x) − u_s(x).

steps.title: Problem
