lessons.title: Sample spaces, events and the axioms

story.title: Rain or shine at the Test match

scenes.text: A commentator says there is a 70% chance of play today. What exactly is that number measuring?
Kolmogorov gave three simple axioms; every probability rule follows from them.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Random experiment**: outcome not known in advance, but set of possible outcomes is known.
- **Sample space S**: set of all outcomes. Toss two coins: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
- **Event**: a subset of S. Mutually exclusive events: A ∩ B = ∅. Exhaustive: A ∪ B ∪ … = S.
- **Classical definition**: P(A) = (favourable outcomes)/(total equally likely outcomes).
- **Axioms (Kolmogorov)**: (i) P(A) ≥ 0; (ii) P(S) = 1; (iii) for pairwise disjoint A₁, A₂, …, P(∪Aᵢ) = ΣP(Aᵢ).

steps.title: Consequences of the axioms
steps.body:
- P(∅) = 0
- P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) (since A and Aᶜ are disjoint with union S)
- A ⊆ B ⇒ P(A) ≤ P(B)
- **Addition theorem**: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Proof: A ∪ B = A ∪ (B ∖ A), disjoint, and P(B ∖ A) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
- Three events: P(A∪B∪C) = ΣP(A) − ΣP(A∩B) + P(A∩B∩C).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive without subtracting the overlap.
- Treating 'sum = 7' outcomes (3,4) and (4,3) as one outcome — the dice are distinguishable.
- Using the classical definition when outcomes are not equally likely.

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.35, then P(Aᶜ) is:
quiz.why: Because A and its complement are disjoint and together form S, P(Aᶜ) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Kolmogorov's axioms?
quiz.why: The product rule holds only for independent events; it is a definition, not an axiom of probability.

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive A, B with P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.3, P(A ∪ B) =
quiz.why: Mutually exclusive events have P(A ∩ B) = 0, so the addition theorem gives 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5.

Knowledge of the first draw shrinks the sample space — that is conditional probability.

steps.title: Definition and multiplication rule
steps.body:
- P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), for P(B) > 0.
- **Multiplication rule**: P(A ∩ B) = P(B)·P(A | B) = P(A)·P(B | A).
- Chain rule: P(A₁A₂A₃) = P(A₁)P(A₂|A₁)P(A₃|A₁A₂).
- **Independence**: A, B independent iff P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).
- A, B, C mutually independent needs all pairwise products AND P(ABC) = P(A)P(B)P(C).

steps.title: Solved: two kings without replacement
steps.body:
- P(K₁) = 4/52, P(K₂ | K₁) = 3/51
- P(both kings) = (4/52)(3/51) = 12/2652 = **1/221 ≈ 0.00452**
- With replacement they are independent: (4/52)² = 1/169.

steps.body: A hits a target with probability 0.6, B with 0.7, independently. P(target hit) = 1 − P(both miss) = 1 − (0.4)(0.3) = 1 − 0.12 = **0.88**.

steps.title: Independent ≠ mutually exclusive
steps.body: If A and B are mutually exclusive with positive probabilities, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B), so they are dependent: knowing A happened tells you B did not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A).
- Assuming pairwise independence implies mutual independence.
- Forgetting to reduce the deck after a draw without replacement.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
Let B₁, …, Bₙ be a partition of S with P(Bᵢ) > 0.

- **Total probability**: P(A) = Σ P(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ).
- **Bayes' theorem**: P(Bₖ | A) = P(Bₖ)P(A | Bₖ) / Σ P(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ).
- P(Bᵢ) are **prior** probabilities; P(Bₖ | A) are **posterior** probabilities.
- Proof: P(Bₖ | A) = P(Bₖ ∩ A)/P(A); numerator by multiplication rule, denominator by total probability.

steps.title: Solved: a medical test
steps.body:
Prevalence 1%, sensitivity P(+ | disease) = 0.95, false-positive rate P(+ | healthy) = 0.05.

- P(+) = 0.01(0.95) + 0.99(0.05) = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059
- P(disease | +) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ **0.161**

Only about 16% of positives are truly ill — the base rate dominates.

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: Spam filters, medical screening, reliability analysis and fault diagnosis all update prior beliefs with evidence using Bayes' rule.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the prior (base-rate fallacy).
- Using events that do not form a partition.
- Forgetting that posteriors must sum to 1 — a quick check.

lessons.title: Discrete random variables, pmf and cdf

scenes.text: A board-game designer wants the chance of getting 0, 1 or 2 sixes in two rolls.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A **random variable** X is a function X: S → ℝ.
- Discrete X: pmf p(x) = P(X = x) with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σp(x) = 1.
- **CDF**: F(x) = P(X ≤ x); non-decreasing, right-continuous, F(−∞) = 0, F(∞) = 1.
- P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). For discrete X, F is a step function with jumps p(x).

- Writing P(X < b) = F(b) for discrete X (that is P(X ≤ b)).
- Accepting a 'pmf' with a negative value.

steps.title: Definitions

- Continuous X has pdf f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫f(x)dx = 1 over ℝ.

steps.title: Definitions and properties

- E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) always; E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) if independent.
- Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
- Raw moments μ′ᵣ = E(Xʳ); central moments μᵣ = E[(X − μ)ʳ]; μ₂ = μ′₂ − μ′₁².
- Skewness β₁ = μ₃²/μ₂³, kurtosis β₂ = μ₄/μ₂² (β₂ = 3 for the normal).

steps.title: MGF
steps.body:
- M_X(t) = E(e^{tX}), when it exists near t = 0.
- μ′ᵣ = M⁽ʳ⁾(0): differentiate r times and put t = 0.
- M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at); for independent X, Y: M_{X+Y} = M_X·M_Y.
- Uniqueness: an MGF determines the distribution.

steps.title: Solved: Bernoulli MGF
steps.body:
X = 1 w.p. p, 0 w.p. q = 1 − p.

- M(t) = q + pe^t
- M′(0) = p ⇒ E(X) = p; M″(0) = p ⇒ E(X²) = p
- Var = p − p² = **pq**

steps.title: Chebyshev's inequality
steps.body:
For any X with mean μ and variance σ², and k > 0:

P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k²

Proof idea: σ² = E(X − μ)² ≥ k²σ²·P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Chebyshev with k ≤ 1 (bound is useless).
- Differentiating the MGF but forgetting to set t = 0.
- Assuming every distribution has an MGF (Cauchy does not).

story.title: Quality check at the bulb factory

scenes.text: 10% of bulbs from a line are defective; an inspector picks 5 at random.
Each bulb is a Bernoulli trial — the count of defectives is binomial.

steps.title: Definition and moments
steps.body:
- n independent trials, each success with probability p (q = 1 − p).
- P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, r = 0, 1, …, n.
- Mean np, variance npq (so variance < mean), MGF (q + pe^t)ⁿ.
- Mode: the integer part of (n + 1)p (two modes if (n + 1)p is an integer).
- Recurrence: P(r + 1) = [(n − r)/(r + 1)]·(p/q)·P(r).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using binomial when trials are dependent (sampling without replacement from a small lot — that is hypergeometric).
- Claiming mean 3, variance 4 for a binomial: impossible, since q = 4/3 > 1.

scenes.text: A bank helpline receives on average 3 calls per minute.
Rare, independent events in a fixed interval follow a Poisson law.

steps.title: Poisson
steps.body:
- P(X = r) = e^{−λ}λʳ/r!, r = 0, 1, 2, …
- Mean = variance = λ; MGF exp[λ(e^t − 1)].
- **Limit of binomial**: n → ∞, p → 0, np = λ fixed.
- Sum of independent Poisson(λ₁), Poisson(λ₂) is Poisson(λ₁ + λ₂).
- Recurrence: P(r + 1) = λ/(r + 1)·P(r).

steps.title: Solved: Poisson approximation
steps.body: 1% of screws are defective; box of 200. λ = np = 2. P(no defective) ≈ e^{−2} ≈ 0.135 (exact 0.99²⁰⁰ ≈ 0.134).

steps.title: Geometric
steps.body: X = number of failures before the first success: P(X = r) = qʳp, r = 0, 1, …; mean q/p, variance q/p². It is the only discrete memoryless distribution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Poisson when the mean is not equal to the variance in the data.
- Forgetting to scale λ to the interval (3 per minute ⇒ 6 per 2 minutes).

steps.title: Properties

- Symmetric about μ; mean = median = mode; points of inflection at μ ± σ.
- Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1); Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z).
- Empirical rule: about 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73% within 1, 2, 3σ.
- MGF exp(μt + σ²t²/2); sums of independent normals are normal.

steps.title: Definitions

- **Uniform U(a, b)**: f = 1/(b − a); mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12.
- **Exponential(λ)**: f(x) = λe^{−λx}, x ≥ 0; F(x) = 1 − e^{−λx}; mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ².
- **Memoryless**: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
- If arrivals are Poisson with rate λ, inter-arrival times are exponential(λ).

steps.title: Solved: LED life
steps.body:
Mean life 2 years ⇒ λ = 0.5 per year.

- P(lasts more than 2 years) = e^{−1} ≈ **0.368**
- P(fails in first year) = 1 − e^{−0.5} ≈ **0.393**
- Given it survived 3 years, P(survives 2 more) = e^{−1} ≈ 0.368 (memoryless).

scenes.text: A teacher records both the minimum and the maximum of two dice rolls.
These two variables move together — covariance measures how.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Joint pmf p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y); marginal p_X(x) = Σ_y p(x, y).
- X, Y independent iff p(x, y) = p_X(x)p_Y(y) for all x, y.
- **Cov(X, Y)** = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y).
- Var(X ± Y) = Var X + Var Y ± 2Cov(X, Y).
- Independent ⇒ Cov = 0; the converse is false (X uniform on {−1, 0, 1}, Y = X²).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding independence from zero covariance.
- Forgetting the 2Cov term in Var(X + Y).

activity.prompt: E(X) = 2, E(Y) = 3, E(XY) = 7.5. Find Cov(X, Y).

quiz.q: Cov(X, Y) = 0 implies:
quiz.why: Zero covariance means no linear relationship, but a non-linear dependence such as Y = X² can still exist.

quiz.q: Var(X − Y) for independent X, Y with variances 4 and 9:
quiz.why: Independence removes the covariance term, and variances add even for a difference: 4 + 9 = 13.

quiz.q: The marginal pmf of X is obtained by:
quiz.why: P(X = x) = Σ_y P(X = x, Y = y) by the law of total probability.

scenes.text: A tutor notes study hours and test scores for five students.
Pearson's r summarises the straight-line association in a single number between −1 and 1.

steps.title: Formula and properties
steps.body:
- r = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) = Σdxdy/√(Σdx²·Σdy²), with dx = x − x̄, dy = y − ȳ.
- −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 (Cauchy–Schwarz); |r| = 1 iff points lie on a line.
- r is unchanged by change of origin and scale (up to sign): r(aX + b, cY + d) = sign(ac)·r(X, Y).
- Probable error PE = 0.6745(1 − r²)/√n.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading correlation as causation.
- Getting |r| > 1 — always a calculation error.
- Using r for clearly curved relationships.

quiz.why: |r| = 1 only when all points lie exactly on a line, and the minus sign means the line slopes downward.

quiz.q: r is a pure number because:
quiz.why: The units of X and Y appear in both numerator and denominator, so r has no units.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
- ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)), d = difference of ranks.
- −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1. Equal to Pearson's r computed on the ranks.
- **Ties**: give average ranks and add (m³ − m)/12 to Σd² for each group of m tied values.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the tie correction.
- Using n² instead of n(n² − 1) in the denominator.

steps.title: Two lines
steps.body:

- **x on y**: x − x̄ = b_xy(y − ȳ), b_xy = r σ_x/σ_y = Sxy/Syy.
- Both pass through (x̄, ȳ); r² = b_yx·b_xy; r has the sign of the coefficients.
- Normal equations for y = a + bx: Σy = na + bΣx, Σxy = aΣx + bΣx².
- The lines coincide iff r = ±1; perpendicular iff r = 0.

lessons.title: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem

scenes.text: A mill's 5 kg rice bags vary in weight; an inspector weighs 25 bags a day.
Daily averages vary far less than single bags, and they look normal — the CLT at work.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Parameter**: population constant (μ, σ, P). **Statistic**: computed from a sample (x̄, s, p̂).
- Sampling distribution of x̄: mean μ, **standard error** σ/√n (with replacement / large population).
- **CLT**: for i.i.d. Xᵢ with mean μ and finite variance σ², (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) → N(0, 1) as n → ∞.
- Proportion: p̂ has mean P and SE √(PQ/n).
- Weak law of large numbers: x̄ → μ in probability.

steps.title: Solved: halving the SE
steps.body: To halve the standard error you must quadruple n, because SE ∝ 1/√n: n = 25 → 100.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ instead of σ/√n for the spread of x̄.
- Thinking the CLT makes the population itself normal — it is about the sample mean.

activity.prompt: A population has σ = 12. What is the standard error of the mean for n = 36?

quiz.q: SE of x̄ for σ = 15, n = 9:
The CLT requires the population to be:
quiz.why: The classical CLT needs i.i.d. observations with finite variance; the population itself can have any shape.

quiz.q: Which is a statistic?
quiz.why: x̄ is computed from the sample, whereas μ, σ and P describe the whole population.

story.title: How long do phone batteries last?

scenes.text: A reviewer tests 64 phones and finds an average battery life of 72 hours.
A single number is a point estimate; a confidence interval shows the uncertainty.

steps.title: Estimators
steps.body:
- **Unbiased**: E(θ̂) = θ. x̄ is unbiased for μ; s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased for σ².
- **Consistent**: θ̂ → θ as n → ∞. **Efficient**: smallest variance among unbiased estimators. **Sufficient**: uses all information about θ.
- Maximum likelihood: maximise L(θ) = Πf(xᵢ; θ). For Poisson, the MLE of λ is x̄.

steps.title: Confidence interval for μ
steps.body:
- σ known or n large: x̄ ± z_{α/2}·σ/√n (z = 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%).
- σ unknown, small n, normal population: x̄ ± t_{α/2, n−1}·s/√n.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'μ lies in this interval with probability 0.95' — μ is fixed; 95% of such intervals cover μ.
- Dividing by n instead of n − 1 for the unbiased sample variance.

activity.prompt: x̄ = 150, σ = 20, n = 100. Find the upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for μ.

quiz.q: An unbiased estimator of σ² divides Σ(x − x̄)² by:
quiz.why: Using n − 1 corrects for estimating the mean from the same data, giving E(s²) = σ².

quiz.q: Raising confidence from 95% to 99% makes the interval:
quiz.why: A higher confidence level needs a larger critical value (2.576 vs 1.96), so the interval widens.

quiz.q: The MLE of λ for a Poisson sample is:
quiz.why: Setting the derivative of the log-likelihood Σxᵢ ln λ − nλ to zero gives λ̂ = x̄.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing and large-sample z tests

scenes.text: A biscuit packet claims 500 g. A consumer group weighs 36 packets: mean 495 g.
Is a 5 g shortfall chance, or evidence of under-filling? A z test decides.

steps.title: Framework
steps.body:
- **H₀** (null): no difference, e.g. μ = 500. **H₁**: μ ≠ 500 (two-tailed) or μ < 500 (left-tailed).
- **Type I error**: reject a true H₀ (probability α, the level of significance). **Type II**: accept a false H₀ (probability β); power = 1 − β.
- Test statistic z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n).
- Critical values: 5% two-tailed ±1.96; 5% one-tailed 1.645; 1% two-tailed ±2.576.

steps.title: Solved: biscuit packets
steps.body:
μ₀ = 500, x̄ = 495, σ = 12, n = 36 ⇒ SE = 2.

- z = (495 − 500)/2 = **−2.5**
- Left-tailed at 5%: −2.5 < −1.645 ⇒ **reject H₀**: packets are under-filled.

steps.title: Solved: a proportion
steps.body: A coin gives 60 heads in 100 tosses. H₀: P = 0.5. SE = √(0.25/100) = 0.05; z = 0.1/0.05 = 2 > 1.96 ⇒ reject H₀ at 5% (two-tailed); the coin appears biased.

steps.title: Solved: two means
steps.body: Two colleges: n₁ = 100, x̄₁ = 68, σ₁ = 10; n₂ = 100, x̄₂ = 65, σ₂ = 10. SE = √(1 + 1) ≈ 1.414; z = 3/1.414 ≈ 2.12 > 1.96 ⇒ significant difference at 5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the claim to be proved as H₀.
- Using a two-tailed critical value for a one-sided question.
- Saying 'H₀ is proved true' — we only fail to reject it.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of a test of significance in order.
items: State H₀ and H₁
Choose the level of significance α
Compute the test statistic from the sample
Find the critical value from the table
Compare and decide to reject or not reject H₀
State the conclusion in context

quiz.q: A type I error is:
quiz.why: Type I error means rejecting H₀ when it is actually true, and its probability is α.

quiz.q: Critical value for a 5% right-tailed z test:
quiz.why: For one tail, all 5% sits on one side, so the cut-off is Φ⁻¹(0.95) = 1.645.

quiz.q: z = 1.5 in a two-tailed 5% test leads to:
quiz.why: |1.5| is less than 1.96, so the result is not significant at 5%.

scenes.text: W. S. Gosset, working at a brewery, had only a handful of samples per batch.
Publishing as 'Student', he found the exact distribution of the small-sample mean ratio.

steps.title: t distribution
steps.body:
- If the population is normal and σ unknown: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with ν = n − 1 degrees of freedom, s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1).
- t is symmetric, heavier-tailed than normal, tends to N(0, 1) as ν → ∞.
- Two independent samples (equal variances): t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/(S√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)), S² = [Σ(x − x̄₁)² + Σ(y − x̄₂)²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2).
- Paired t: work with differences d, t = d̄/(s_d/√n).

steps.title: Solved: paired t
steps.body:
Weights before/after a diet for 5 people give d = 2, 3, 1, 4, 0. d̄ = 2, s_d² = (0 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 4)/4 = 2.5, s_d ≈ 1.581.

t = 2/(1.581/√5) = 2/0.707 ≈ **2.83**; t₀.₀₅,₄ one-tailed = 2.132 ⇒ the diet reduces weight (5% level).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using n instead of n − 1 for the degrees of freedom.
- Using an independent-samples t test on paired data.

activity.prompt: n = 16, x̄ = 41.5, s = 6, H₀: μ = 40. Compute t.

quiz.why: One degree of freedom is used up by estimating the mean, so ν = n − 1 = 11.

quiz.q: As ν → ∞ the t distribution approaches:
quiz.why: Its heavier tails shrink as s becomes a precise estimate of σ, and it tends to N(0, 1).

quiz.why: For the pooled two-sample t test ν = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 16.

lessons.title: Chi-square test of goodness of fit and independence

scenes.text: A die rolled 60 times shows 8, 12, 9, 11, 6, 14 for faces 1 to 6.
χ² compares observed and expected counts across all faces at once.

steps.title: The statistic
steps.body:
- χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
- Goodness of fit: ν = k − 1 − (number of parameters estimated).
- Independence in an r × c table: E = (row total × column total)/N, ν = (r − 1)(c − 1).
- Conditions: expected frequencies at least 5 (pool small classes).

steps.title: Solved: the die
steps.body:
E = 10 each. (O − E)²: 4, 4, 1, 1, 16, 16 ⇒ χ² = 42/10 = **4.2**.

ν = 5, χ²₀.₀₅ = 11.07 ⇒ 4.2 < 11.07 ⇒ the die is consistent with fairness.

steps.title: Solved: 2 × 2 independence

courses.title: Unit 1 · The real number system
courses.summary: ℝ as a complete ordered field: algebraic and order properties, absolute value and inequalities, supremum and infimum, the completeness axiom, the Archimedean property, density of rationals, countability, and the basic topology of ℝ.
outcomes: Manipulate inequalities and absolute values rigorously

scenes.text: An engineering drawing says a bolt is 30 ± 0.2 mm.
That is the statement |x − 30| ≤ 0.2 — absolute value turns tolerances into precise inequalities.

steps.title: Axioms in brief
steps.body:
ℝ is a field (addition and multiplication with the usual laws) with an order < satisfying trichotomy, transitivity, a < b ⇒ a + c < b + c, and a < b, c > 0 ⇒ ac < bc. Completeness (next lesson) distinguishes ℝ from ℚ.

|x| = x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0.

steps.title: Key inequalities
steps.body:
- |ab| = |a||b|; |x| < a ⇔ −a < x < a.
- Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|; reverse: ||a| − |b|| ≤ |a − b|.
- Bernoulli: (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx for x ≥ −1, n ∈ ℕ (induction).
- AM–GM: (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) for a, b ≥ 0, since (√a − √b)² ≥ 0.

steps.title: Solved: proof of the triangle inequality
steps.body: −|a| ≤ a ≤ |a| and −|b| ≤ b ≤ |b|. Adding: −(|a| + |b|) ≤ a + b ≤ |a| + |b|, which is |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. ∎

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying an inequality by a negative number without reversing it.
- Writing |a − b| ≤ |a| − |b| (false; use the reverse triangle inequality).
- Solving |x| > a as −a > x > a (impossible); it is x > a or x < −a.

Which is always true?
quiz.why: This is the reverse triangle inequality, obtained by applying the triangle inequality to a = (a − b) + b.

quiz.q: Bernoulli's inequality states (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx for:

scenes.text: The rationals with x² < 2 creep up towards √2, but no rational number sits at the top.
ℝ fills every such gap — that is the completeness axiom.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For non-empty S ⊆ ℝ:
- u is an upper bound if s ≤ u for all s ∈ S.
- sup S (least upper bound) is an upper bound smaller than every other upper bound; inf S similarly.
- Completeness axiom: every non-empty set bounded above has a supremum in ℝ.
- ε-characterisation: u = sup S ⇔ (i) u is an upper bound and (ii) for every ε > 0 there is s ∈ S with s > u − ε.

steps.title: Solved: S = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ}
steps.body:
- Elements 0, 1/2, 2/3, … ⇒ inf S = 0 (attained at n = 1, so it is the minimum).
- 1 is an upper bound. Given ε > 0, choose n > 1/ε; then 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε. Hence sup S = 1, not attained.

steps.title: Solved: ℚ is not complete
steps.body: A = {x ∈ ℚ : x > 0, x² < 2} is bounded above in ℚ (by 2) but has no rational supremum: if r = p/q were the sup, either r² < 2 (then a slightly larger rational still has square < 2) or r² > 2 (then a slightly smaller rational is still an upper bound); r² = 2 is impossible for rational r. In ℝ, sup A = √2.

steps.title: Useful rules
steps.body:
- sup(A + B) = sup A + sup B.
- sup(cA) = c sup A for c > 0; sup(−A) = −inf A.
- If A ⊆ B, then sup A ≤ sup B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the supremum belongs to the set.
- Forgetting the 'non-empty' hypothesis.
- Proving only that u is an upper bound without showing it is the least one.

activity.prompt: For S = {n/(n + 1) : n ∈ ℕ}, find inf S.

quiz.q: The completeness axiom is what distinguishes ℝ from:
quiz.why: ℚ is also an ordered field, but sets like {x ∈ ℚ : x² < 2} have no rational supremum.

steps.title: Archimedean property
steps.body:
For any x > 0 and y ∈ ℝ there is n ∈ ℕ with nx > y. Equivalently ℕ is not bounded above, and for every ε > 0 there is n with 1/n < ε.

Proof: if ℕ were bounded above, let u = sup ℕ. Then u − 1 is not an upper bound, so some m > u − 1, giving m + 1 > u with m + 1 ∈ ℕ — contradiction. ∎

steps.title: Density of ℚ
steps.body:
Between any two reals a < b there is a rational.

Proof: choose n with 1/n < b − a (Archimedean). Let m be the least integer with m > na. Then m − 1 ≤ na < m, so na < m ≤ na + 1 < nb, i.e. a < m/n < b. ∎

Corollary: irrationals are dense too (apply to a/√2, b/√2 and multiply by √2).

steps.title: Solved: √2 is irrational
steps.body: Suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, hence p is even: p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q² ⇒ q² = 2k² ⇒ q even — contradicting lowest terms. ∎

steps.title: Solved: inf{1/n} = 0
steps.body: 0 is a lower bound. For ε > 0, the Archimedean property gives n with 1/n < ε, so no ε > 0 is a lower bound. Hence inf = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the sum of two irrationals is irrational (√2 + (1 − √2) = 1).
- Using decimals to 'prove' density instead of the Archimedean argument.
- Forgetting that the product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational (true) while the product of two irrationals can be rational.

quiz.q: The product of two irrational numbers is:

lessons.title: Countability and the topology of ℝ

scenes.text: A full hotel with infinitely many rooms can still admit a new guest — everyone moves up one room.
Some infinities can be listed like rooms; the real numbers cannot.

steps.title: Countable and uncountable
steps.body:
- A set is countable if it is finite or in bijection with ℕ.
- ℤ is countable (0, 1, −1, 2, −2, …); ℚ is countable (list p/q by p + q, skipping repeats); a countable union of countable sets is countable.
- ℝ (even (0, 1)) is uncountable — Cantor's diagonal argument: given any list of decimals in (0, 1), build a number whose nth digit differs from the nth digit of the nth number; it is not on the list.

steps.title: Neighbourhoods, open and closed sets
steps.body:
- Neighbourhood of x: a set containing (x − ε, x + ε) for some ε > 0.
- Interior point of S: S is a neighbourhood of it. S is open if every point is interior.
- Limit (accumulation) point of S: every neighbourhood contains a point of S other than x. Derived set S' = set of limit points.
- S is closed if S' ⊆ S; equivalently its complement is open.
- Bolzano–Weierstrass (sets): every bounded infinite subset of ℝ has a limit point.

steps.title: Solved: S = {1/n : n ∈ ℕ}
steps.body:
- Interior: empty (every interval around 1/n contains irrationals not in S) ⇒ S is not open.
- S' = {0}: every (−ε, ε) contains 1/n for large n; points 1/n are isolated.
- 0 ∉ S ⇒ S is not closed. S ∪ {0} is closed.

steps.title: Solved: intervals
steps.body:
- (0, 1) is open; [0, 1] is closed; [0, 1) is neither (interior (0, 1), derived set [0, 1]).
- ℝ and ∅ are both open and closed.
- ℚ has empty interior and derived set ℝ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'not open' means 'closed'.
- Requiring a limit point to belong to the set.
- Believing every infinite set has a limit point (ℕ has none; boundedness is needed).

activity.prompt: How many limit points does S = {1/n : n ∈ ℕ} have?

quiz.q: Which set is uncountable?
quiz.why: Cantor's diagonal argument shows no list can contain every number in (0, 1).

quiz.q: The derived set of ℤ is:
quiz.why: Around each integer there is an interval containing no other integer, and non-integers also have such intervals, so ℤ has no limit points.

quiz.q: A set is closed iff:
options: it contains all its limit points
quiz.why: Closed means S' ⊆ S, equivalently the complement is open.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Sequences of real numbers
courses.summary: Convergence of sequences by ε–N, limit theorems and the squeeze theorem, monotone sequences and recursive limits, subsequences, Bolzano–Weierstrass, limit superior and inferior, and Cauchy sequences.
outcomes: Prove convergence directly from the ε–N definition
Use limit theorems, the squeeze theorem and standard limits
Apply the monotone convergence theorem to recursive sequences
Find subsequential limits, lim sup and lim inf
Use the Cauchy criterion to prove convergence or divergence

scenes.text: An archer's arrows land 1 m, 0.5 m, 0.33 m, 0.25 m … from the centre.
For any target ring, however small, from some arrow on every arrow lands inside it — that is convergence.

steps.title: Definition and first results
steps.body:
(aₙ) → L if for every ε > 0 there is N ∈ ℕ with |aₙ − L| < ε for all n ≥ N.

- Limits are unique.
- Every convergent sequence is bounded (the converse fails: (−1)ⁿ).
- Algebra of limits: aₙ → a, bₙ → b ⇒ aₙ ± bₙ → a ± b, aₙbₙ → ab, aₙ/bₙ → a/b if b ≠ 0.
- Squeeze: aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ cₙ with aₙ, cₙ → L ⇒ bₙ → L.

steps.title: Solved: ε–N proof
steps.body:
Prove n/(n + 1) → 1.

- |n/(n + 1) − 1| = 1/(n + 1).
- 1/(n + 1) < ε ⇔ n > 1/ε − 1.
- Choose N > 1/ε − 1 (Archimedean). Then n ≥ N ⇒ |aₙ − 1| < ε. ∎
- For ε = 0.01 we need n + 1 > 100, i.e. N = 100 works.

steps.title: Solved: squeeze
steps.body: −1/n ≤ sin n/n ≤ 1/n and both bounds → 0, so sin n/n → 0.

steps.title: Standard limits
steps.body:
- aⁿ → 0 if |a| < 1
- n^{1/n} → 1; a^{1/n} → 1 for a > 0
- nᵏ/aⁿ → 0 for a > 1 (exponentials beat powers)
- (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e; (1 + x/n)ⁿ → eˣ
- aⁿ/n! → 0 for every real a

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting N depend on n (it may depend only on ε).
- Assuming bounded ⇒ convergent.
- Splitting lim(aₙbₙ) when one factor diverges (e.g. n·(1/n)).

scenes.text: A balloon keeps rising but never passes a ceiling.
An increasing sequence bounded above must settle at its supremum.

steps.title: Monotone convergence theorem
steps.body:
A monotone sequence converges iff it is bounded. If (aₙ) is increasing and bounded above, aₙ → sup{aₙ}; if decreasing and bounded below, aₙ → inf{aₙ}.

Proof (increasing case): let L = sup{aₙ}. For ε > 0 some a_N > L − ε; for n ≥ N, L − ε < a_N ≤ aₙ ≤ L. ∎

steps.title: Solved: a₁ = √2, aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ)
steps.body:
- Bounded: if aₙ < 2 then aₙ₊₁ < √4 = 2; a₁ < 2, so by induction aₙ < 2.
- Increasing: aₙ₊₁² − aₙ² = 2 + aₙ − aₙ² = (2 − aₙ)(1 + aₙ) > 0.
- So aₙ → L with L = √(2 + L) ⇒ L² − L − 2 = 0 ⇒ L = 2 (L = −1 rejected since aₙ > 0).

steps.title: Solved: (1 + 1/n)ⁿ converges
steps.body: By the binomial theorem, aₙ = Σₖ (1/k!)(1 − 1/n)(1 − 2/n)…(1 − (k − 1)/n). Each term grows with n and there are more terms, so (aₙ) is increasing. Also aₙ ≤ Σ 1/k! ≤ 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … < 3. Hence it converges; its limit is called e.

lessons.title: Subsequences, Bolzano–Weierstrass, lim sup and lim inf

scenes.text: A sequence alternates between cars heading to 1 and cars heading to −1.
Each lane converges even though the full sequence does not — those are subsequences.

steps.title: Definitions and theorems
steps.body:
- A subsequence (a_{n_k}) uses indices n₁ < n₂ < …. If aₙ → L, every subsequence → L.
- Divergence test: two subsequences with different limits ⇒ (aₙ) diverges.
- Every sequence has a monotone subsequence.
- Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.
- lim sup aₙ = largest subsequential limit = lim_{n→∞} sup_{k≥n} a_k; lim inf similarly.
- (aₙ) converges ⇔ it is bounded and lim sup = lim inf.

- Note sup{aₙ} = a₂ = 3/2 ≠ lim sup.

steps.title: Definition and criterion
steps.body:
(aₙ) is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there is N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

- Every convergent sequence is Cauchy (triangle inequality).
- Every Cauchy sequence is bounded.
- Cauchy criterion: in ℝ, a sequence converges ⇔ it is Cauchy (uses Bolzano–Weierstrass, hence completeness). In ℚ this fails: decimal approximations of √2 are Cauchy but have no rational limit.

steps.title: Solved: harmonic partial sums diverge
steps.body:
Hₙ = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n. Then H₂ₙ − Hₙ = 1/(n + 1) + … + 1/(2n) ≥ n·1/(2n) = 1/2.

So for ε = 1/2 no N works: (Hₙ) is not Cauchy and diverges.

- Forgetting that the Cauchy criterion depends on completeness.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Infinite series and convergence tests
courses.summary: Series as limits of partial sums, geometric, telescoping and p-series, the nth-term test, comparison and limit comparison, integral and Cauchy condensation tests, ratio, root and Raabe's tests, and alternating series with absolute and conditional convergence.
outcomes: Sum geometric and telescoping series and apply the nth-term test
Use comparison, limit comparison, integral and condensation tests
Choose and apply the ratio, root or Raabe test
Test alternating series with Leibniz's test and estimate the error
Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence

scenes.text: To cross a 1 km track, a runner covers half, then a quarter, then an eighth …
Infinitely many pieces, yet the total is exactly 1 km — an infinite series can have a finite sum.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Σaₙ converges to S if the partial sums sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ → S.

- nth-term test: Σaₙ converges ⇒ aₙ → 0. So aₙ ↛ 0 ⇒ divergence. (aₙ → 0 is not sufficient.)
- Geometric: Σ_{n=0}^{∞} rⁿ = 1/(1 − r) for |r| < 1, diverges for |r| ≥ 1.
- p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p > 1.

steps.title: Cauchy condensation test
steps.body:
If aₙ ≥ 0 is decreasing, Σaₙ and Σ2ᵏa_{2ᵏ} converge or diverge together.

For aₙ = 1/nᵖ: Σ2ᵏ/2^{kp} = Σ(2^{1−p})ᵏ, geometric with ratio 2^{1−p} < 1 ⇔ p > 1. This proves the p-series result.

steps.title: Solved: nth-term test
steps.body:
Σ n/(n + 1): terms → 1 ≠ 0 ⇒ diverges.
Σ 1/n: terms → 0, yet it diverges (p = 1), so the test is one-way only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding convergence from aₙ → 0.
- Starting the geometric formula at n = 1 without adjusting: Σ_{n=1}^{∞} rⁿ = r/(1 − r).
- Treating p = 1 as convergent.

quiz.why: It is a p-series with p = 1.01 > 1, so it converges (slowly).

quiz.q: Σ cos(1/n) is:
quiz.why: cos(1/n) → 1 ≠ 0, so the terms do not tend to zero and the series diverges.

scenes.text: You cannot sum Σ1/(n² + 1) exactly, but its terms are smaller than 1/n².
If the bigger series converges, the smaller one must too.

steps.title: Tests for non-negative series
steps.body:
- Comparison: 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ. Σbₙ converges ⇒ Σaₙ converges; Σaₙ diverges ⇒ Σbₙ diverges.
- Limit comparison: aₙ, bₙ > 0, aₙ/bₙ → L with 0 < L < ∞ ⇒ both converge or both diverge.
- Integral test: f positive, continuous, decreasing on [1, ∞), aₙ = f(n). Then Σaₙ and ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx converge or diverge together.

steps.title: Solved: comparison
steps.body:
- Σ 1/(n² + 1) ≤ Σ 1/n² ⇒ converges.
- Σ 1/√(n(n + 1)): compare with 1/n: ratio = n/√(n² + n) → 1 ⇒ diverges (limit comparison).

steps.title: Solved: integral test
steps.body:
Σ_{n≥2} 1/(n ln n): ∫₂^∞ dx/(x ln x) = [ln ln x]₂^∞ = ∞ ⇒ diverges.
Σ_{n≥2} 1/(n (ln n)²): ∫ = [−1/ln x]₂^∞ = 1/ln 2 < ∞ ⇒ converges.

steps.title: Solved: choosing bₙ
steps.body: Σ (2n + 1)/(n³ + 4): leading behaviour 2n/n³ = 2/n². With bₙ = 1/n², aₙ/bₙ → 2 ⇒ converges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing in the wrong direction (smaller than a divergent series proves nothing).
- Using the integral test for non-monotone f.
- Getting L = 0 or ∞ in limit comparison and still concluding 'same behaviour'.

activity.prompt: Convergent or divergent?

quiz.why: Limit comparison with 1/n gives ratio → 1/3, and Σ1/n diverges.

quiz.q: In the limit comparison test, if aₙ/bₙ → 0 and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ:
quiz.why: Eventually aₙ ≤ bₙ, so ordinary comparison gives convergence.

quiz.q: The integral test requires f to be positive, continuous and:
quiz.why: Monotone decrease lets the sum be squeezed between integrals of f.

scenes.text: Terms like n!/nⁿ or 3ⁿ/n! mix factorials and powers; comparison is clumsy.
The ratio test looks at how each term compares with the next.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
For positive terms:
- D'Alembert ratio test: L = lim aₙ₊₁/aₙ. L < 1 converges; L > 1 diverges; L = 1 inconclusive.
- Cauchy root test: L = lim aₙ^{1/n} (or lim sup). Same conclusions.
- Raabe's test (when the ratio gives 1): R = lim n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁ − 1). R > 1 converges; R < 1 diverges; R = 1 inconclusive.

steps.title: Solved: ratio test
steps.body:
- Σ n²/2ⁿ: ratio = (n + 1)²/(2n²) → 1/2 < 1 ⇒ converges.
- Σ n!/nⁿ: ratio = (n + 1)nⁿ/(n + 1)^{n+1} = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ → 1/e < 1 ⇒ converges.
- Σ 2ⁿ/n: ratio = 2n/(n + 1) → 2 > 1 ⇒ diverges.

steps.title: Solved: Raabe's test
steps.body:
Σ 1/n²: the ratio → 1. Raabe: n((n + 1)²/n² − 1) = n(2n + 1)/n² = (2n + 1)/n → 2 > 1 ⇒ converges.

Similarly Σ 1/n gives R = 1 (inconclusive), consistent with its slow divergence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming divergence when the ratio limit equals 1.
- Inverting the ratio in Raabe's test (it uses aₙ/aₙ₊₁).
- Using the ratio test on p-series (always inconclusive).

activity.prompt: For Σ (n/(2n + 1))ⁿ, what is lim aₙ^{1/n} in the root test?

quiz.q: For Σ 3ⁿ/n!, the ratio-test limit is:
quiz.why: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = 3/(n + 1) → 0 < 1, so the series converges.

quiz.q: The ratio test on Σ 1/n³ gives:
quiz.why: (n/(n + 1))³ → 1, so the ratio test cannot decide; the p-test shows convergence.

quiz.q: Raabe's limit R = 3/2 implies the series:
quiz.why: Raabe's test gives convergence whenever R > 1.

lessons.title: Alternating series, absolute and conditional convergence

scenes.text: A walker steps 1 m forward, 1/2 back, 1/3 forward, 1/4 back …
The swings shrink, and the walker settles at ln 2 ≈ 0.693 m.

steps.title: Leibniz's test
steps.body:
If uₙ ≥ 0 is decreasing and uₙ → 0, then Σ(−1)^{n+1}uₙ converges. Error bound: |S − sₙ| ≤ uₙ₊₁.

Proof idea: even partial sums increase, odd ones decrease, both bounded, and their difference uₙ → 0.

steps.title: Absolute vs conditional
steps.body:
- Σaₙ is absolutely convergent if Σ|aₙ| converges; absolute convergence ⇒ convergence.
- Conditionally convergent: Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges.
- Absolutely convergent series can be rearranged freely; Riemann's theorem: a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to sum to any real number, or to diverge.

steps.title: Solved: classic examples
steps.body:
- Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n: Leibniz ⇒ converges (to ln 2); Σ1/n diverges ⇒ conditionally convergent.
- Σ(−1)ⁿ/n²: Σ1/n² converges ⇒ absolutely convergent.
- Σ(−1)ⁿ n/(n + 1): terms ↛ 0 ⇒ diverges.

steps.title: Solved: error estimate
steps.body:
For Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n², how many terms guarantee error < 0.01?

Need uₙ₊₁ = 1/(n + 1)² < 0.01 ⇒ n + 1 > 10 ⇒ n = 10 terms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the 'decreasing' check in Leibniz's test.
- Calling Σ(−1)ⁿ/n absolutely convergent.
- Rearranging conditionally convergent series and expecting the same sum.

activity.prompt: How many terms of Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n² guarantee an error below 0.01 by the Leibniz bound?

quiz.why: Leibniz's test gives convergence, but Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 and diverges.

quiz.q: Absolute convergence implies:
quiz.why: By the Cauchy criterion, |aₘ₊₁ + … + aₙ| ≤ |aₘ₊₁| + … + |aₙ|, so Σaₙ is Cauchy.

quiz.q: Riemann's rearrangement theorem applies to series that are:
quiz.why: Only conditionally convergent series have positive and negative parts that both diverge, allowing any rearranged sum.

questions.q: Σ 1/(n(n + 1)) equals:
questions.why: Telescoping gives sₙ = 1 − 1/(n + 1) → 1.

questions.q: Σ 1/nᵖ converges iff:
questions.why: Cauchy condensation turns it into a geometric series with ratio 2^{1−p}, which needs p > 1.

questions.q: Σ sin(1/n) is:
questions.why: sin(1/n)/(1/n) → 1, so limit comparison with the harmonic series gives divergence.

questions.q: Σ 1/(n ln n), n ≥ 2, is:
questions.why: The integral of 1/(x ln x) is ln ln x, which grows without bound.

questions.q: For Σ n!/nⁿ the ratio-test limit is:
questions.why: The ratio simplifies to (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e.

questions.q: Σ n²/2ⁿ is:
questions.why: The ratio (n + 1)²/(2n²) → 1/2 < 1.

questions.q: Σ nⁿ/n! is:
questions.why: The ratio is (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e > 1, so the series diverges.

questions.q: For Σ 1/n², Raabe's limit is:
Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n converges to:
questions.why: This alternating harmonic series is the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x) at x = 1.

questions.q: Σ(−1)ⁿ/n² is:
questions.why: Σ1/n² converges, so the series converges absolutely.
Its terms have modulus tending to 1, not 0, so the nth-term test gives divergence.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Limits, continuity and uniform continuity
courses.summary: Limits of functions by ε–δ and the sequential criterion, continuity and the major theorems on closed bounded intervals, uniform continuity and the Heine–Cantor theorem, and discontinuities of monotone and pathological functions.
outcomes: Prove or disprove limits using ε–δ and sequences
Apply the boundedness, extreme value and intermediate value theorems
Decide whether a function is uniformly continuous
Classify discontinuities, including those of monotone functions

lessons.title: Limits of functions and the sequential criterion

scenes.text: A town is reachable by many roads; the temperature you feel as you arrive should not depend on the road.
The sequential criterion: a limit exists only if every sequence xₙ → a gives the same f(xₙ) → L.

steps.title: Two equivalent definitions
steps.body:
Let a be a limit point of the domain D.

- ε–δ: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0: x ∈ D, 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε.
- Sequential (Heine): lim f(x) = L iff for every sequence xₙ ∈ D∖{a} with xₙ → a, f(xₙ) → L.

The sequential form is ideal for proving that a limit does NOT exist: find two sequences giving different limits.

steps.title: Solved: sin(1/x) at 0
steps.body:
- xₙ = 1/(nπ) → 0 and sin(1/xₙ) = sin(nπ) = 0.
- yₙ = 1/(2nπ + π/2) → 0 and sin(1/yₙ) = 1.
- Different limits ⇒ lim_{x→0} sin(1/x) does not exist.

steps.title: Solved: x sin(1/x) at 0
steps.body: |x sin(1/x) − 0| ≤ |x|. Given ε, take δ = ε. Then 0 < |x| < δ ⇒ |f(x)| < ε. So the limit is 0.

steps.title: Solved: Dirichlet's function
steps.body: D(x) = 1 for x ∈ ℚ, 0 for x ∉ ℚ. At any a, take rationals rₙ → a and irrationals sₙ → a (density): D(rₙ) = 1, D(sₙ) = 0. No limit exists anywhere, so D is discontinuous at every point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using one sequence to prove a limit exists (all sequences are needed).
- Including x = a itself in the ε–δ condition.
- Forgetting that δ may depend on a and ε but not on x.

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x).

quiz.q: To prove lim_{x→a} f(x) does not exist, it suffices to find:
options: one sequence xₙ → a with f(xₙ) divergent or two with different limits
quiz.why: By the sequential criterion, any such failure means not every sequence gives the same limit.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} cos(1/x):
quiz.why: Along xₙ = 1/(2nπ) the values are 1, and along 1/((2n + 1)π) they are −1.

quiz.q: For lim_{x→2} (3x + 1) = 7, δ = ε/3 works because:
quiz.why: |f(x) − 7| = 3|x − 2| < 3δ = ε whenever |x − 2| < δ.

scenes.text: A monk climbs a mountain one day and descends by the same path the next, starting at the same hour.
By the intermediate value theorem, there is a spot he passes at the same time on both days.

steps.title: Main theorems
steps.body:
Let f be continuous on [a, b].

- Boundedness theorem: f is bounded. (Proof: else pick xₙ with |f(xₙ)| > n; Bolzano–Weierstrass gives xₙₖ → c ∈ [a, b], and continuity gives f(xₙₖ) → f(c), contradicting unboundedness.)
- Extreme value theorem: f attains its sup and inf.
- Intermediate value theorem: f takes every value between f(a) and f(b).
- So f([a, b]) = [m, M].

steps.title: Solved: x = cos x has a root
steps.body: g(x) = x − cos x is continuous on [0, 1]; g(0) = −1 < 0, g(1) = 1 − cos 1 ≈ 0.46 > 0. By IVT a root lies in (0, 1); since g'(x) = 1 + sin x > 0 on (0, 1), it is unique (≈ 0.739).

steps.title: Solved: fixed-point theorem
steps.body:
If f: [0, 1] → [0, 1] is continuous, then f(c) = c for some c.

Let g(x) = f(x) − x. g(0) = f(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0. By IVT g(c) = 0 for some c ∈ [0, 1]. ∎

steps.title: Solved: when hypotheses fail
steps.body:
- f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1]: continuous but unbounded (interval not closed).
- f(x) = x on [0, 1): bounded but sup = 1 is not attained.
- f(x) = sgn x on [−1, 1]: discontinuous; skips the value 1/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the extreme value theorem on open intervals.
- Using IVT to claim a unique root (it gives existence only).
- Forgetting to check continuity at every point of the closed interval.

activity.prompt: How many real roots does x⁵ + x − 1 = 0 have?

quiz.q: A continuous function on [a, b]:
quiz.why: This is the extreme value theorem, which relies on compactness of [a, b].

quiz.q: f(x) = x² on (0, 1) attains:
quiz.why: Its sup 1 and inf 0 occur only at the excluded endpoints.

quiz.q: The image of [a, b] under a continuous f is:
quiz.why: By the extreme value and intermediate value theorems, f([a, b]) = [m, M].

story.title: One tolerance for the whole factory

scenes.text: A factory wants one input tolerance δ that guarantees output accuracy ε on every machine setting.
If such a single δ exists for the whole domain, the function is uniformly continuous.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f is uniformly continuous on D if ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 such that x, y ∈ D, |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. Here δ depends only on ε, not on the point.

Negation (sequential): there exist ε₀ > 0 and xₙ, yₙ ∈ D with |xₙ − yₙ| → 0 but |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε₀.

steps.title: Solved: x² on [0, 1] vs ℝ
steps.body:
- On [0, 1]: |x² − y²| = |x + y||x − y| ≤ 2|x − y|; δ = ε/2 works.
- On ℝ: xₙ = n + 1/n, yₙ = n: |xₙ − yₙ| → 0 but xₙ² − yₙ² = 2 + 1/n² ≥ 2. Not uniformly continuous.

steps.title: Solved: 1/x on (0, 1)
steps.body: xₙ = 1/n, yₙ = 1/(n + 1): |xₙ − yₙ| = 1/(n(n + 1)) → 0 but |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| = 1. Not uniformly continuous, though continuous.

steps.title: Key theorems
steps.body:
- Heine–Cantor: continuous on a closed bounded interval ⇒ uniformly continuous.
- Lipschitz (|f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y|) ⇒ uniformly continuous; bounded derivative ⇒ Lipschitz (MVT).
- √x is uniformly continuous on [0, ∞) (|√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|) but not Lipschitz near 0.
- Uniformly continuous functions map Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting δ depend on x.
- Concluding 'not uniformly continuous' because f is unbounded (x is unbounded but uniformly continuous on ℝ).
- Assuming uniform continuity requires differentiability.

activity.prompt: Uniformly continuous on the given domain?

quiz.q: Heine–Cantor applies to continuous functions on:
quiz.why: Compactness of [a, b] is what upgrades continuity to uniform continuity.

quiz.q: sin x is uniformly continuous on ℝ because:
quiz.why: By the MVT it is Lipschitz with constant 1, and δ = ε works everywhere.

quiz.q: A uniformly continuous function on (0, 1) maps Cauchy sequences to:
quiz.why: Given ε, the δ from uniform continuity and the Cauchy N for δ together make f(xₙ) Cauchy.

scenes.text: An electricity bill jumps to a higher rate at fixed slabs of units used.
A monotone function can only jump — it can never oscillate wildly.

steps.title: Types of discontinuity
steps.body:
At c, let f(c⁻) and f(c⁺) be the one-sided limits.
- Removable: f(c⁻) = f(c⁺) ≠ f(c) (or f(c) undefined).
- First kind (jump): both exist, unequal.
- Second kind: at least one one-sided limit fails to exist.

steps.title: Monotone functions
steps.body:
If f is monotone on (a, b):
- f(c⁻) and f(c⁺) exist at every c (they are sup/inf of values on each side).
- All discontinuities are jumps (first kind).
- The set of discontinuities is countable: assign each jump interval (f(c⁻), f(c⁺)) a distinct rational.

steps.title: Solved: f continuous at only one point
steps.body:
f(x) = x for x ∈ ℚ, 0 for x ∉ ℚ.
- At 0: |f(x)| ≤ |x| ⇒ continuous.
- At a ≠ 0: rationals rₙ → a give f → a, irrationals give f → 0 ⇒ discontinuous (second kind).

steps.title: Solved: classifying
steps.body:

- (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at 1: removable (limit 2).
- sin(1/x) at 0: second kind.
- e^{1/x} at 0: f(0⁻) = 0, f(0⁺) = ∞ ⇒ second kind.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling an infinite one-sided limit a jump.
- Believing a monotone function can be discontinuous on an interval (its discontinuities are only countable).
- Forgetting the function value when classifying a removable discontinuity.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Riemann integration
courses.summary: Partitions and upper and lower Darboux sums, Riemann's criterion for integrability, classes of integrable functions, integrals as limits of Riemann sums, properties and the mean value theorems for integrals, the fundamental theorems of calculus and an introduction to improper integrals.
outcomes: Compute upper and lower sums and prove integrability from the definition
Apply Riemann's criterion and recognise integrable classes
Evaluate limits of sums as definite integrals
Use the mean value theorem for integrals and integral inequalities
Apply both fundamental theorems and test simple improper integrals

scenes.text: To measure the area under a curve, you can stack rectangles just under it and just over it.
As the rectangles get thinner, the two estimates squeeze together onto the true area.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
f bounded on [a, b]. A partition P = {a = x₀ < x₁ < … < xₙ = b}, Δxᵢ = xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁.

- Mᵢ = sup f on [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ], mᵢ = inf f there.
- Upper sum U(P, f) = ΣMᵢΔxᵢ; lower sum L(P, f) = ΣmᵢΔxᵢ.
- Refining P raises L and lowers U; always L(P₁, f) ≤ U(P₂, f).
- Upper integral = inf over P of U; lower integral = sup of L. f is Riemann integrable if they are equal.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x on [0, 1]
steps.body:
Uniform partition into n parts, xᵢ = i/n. f increasing ⇒ Mᵢ = i/n, mᵢ = (i − 1)/n.

- U = Σ (i/n)(1/n) = n(n + 1)/(2n²) = (n + 1)/(2n).
- L = Σ ((i − 1)/n)(1/n) = (n − 1)/(2n).
- U − L = 1/n → 0 and both → 1/2 ⇒ ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using endpoint values as Mᵢ for non-monotone functions (you need the sup on each piece).
- Forgetting that f must be bounded for Darboux sums to make sense.
- Thinking U(P) ≥ L(P) only for the same partition (it holds for any two partitions).

activity.prompt: For f(x) = x on [0, 1] with 4 equal subintervals, compute U(P, f).

quiz.q: Refining a partition:
quiz.why: Splitting an interval cannot raise a sup or lower an inf on the pieces, so U decreases and L increases (weakly).

quiz.q: For f(x) = x on [0, 1] with n equal parts, U − L equals:
quiz.why: U = (n + 1)/(2n) and L = (n − 1)/(2n) differ by 2/(2n) = 1/n.

quiz.q: For a constant function c on [a, b], U(P) equals:
quiz.why: Every Mᵢ = c, so U = cΣΔxᵢ = c(b − a).

scenes.text: Dirichlet's function jumps between 0 and 1 in every tiny interval.
Its upper and lower sums never meet, so it has no Riemann integral.

steps.title: Riemann's criterion
steps.body:
A bounded f is integrable on [a, b] iff for every ε > 0 there is a partition P with U(P, f) − L(P, f) < ε.

Integrable classes:
- Continuous functions (use uniform continuity: make each Mᵢ − mᵢ < ε/(b − a)).
- Monotone functions (U − L = |f(b) − f(a)|(b − a)/n for n equal parts).
- Bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities.
- Sums, products, |f| of integrable functions.

steps.title: Solved: Dirichlet's function
steps.body: D = 1 on ℚ, 0 elsewhere, on [0, 1]. Every subinterval contains rationals and irrationals ⇒ Mᵢ = 1, mᵢ = 0 ⇒ U = 1, L = 0 for every P. Not integrable.

steps.title: Integral as a limit of sums
steps.body:
If f is integrable, Riemann sums Σf(tᵢ)Δxᵢ (any tᵢ in the ith piece) → ∫f as the mesh → 0. In particular

lim (1/n) Σ_{k=1}^{n} f(k/n) = ∫₀¹ f(x) dx.

steps.title: Solved: limits of sums
steps.body:
- lim Σ_{k=1}^{n} 1/(n + k) = lim (1/n)Σ 1/(1 + k/n) = ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x) = ln 2.
- lim Σ_{k=1}^{n} n/(n² + k²) = ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) = π/4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking every bounded function is integrable.
- Writing the sum as ∫₀¹ but forgetting to factor out exactly 1/n.
- Believing an integrable function must be continuous (step functions are integrable).

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim (1/n) Σ_{k=1}^{n} (k/n)² (three decimals).

quiz.q: Which function is NOT Riemann integrable on [0, 1]?
quiz.why: Its upper sums are always 1 and lower sums always 0.

quiz.q: lim Σ_{k=1}^{n} n/(n² + k²) equals:
quiz.why: It is (1/n)Σ 1/(1 + (k/n)²) → ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) = π/4.

quiz.q: A bounded function with finitely many discontinuities on [a, b] is:
options: integrable only if continuous at a
quiz.why: Each discontinuity can be enclosed in a tiny interval contributing less than ε/k to U − L.

lessons.title: Properties and mean value theorems for integrals

scenes.text: A train's speed varies, but over the trip it covers the distance an average-speed train would.
The mean value theorem for integrals says the train actually moved at that average speed at some instant.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
For integrable f, g on [a, b]:
- Linearity: ∫(αf + βg) = α∫f + β∫g.
- Additivity: ∫_a^b = ∫_a^c + ∫_c^b.
- Monotonicity: f ≤ g ⇒ ∫f ≤ ∫g; m ≤ f ≤ M ⇒ m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a).
- |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|.

steps.title: Mean value theorems
steps.body:
- First MVT: f continuous on [a, b] ⇒ ∫_a^b f = f(c)(b − a) for some c ∈ [a, b]. (Proof: m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a), then IVT.)
- Generalised: f continuous, g ≥ 0 integrable ⇒ ∫fg = f(c)∫g.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the first MVT to discontinuous functions (c may not exist).
- Forgetting the factor (b − a).
- Using |∫f| = ∫|f| (only an inequality).

activity.prompt: Find c from the mean value theorem for f(x) = x³ on [0, 2] (three decimals).

quiz.q: The average value of f(x) = x on [0, 4] is:
If 0 ≤ f ≤ 3 on [1, 5], then ∫₁⁵ f lies in:
|∫f| ≤ ∫|f| holds because:
quiz.why: Integrating −|f| ≤ f ≤ |f| gives −∫|f| ≤ ∫f ≤ ∫|f|.

scenes.text: Differentiation and integration look like separate subjects.
The fundamental theorem shows each undoes the other — the most useful theorem in calculus.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
Let f be integrable on [a, b] and F(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt.

- F is continuous (indeed Lipschitz if |f| ≤ M).
- FTC I: if f is continuous at c, F'(c) = f(c).
- FTC II: if G' = f on [a, b] and f is integrable, ∫_a^b f = G(b) − G(a).
- Leibniz rule: d/dx ∫_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f(t) dt = f(v)v' − f(u)u'.

steps.title: Solved: differentiating an integral
steps.body:
- d/dx ∫₀^{x²} sin t dt = 2x sin(x²).
- d/dx ∫_x^{x³} e^{t²} dt = 3x² e^{x⁶} − e^{x²}.

steps.title: Solved: a limit using FTC
steps.body: lim_{x→0} (∫₀^x sin(t²) dt)/x³: 0/0, L'Hôpital with FTC ⇒ sin(x²)/(3x²) → 1/3.

steps.title: Improper integrals
steps.body:
∫_a^∞ f = lim_{R→∞} ∫_a^R f; for an unbounded integrand at a, ∫_a^b f = lim_{ε→0⁺} ∫_{a+ε}^b f.

- ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges iff p > 1 (value 1/(p − 1)).
- ∫₀¹ dx/xᵖ converges iff p < 1 (value 1/(1 − p)).
- Comparison tests work as for series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor v'(x) in the Leibniz rule.
- Applying FTC II across a point where the integrand blows up (e.g. ∫_{−1}^{1} dx/x²).
- Mixing up the convergence conditions p > 1 (at ∞) and p < 1 (at 0).

quiz.why: By FTC I the derivative of the integral with variable upper limit is the integrand at x.

quiz.why: lim (1 − 1/R) = 1, matching 1/(p − 1) with p = 2.

questions.why: Left endpoints give Σ(i − 1)/n² = (n − 1)/(2n).

questions.why: Integrability is equivalent to being able to make U − L arbitrarily small.

questions.why: Every subinterval has sup 1 and inf 0.

questions.q: lim Σ_{k=1}^{n} 1/(n + k) equals:
questions.why: It is (1/n)Σ 1/(1 + k/n) → ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x) = ln 2.

questions.q: Which class is always Riemann integrable?
questions.why: For monotone f, U − L = |f(b) − f(a)|(b − a)/n → 0.

questions.q: The mean value c for f(x) = x² on [0, 3] is:

uni-bsc-math-ring-linear-algebra.title: Ring Theory & Linear Algebra (B.Sc Mathematics)
uni-bsc-math-ring-linear-algebra.description: Rings, integral domains and fields, ideals and quotient rings, ring homomorphisms, vector spaces, bases and dimension, linear transformations and rank–nullity, eigenvalues, diagonalisation and inner product spaces. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc (Hons) Mathematics programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Rings, integral domains and fields
courses.summary: Definition and examples of rings, subrings, units and zero divisors, integral domains, fields, characteristic of a ring, and the results that finite integral domains are fields and ℤₙ is a field iff n is prime.
outcomes: Verify ring axioms and identify commutative rings with unity
Find units and zero divisors in ℤₙ and matrix rings
Prove that a finite integral domain is a field
Compute the characteristic of a ring
Apply the subring test

scenes.text: Groups capture one operation. But integers can be added AND multiplied, and the two interact through the distributive law.
A ring is the structure that captures this pair of operations.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A ring (R, +, ·) is a set with two binary operations such that (R, +) is an abelian group, · is associative, and a(b + c) = ab + ac, (b + c)a = ba + ca. R is commutative if ab = ba; it has unity 1 if 1·a = a·1 = a with 1 ≠ 0.

steps.title: Standard examples
steps.body: ℤ, ℚ, ℝ, ℂ (commutative with unity); ℤₙ; 2ℤ (commutative, no unity); M₂(ℝ) (non-commutative with unity I); ℤ[x] polynomials; ℤ[i] = {a + bi : a, b ∈ ℤ} Gaussian integers; C[0,1] continuous functions under pointwise operations.

steps.title: Basic properties
steps.body: For all a, b in R: a·0 = 0·a = 0; a(−b) = (−a)b = −(ab); (−a)(−b) = ab. Proof of the first: a·0 = a(0 + 0) = a·0 + a·0, then cancel a·0 in the group (R, +).

steps.title: Subring test
steps.body: A non-empty S ⊆ R is a subring iff a − b ∈ S and ab ∈ S for all a, b ∈ S. Example: {0, 2, 4} in ℤ₆ is a subring; ℤ is a subring of ℚ; the diagonal matrices form a subring of M₂(ℝ).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: A subring need not contain the unity of R (2ℤ ⊂ ℤ). In {0,2,4} ⊂ ℤ₆, 4 acts as unity (4·2 = 8 ≡ 2, 4·4 = 16 ≡ 4), different from 1 in ℤ₆.

activity.prompt: Classify the ring.

quiz.q: In any ring, a·0 equals:
quiz.why: From a·0 = a·0 + a·0 we cancel a·0 additively to get a·0 = 0.

quiz.q: Which ring has no unity?
quiz.why: No element e of 5ℤ satisfies e·5 = 5, since that forces e = 1 ∉ 5ℤ.

quiz.q: M₂(ℝ) is:
quiz.why: Matrix multiplication does not commute in general, and the identity matrix is the unity.

quiz.q: The unity of the subring {0, 3} of ℤ₆ is:
quiz.why: 3·3 = 9 ≡ 3 (mod 6) and 3·0 = 0, so 3 acts as unity inside {0, 3}.

lessons.title: Units, zero divisors and integral domains

scenes.text: In ℤ₆, 2·3 = 0 even though 2 ≠ 0 and 3 ≠ 0.
Such elements are zero divisors; rings without them behave like the integers and are called integral domains.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse. a ≠ 0 is a zero divisor if ab = 0 for some b ≠ 0. An integral domain is a commutative ring with unity and no zero divisors. A field is a commutative ring with unity in which every non-zero element is a unit.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ₁₂
steps.body: Units are k with gcd(k,12) = 1: 1, 5, 7, 11. Zero divisors are the other non-zero elements: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 (e.g. 4·3 = 12 ≡ 0, 9·4 = 36 ≡ 0). In ℤₙ every non-zero element is either a unit or a zero divisor.

steps.title: Cancellation
steps.body: A commutative ring with unity is an integral domain iff ab = ac with a ≠ 0 implies b = c. Proof: ab = ac ⇒ a(b − c) = 0 ⇒ b − c = 0.

steps.title: Worked example: units in ℤ[i]
steps.body: If (a + bi)(c + di) = 1, taking norms N(z) = a² + b² gives N(z)N(w) = 1, so a² + b² = 1. Units are ±1, ±i.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying ℤ is a field — 2 has no inverse in ℤ; ℤ is an integral domain. M₂(ℝ) has zero divisors: [[1,0],[0,0]]·[[0,0],[0,1]] = 0.

activity.prompt: How many zero divisors (non-zero) does ℤ₂₀ have?

quiz.q: Units of ℤ₁₀:
quiz.why: Units of ℤₙ are the residues coprime to n; for n = 10 these are 1, 3, 7, 9.

quiz.q: ℤ is:
options: an integral domain but not a field
quiz.why: ℤ has no zero divisors, but only ±1 are units, so it is not a field.

quiz.q: Units of ℤ[i] are:
quiz.why: A unit must have norm a² + b² = 1, which allows only ±1 and ±i.

quiz.q: Which is a zero divisor in ℤ₁₅?

scenes.text: In ℤ₇ every non-zero number has an inverse: 3·5 = 15 ≡ 1.
Finite fields like ℤₚ power modern cryptography and error-correcting codes.

steps.title: Theorem: a finite integral domain is a field
steps.body: Let D be finite and a ≠ 0. The map x ↦ ax is injective (cancellation), hence surjective because D is finite. So ax = 1 for some x, i.e. a is a unit.

steps.title: Corollary
steps.body: ℤₙ is a field ⇔ ℤₙ is an integral domain ⇔ n is prime. If n = rs with 1 < r, s < n then r·s = 0 gives zero divisors.

steps.title: Characteristic
steps.body: char R is the least positive n with n·a = 0 for all a ∈ R (0 if none). For a ring with unity, char R = additive order of 1. char ℤₙ = n; char ℤ = char ℚ = char ℝ = 0. The characteristic of an integral domain is 0 or a prime.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ₃ × ℤ₄
steps.body: Unity (1,1) has additive order lcm(3,4) = 12, so char(ℤ₃ × ℤ₄) = 12. This ring has zero divisors, e.g. (1,0)(0,1) = (0,0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking a field can have characteristic 6 — characteristic of an integral domain is prime or 0. In characteristic p, (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ, not in general rings.

quiz.why: ℤₙ has zero divisors exactly when n is composite, and a finite integral domain is a field.

quiz.q: char(ℤ₆ × ℤ₁₀) equals:
quiz.why: The unity (1,1) has additive order lcm(6,10) = 30.

quiz.q: Inverse of 4 in ℤ₁₃:
Characteristic of ℚ:
quiz.why: No positive multiple n·1 equals 0 in ℚ, so the characteristic is defined to be 0.

lessons.title: Lab: Ring tables and exam drill

scenes.text: Writing the full multiplication table of ℤ₆ reveals every unit and zero divisor at a glance.
A row containing 1 means a unit; a row containing an extra 0 means a zero divisor.

steps.title: Multiplication table of ℤ₆ (non-zero part)
steps.body: Row 1: 1 2 3 4 5. Row 2: 2 4 0 2 4. Row 3: 3 0 3 0 3. Row 4: 4 2 0 4 2. Row 5: 5 4 3 2 1. Rows 1 and 5 contain 1 → units {1, 5}. Rows 2, 3, 4 contain 0 → zero divisors {2, 3, 4}.

steps.title: Idempotents and nilpotents
steps.body: a is idempotent if a² = a; nilpotent if aⁿ = 0 for some n. In ℤ₆ idempotents are 0, 1, 3, 4 (3² = 9 ≡ 3, 4² = 16 ≡ 4). In ℤ₈, 2 is nilpotent (2³ = 0), and the nilpotents are 0, 2, 4, 6.

steps.title: Exam pattern
steps.body: Questions like 'Show that ℤ[√2] = {a + b√2} is an integral domain' need: subring of ℝ (closure under − and ·), contains 1, commutative, no zero divisors since ℝ has none.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Show that the only idempotents of an integral domain are 0 and 1: a² = a ⇒ a(a − 1) = 0 ⇒ a = 0 or a = 1.

activity.prompt: In ℤ₁₀, complete the facts.

quiz.why: a² = a gives a(a − 1) = 0, and with no zero divisors a = 0 or a = 1.

quiz.q: Nilpotent elements of ℤ₈:
quiz.why: Every even residue x satisfies x³ ≡ 0 mod 8, while odd residues are units.
It is a subring of ℝ containing 1, commutative, and inherits the absence of zero divisors from ℝ.

questions.why: 11 is prime, so ℤ₁₁ is a field.

questions.why: ℤ₇ is a field, so it has no zero divisors.

questions.why: {0,4,8} is closed under subtraction and multiplication (4·8 = 32 ≡ 8).

questions.why: Multiplication by a ≠ 0 is injective, hence surjective on a finite set, so a has an inverse.

The Gaussian integers ℤ[i] have exactly how many units?
questions.why: Units satisfy a² + b² = 1, giving ±1 and ±i.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Ideals, quotient rings and ring homomorphisms
courses.summary: Ideals and the ideal test, principal ideals, factor rings, prime and maximal ideals, ring homomorphisms and the first isomorphism theorem for rings, and polynomial rings over fields with the division algorithm and irreducibility.
outcomes: Apply the ideal test and identify principal ideals
Construct factor rings R/I and compute in them
Characterise prime and maximal ideals via R/I
Use the first isomorphism theorem for rings
Test small polynomials over ℤₚ for irreducibility

scenes.text: Multiply any integer by an even number and the result is even: the evens 'absorb' multiplication.
Subrings with this absorbing property are ideals, and they let us build factor rings like ℤ/nℤ.

steps.title: Definition and test
steps.body: A subring I of R is an ideal if rI ⊆ I and Ir ⊆ I for all r ∈ R. Ideal test: I non-empty, a − b ∈ I for a, b ∈ I, and ra, ar ∈ I for a ∈ I, r ∈ R. ⟨a⟩ = {ra : r ∈ R} is the principal ideal generated by a (R commutative with unity).

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: nℤ is an ideal of ℤ, and every ideal of ℤ is of this form (ℤ is a principal ideal domain). ⟨x⟩ in ℝ[x] = polynomials with zero constant term. ℤ is a subring of ℚ but not an ideal: (1/2)·1 ∉ ℤ.

steps.title: Factor ring
steps.body: For an ideal I, R/I = {a + I} is a ring with (a + I) + (b + I) = (a + b) + I and (a + I)(b + I) = ab + I. Absorption is what makes multiplication well defined.

steps.title: Worked example: ℤ[i]/⟨2 − i⟩
steps.body: In ℤ[i]/⟨2 − i⟩ we have i ≡ 2. Then −1 = i² ≡ 4, so 5 ≡ 0. Every a + bi ≡ a + 2b mod 5. Hence ℤ[i]/⟨2 − i⟩ ≅ ℤ₅, a field with 5 elements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: An ideal containing a unit is the whole ring (u ∈ I ⇒ 1 = u⁻¹u ∈ I ⇒ I = R). So a field has only the ideals {0} and itself.

activity.prompt: Is I an ideal of R?

quiz.q: An ideal containing 1 is:
quiz.why: For any r, r = r·1 lies in the ideal by absorption, so I = R.

quiz.q: Ideals of a field F:
quiz.why: Any non-zero ideal contains a unit and therefore equals F.

quiz.q: |ℤ/12ℤ| equals:
quiz.why: The cosets are 0 + 12ℤ, …, 11 + 12ℤ — twelve in total.

quiz.q: ℤ[i]/⟨2 − i⟩ is isomorphic to:
quiz.why: Setting i = 2 forces 5 = 0, so every class is represented by a + 2b mod 5.

scenes.text: If a prime p divides ab then p divides a or b. The ideal pℤ inherits this behaviour.
Maximal ideals are as large as possible without being the whole ring.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: In a commutative ring R with unity, a proper ideal P is prime if ab ∈ P ⇒ a ∈ P or b ∈ P. A proper ideal M is maximal if M ⊆ I ⊆ R (I an ideal) implies I = M or I = R.

steps.title: Key theorems
steps.body: R/P is an integral domain ⇔ P is prime. R/M is a field ⇔ M is maximal. Since every field is an integral domain, maximal ⇒ prime.

steps.title: Worked example: ideals of ℤ
steps.body: nℤ is prime ⇔ n is prime or n = 0. {0} is prime (ℤ is a domain) but not maximal ({0} ⊂ 2ℤ). For a prime p, ℤ/pℤ ≅ ℤₚ is a field, so pℤ is maximal.

steps.title: Worked example: ℝ[x]/⟨x² + 1⟩
steps.body: x² + 1 has no real root, so it is irreducible over ℝ and ⟨x² + 1⟩ is maximal. The factor ring is ≅ ℂ, via x + ⟨x² + 1⟩ ↦ i.

steps.title: Worked example: ⟨x⟩ in ℤ[x]
steps.body: ℤ[x]/⟨x⟩ ≅ ℤ (evaluate at 0), an integral domain but not a field. So ⟨x⟩ is prime but not maximal; it lies inside the maximal ideal ⟨2, x⟩.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying every prime ideal is maximal — true in ℤ for non-zero ideals and in finite rings, false in ℤ[x]. Forgetting 'proper' in the definitions.

activity.prompt: Classify the ideal.

quiz.q: R/M is a field iff M is:
quiz.why: This is the standard characterisation: a commutative ring with unity modulo M is a field exactly when M is maximal.

quiz.q: ⟨x² − 1⟩ in ℝ[x] is not prime because:
options: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) with neither factor in the ideal
quiz.why: (x − 1)(x + 1) lies in the ideal but neither factor does, since both have degree 1.

quiz.q: In ℤ₁₂, the ideal ⟨3⟩ is:
quiz.why: ℤ₁₂/⟨3⟩ ≅ ℤ₃ is a field, so ⟨3⟩ is maximal.

quiz.q: Maximal ideals are always:
quiz.why: R/M is a field, and every field is an integral domain, so M is prime.

scenes.text: Plugging x = 2 into polynomials respects sums and products: (f + g)(2) = f(2) + g(2), (fg)(2) = f(2)g(2).
Its kernel is ⟨x − 2⟩, so ℝ[x]/⟨x − 2⟩ ≅ ℝ.

steps.title: Ring homomorphisms
steps.body: φ : R → S with φ(a + b) = φ(a) + φ(b) and φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b). ker φ is an ideal of R. First isomorphism theorem: R/ker φ ≅ φ(R).

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: (1) ℤ → ℤₙ, k ↦ k mod n, kernel nℤ. (2) Evaluation ℝ[x] → ℝ, f ↦ f(a), kernel ⟨x − a⟩. (3) ℂ → M₂(ℝ), a + bi ↦ [[a, −b],[b, a]] is an injective homomorphism.

steps.title: Polynomials over a field
steps.body: F[x] has a division algorithm: f = qg + r with deg r < deg g. Factor theorem: (x − a) | f ⇔ f(a) = 0. A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over F is irreducible iff it has no root in F. F[x] is a PID, and ⟨p(x)⟩ is maximal iff p is irreducible.

steps.title: Worked example: irreducibility over ℤ₃
steps.body: f(x) = x² + 1: f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 5 ≡ 2. No roots, so f is irreducible over ℤ₃ and ℤ₃[x]/⟨x² + 1⟩ is a field with 3² = 9 elements.

steps.title: Worked example: Eisenstein
steps.body: x⁴ + 6x² + 3 over ℚ: p = 3 divides 6 and 3, does not divide the leading coefficient 1, and 3² = 9 ∤ 3. By Eisenstein's criterion it is irreducible over ℚ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 'no roots ⇒ irreducible' for degree 4: x⁴ + 2x² + 1 = (x² + 1)² has no real roots yet is reducible over ℝ.

activity.prompt: How many elements does the field ℤ₅[x]/⟨x² + 2⟩ have? (x² + 2 has no root in ℤ₅.)

quiz.q: Kernel of evaluation at 3, ℝ[x] → ℝ:
quiz.why: f(3) = 0 iff (x − 3) divides f, by the factor theorem.

quiz.q: Over ℤ₂, x² + x + 1 is:
quiz.why: Its values at 0 and 1 are both 1 ≠ 0, so a degree-2 polynomial without roots is irreducible.

quiz.q: Over ℤ₅, x² + 1 factors because:
quiz.why: 2² + 1 = 5 ≡ 0 mod 5, so x² + 1 = (x − 2)(x − 3) over ℤ₅.

quiz.q: ℝ[x]/⟨x − 5⟩ is isomorphic to:
quiz.why: Evaluation at 5 maps ℝ[x] onto ℝ with kernel ⟨x − 5⟩.

scenes.text: Ring theory papers reward clean, step-by-step proofs.
Practise the standard ones in the right order.

steps.title: Proof: intersection of ideals is an ideal
steps.body: Let I, J be ideals. 0 ∈ I ∩ J. If a, b ∈ I ∩ J then a − b ∈ I and ∈ J. For r ∈ R, ra ∈ I and ra ∈ J. Hence I ∩ J is an ideal. (Sum I + J is also an ideal; the union need not be.)

steps.title: Proof: ker φ is an ideal
steps.body: φ(0) = 0 so 0 ∈ ker φ. φ(a − b) = φ(a) − φ(b) = 0. φ(ra) = φ(r)φ(a) = φ(r)·0 = 0. So ker φ is an ideal.

steps.title: Useful facts for ℤ
steps.body: mℤ + nℤ = gcd(m, n)ℤ, mℤ ∩ nℤ = lcm(m, n)ℤ, and mℤ·nℤ = mnℤ.

activity.prompt: Order the proof that R/M is a field when M is maximal.
items: Take a + M ≠ M in R/M, so a ∉ M
Form the ideal I = {m + ra : m ∈ M, r ∈ R}
Note M ⊊ I, so maximality gives I = R
Write 1 = m + ba for some m ∈ M, b ∈ R
Conclude (b + M)(a + M) = 1 + M, so a + M is a unit

quiz.why: 2ℤ ∪ 3ℤ contains 2 and 3 but not 5, so it is not even closed under addition.

questions.why: ℤ is a PID: every ideal is nℤ for some n ≥ 0.

questions.why: f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 1, so a cubic with no roots over ℤ₂ is irreducible.

questions.why: Classes are polynomials of degree < 3 over ℤ₂: 2³ = 8.

questions.why: A unit u ∈ I gives 1 = u⁻¹u ∈ I, and conversely 1 is a unit.

questions.why: nℤ is prime iff ℤ/nℤ is an integral domain, i.e. n = 0 or n prime.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Vector spaces, subspaces, basis and dimension
courses.summary: Vector space axioms over a field, subspaces, linear span, linear independence, basis and dimension, coordinates, and the dimension formula for sums of subspaces.
outcomes: Verify vector space axioms and test subspaces
Decide linear independence by row reduction
Find a basis and the dimension of a subspace
Use dim(U + W) = dim U + dim W − dim(U ∩ W)
Find coordinates of a vector relative to a basis

scenes.text: Arrows in the plane can be added and scaled. So can polynomials, matrices and audio signals.
A vector space is any collection where 'add' and 'scale' behave like arrows.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A vector space V over a field F is an abelian group (V, +) with scalar multiplication F × V → V satisfying a(u + v) = au + av, (a + b)v = av + bv, (ab)v = a(bv) and 1v = v. Examples: Fⁿ, Mₘₓₙ(F), Pₙ (polynomials of degree ≤ n), C[a, b].

steps.title: Subspace test
steps.body: W ⊆ V is a subspace iff W ≠ ∅ and au + bv ∈ W for all u, v ∈ W, a, b ∈ F. Every subspace contains 0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: W = {(x, y, z) ∈ ℝ³ : x + 2y − z = 0} is a subspace: if u, v satisfy the equation, so does au + bv by linearity. W' = {(x, y, z) : x + y = 1} is not: (0,0,0) ∉ W'. The solution set of any homogeneous system Ax = 0 is a subspace (the null space).

steps.title: Worked example: symmetric matrices
steps.body: Sym₂(ℝ) = {A : Aᵀ = A} is a subspace of M₂(ℝ): (aA + bB)ᵀ = aAᵀ + bBᵀ = aA + bB. But invertible matrices do not form a subspace (0 is not invertible).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The union of two subspaces is generally not a subspace (x-axis ∪ y-axis in ℝ²). The set {(x, x²)} is not a subspace — check closure under addition.

activity.prompt: Subspace of the given space?

quiz.q: Every subspace must contain:
quiz.why: Taking a = b = 0 in the subspace test gives 0 ∈ W.

quiz.q: {A ∈ M₂(ℝ) : det A = 0} is not a subspace because:
options: it is not closed under addition
quiz.why: diag(1,0) and diag(0,1) are singular, but their sum I is invertible.

quiz.q: The solution set of Ax = 0 is:
quiz.why: A(au + bv) = aAu + bAv = 0, so it is closed under linear combinations and contains 0.
The zero polynomial has p(0) = 0 ≠ 1, so the set does not contain 0.

scenes.text: A drone controller has three joysticks, but one is just a mix of the other two — it adds no new direction.
Linear independence is the mathematical test for such redundancy.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: span S = all finite linear combinations of vectors in S; it is the smallest subspace containing S. S = {v₁, …, v_k} is linearly independent if c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k = 0 forces all cᵢ = 0; otherwise dependent.

steps.title: Row-reduction method
steps.body: Put the vectors as columns of a matrix A and row reduce. They are independent iff every column has a pivot, i.e. rank A = k. In ℝⁿ, n vectors are independent iff det ≠ 0; more than n vectors are always dependent.

steps.title: Worked example: polynomials
steps.body: Are 1 + x, 1 − x, x² independent in P₂? a(1 + x) + b(1 − x) + cx² = 0 gives a + b = 0, a − b = 0, c = 0, so a = b = c = 0. Independent, and since dim P₂ = 3 they form a basis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Any set containing 0 is dependent. Two vectors are dependent iff one is a scalar multiple of the other — but for three or more vectors, no two need be parallel for dependence.

activity.prompt: For which value of k are (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1) and (1, 0, k) linearly dependent?

quiz.q: Four vectors in ℝ³ are:
quiz.why: ℝ³ has dimension 3, so any set of more than 3 vectors is linearly dependent.
(2,4) = 2(1,2), so one vector is a multiple of the other.

quiz.q: A set containing the zero vector is:
quiz.why: 1·0 = 0 is a non-trivial combination equal to zero.
Combinations a(1,0,0) + b(0,1,0) = (a, b, 0) fill exactly the plane z = 0.

scenes.text: A basis is a toolkit with no redundant tools that can still build every vector.
Every basis of the same space has the same size — the dimension.

steps.title: Basis and dimension
steps.body: A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. All bases of V have the same number of elements, dim V. dim Fⁿ = n, dim Pₙ = n + 1, dim Mₘₓₙ = mn, dim Sym₂(ℝ) = 3. In an n-dimensional space, any n independent vectors form a basis, and any n spanning vectors form a basis.

steps.title: Dimension of a sum
steps.body: For subspaces U, W of a finite-dimensional V: dim(U + W) = dim U + dim W − dim(U ∩ W). Example: two distinct planes through 0 in ℝ³ meet in a line: 2 + 2 − 1 = 3.

steps.title: Worked example: basis of a null space
Common mistakes
steps.body: dim Pₙ is n + 1, not n. Counting equations instead of free variables: dimension of the null space = number of unknowns − rank.

activity.prompt: U and W are subspaces of ℝ⁵ with dim U = 3, dim W = 4 and U + W = ℝ⁵. Find dim(U ∩ W).

quiz.q: dim M₂ₓ₃(ℝ):
quiz.why: A 2 × 3 matrix has 6 independent entries, so the standard basis has 6 matrix units.

quiz.q: dim P₄:
quiz.why: 1, x, x², x³, x⁴ form a basis — five polynomials.

quiz.q: Coordinates of (4, 2) in basis {(1,1),(1,−1)}:
quiz.why: a + b = 4 and a − b = 2 give a = 3, b = 1.

quiz.q: dim of skew-symmetric 3 × 3 real matrices:
quiz.why: The diagonal is zero and the three entries above it determine those below, so dimension 3.

lessons.title: Lab: Row reduction to find bases

scenes.text: Row-reducing a matrix reveals its pivot columns, its rank and its null space in one go.
This lab follows the full procedure on a real exam-style matrix.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A = [[1,2,1],[2,4,3],[3,6,4]]. R₂ − 2R₁ → (0,0,1); R₃ − 3R₁ → (0,0,1); R₃ − R₂ → (0,0,0). Echelon form [[1,2,1],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]]. Pivots in columns 1 and 3, rank 2. Column space basis: original columns 1 and 3: (1,2,3), (1,3,4). Row space basis: (1,2,1), (0,0,1).

steps.title: Null space of the same A
steps.body: From the echelon form: z = 0, x + 2y = 0. Free variable y: (x,y,z) = y(−2, 1, 0). Null space basis {(−2,1,0)}, nullity 1. Check: rank + nullity = 2 + 1 = 3 = number of columns ✔

steps.title: Key point
steps.body: Take column-space basis vectors from the ORIGINAL matrix's pivot columns, but row-space basis vectors from the echelon form's non-zero rows.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find a basis of the column space of A.
items: Row reduce A to echelon form
Identify the pivot columns
Return to the original matrix A
Take its pivot columns as the basis
Record rank = number of pivots

quiz.why: Nullity = number of columns − rank = 6 − 3 = 3.

quiz.why: Row operations change the column space but preserve which columns are independent, so we read pivot positions and take the original columns.

questions.why: The coefficients in the order 1, x, x² are 3, 2, 1.

questions.why: If u ∈ U \ W and w ∈ W \ U, then u + w lies in neither.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Linear transformations, rank–nullity and matrices
courses.summary: Linear transformations, kernel and range, the rank–nullity theorem, isomorphisms, the matrix of a linear map relative to bases, change of basis and similar matrices.
outcomes: Check linearity and compute kernel and range
Apply the rank–nullity theorem
Write the matrix of a linear map relative to given bases
Use change-of-basis matrices and recognise similar matrices
Decide when a linear map is an isomorphism

scenes.text: Shining a light straight down turns a 3D object into a 2D shadow — a projection.
Everything on the vertical line through the origin lands on the same point: that line is the kernel.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: T : V → W is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(av) = aT(v). Then T(0) = 0. ker T = {v : T(v) = 0} ⊆ V and range T = T(V) ⊆ W are subspaces. T is one-one iff ker T = {0}.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: T : ℝ³ → ℝ², T(x, y, z) = (x + y, y + z). Kernel: x + y = 0, y + z = 0 ⇒ (x,y,z) = t(1, −1, 1), nullity 1. Range: T(1,0,0) = (1,0), T(0,0,1) = (0,1), so range = ℝ², rank 2. Check 2 + 1 = 3 ✔

steps.title: Non-examples
steps.body: T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) is not linear since T(0,0) = (1,0) ≠ 0. T(x, y) = (xy, x) is not linear: T(2(1,1)) = (4, 2) but 2T(1,1) = (2, 2).

steps.title: Derivative map
steps.body: D : P₃ → P₃, D(p) = p′. ker D = constants (nullity 1), range = P₂ (rank 3). 1 + 3 = 4 = dim P₃ ✔. D is neither one-one nor onto.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Checking only T(0) = 0 is not enough to prove linearity. The kernel lives in the domain, the range in the codomain.

activity.prompt: Linear or not?

quiz.q: ker T for T(x, y) = (x − y, 2x − 2y):
quiz.why: x − y = 0 gives (x, y) = t(1, 1); the second equation is the same condition.

quiz.q: T is one-one iff:
quiz.why: T(u) = T(v) ⇔ u − v ∈ ker T, so a trivial kernel forces u = v.

quiz.q: The trace map M₂(ℝ) → ℝ has nullity:
quiz.why: It is onto ℝ (rank 1), so nullity = 4 − 1 = 3.

quiz.q: Kernel of D on P₃:
quiz.why: p′ = 0 exactly when p is constant.

scenes.text: Whatever dimension a linear map 'loses' into its kernel, it keeps in its range.
rank + nullity always equals the dimension of the domain.

steps.title: Theorem
steps.body: For T : V → W with V finite-dimensional, dim V = rank T + nullity T. Proof idea: extend a basis {u₁,…,u_k} of ker T to a basis {u₁,…,u_k, v₁,…,v_r} of V; then {T(v₁),…,T(v_r)} is a basis of range T.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body: If dim V = dim W (finite), T is one-one ⇔ onto ⇔ isomorphism. V ≅ W ⇔ dim V = dim W. So every n-dimensional real space is ≅ ℝⁿ (e.g. P₃ ≅ ℝ⁴, M₂ ≅ ℝ⁴).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: T : ℝ⁵ → ℝ³ with rank 3: nullity = 5 − 3 = 2; T is onto but not one-one. A map ℝ³ → ℝ⁵ can never be onto (rank ≤ 3).

steps.title: Worked example: isomorphism P₂ → ℝ³
steps.body: T(a + bx + cx²) = (a, a + b, a + b + c). Kernel: a = 0, b = 0, c = 0 ⇒ ker T = {0}. Since dim P₂ = dim ℝ³ = 3, T is an isomorphism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the dimension of the codomain in rank–nullity. A one-one map between spaces of different dimensions is not an isomorphism.

quiz.why: Nullity 0 gives rank 7 = dim of codomain, so T is onto as well.

quiz.q: Can a linear map ℝ² → ℝ³ be onto?
quiz.why: rank ≤ dim domain = 2 < 3, so the range cannot be all of ℝ³.

quiz.q: P₄ is isomorphic to:
quiz.why: dim P₄ = 5, and spaces of equal finite dimension over ℝ are isomorphic.
