lessons.title: Matrix of a linear map and change of basis

scenes.text: A linear map is a geometric object; its matrix depends on the coordinate system you wear.
Changing basis changes the matrix to P⁻¹AP — a similar matrix.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Given bases B = {v₁,…,vₙ} of V and C of W, the matrix [T]_C,B has j-th column [T(vⱼ)]_C. Then [T(v)]_C = [T]_C,B [v]_B. Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication.

steps.title: Change of basis
steps.body: If P has columns = new basis vectors written in old coordinates, then [T]_new = P⁻¹ [T]_old P. Matrices A and B = P⁻¹AP are similar; they share determinant, trace, rank, characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: T(x, y) = (3x + y, x + 3y), standard matrix A = [[3,1],[1,3]]. New basis (1,1), (1,−1): T(1,1) = (4,4) = 4(1,1), T(1,−1) = (2,−2) = 2(1,−1). So in the new basis [T] = diag(4, 2) — a much simpler picture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing images as rows instead of columns. Order of bases matters — reordering basis vectors permutes the matrix columns/rows.

activity.prompt: T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − y). Fill in its standard matrix [[a, b], [c, d]].

quiz.q: The j-th column of [T] is:
options: T applied to the j-th basis vector, in coordinates
quiz.why: By construction, column j records the coordinates of T(vⱼ) in the target basis.

quiz.q: Similar matrices always share:
quiz.why: det(P⁻¹AP − λI) = det(A − λI), so the characteristic polynomial and hence eigenvalues agree.

quiz.q: Matrix of rotation by 90° in ℝ² (standard basis):
quiz.why: e₁ ↦ (0,1) and e₂ ↦ (−1,0), giving columns (0,1) and (−1,0).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: (1) Verify linearity. (2) Compute images of basis vectors → matrix. (3) Row reduce the matrix. (4) Pivots → rank and a basis for the range (original columns). (5) Free variables → kernel basis. (6) Check rank + nullity = dim V.

scenes.text: Stretch a rubber sheet: most arrows drawn on it change direction, but a few special ones only get longer or shorter.
Those are eigenvectors, and the stretch factors are eigenvalues.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: λ is an eigenvalue of A if Av = λv for some v ≠ 0 (an eigenvector). Equivalently det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic equation. For 2 × 2: λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0. Sum of eigenvalues = trace, product = determinant.

steps.title: Worked example: triangular 3 × 3
steps.body: A = [[2,1,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,3]]. Eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 2, 2, 3. For λ = 2: A − 2I = [[0,1,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]] ⇒ y = 0, z = 0, eigenvectors t(1,0,0) — only one independent eigenvector for the double eigenvalue.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body: Eigenvalues of Aᵏ are λᵏ; of A⁻¹ are 1/λ; of A + cI are λ + c. A is invertible iff 0 is not an eigenvalue. Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Accepting v = 0 as an eigenvector. Forgetting that eigenvalues of a real matrix may be complex: [[0,−1],[1,0]] has λ = ±i.

steps.title: Criterion
steps.body: An n × n matrix is diagonalisable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, iff for each eigenvalue geometric multiplicity (dim of eigenspace) = algebraic multiplicity. Distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalisable. Then P = [eigenvectors], D = diag(eigenvalues), A = PDP⁻¹.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A = [[4,1],[2,3]], P = [[1,1],[1,−2]], D = diag(5, 2). det P = −3, P⁻¹ = (1/3)[[2,1],[1,−1]]. Aⁿ = P diag(5ⁿ, 2ⁿ) P⁻¹. The matrix [[2,1,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,3]] from Lesson 1 is NOT diagonalisable: λ = 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2 but geometric multiplicity 1.

steps.title: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
steps.body: Every square matrix satisfies its characteristic equation. For 2 × 2: A² − (tr A)A + (det A)I = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming repeated eigenvalues mean non-diagonalisable — the identity matrix has λ = 1 repeated and is already diagonal. The columns of P must be in the same order as the entries of D.

steps.title: Inner product
steps.body: On a real vector space, ⟨u, v⟩ is symmetric, linear in each argument and positive definite (⟨v, v⟩ > 0 for v ≠ 0). Examples: dot product on ℝⁿ; ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f(x)g(x) dx on C[0,1]. Norm ‖v‖ = √⟨v, v⟩.

steps.title: Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequality
steps.body: |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖, with equality iff u, v are dependent. Hence ‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ and cos θ = ⟨u, v⟩/(‖u‖‖v‖) is well defined.

steps.title: Gram–Schmidt
steps.body: u₁ = v₁; u₂ = v₂ − (⟨v₂,u₁⟩/⟨u₁,u₁⟩)u₁; u₃ = v₃ − (⟨v₃,u₁⟩/⟨u₁,u₁⟩)u₁ − (⟨v₃,u₂⟩/⟨u₂,u₂⟩)u₂; then normalise eᵢ = uᵢ/‖uᵢ‖.

steps.title: Worked example: functions
steps.body: On C[0,1] with ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫₀¹ fg dx: ⟨1, x⟩ = ½, ‖1‖² = 1. Orthogonalising {1, x}: u₂ = x − ½. Check ∫₀¹ (x − ½) dx = ½ − ½ = 0 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Projecting onto the original vᵢ instead of the new uᵢ. Forgetting to normalise when an orthonormal basis is asked for.

steps.title: Ring theory key points
steps.body: ℤₙ field ⇔ n prime. Finite integral domain ⇒ field. char of a domain is 0 or prime. R/P domain ⇔ P prime; R/M field ⇔ M maximal. F[x]/⟨p⟩ field ⇔ p irreducible; it has qⁿ elements if F = ℤ_q, deg p = n. First isomorphism theorem: R/ker φ ≅ φ(R).

steps.title: Linear algebra key points
steps.body: dim(U + W) = dim U + dim W − dim(U ∩ W). rank + nullity = dim V. Similar ⇒ same det, trace, eigenvalues. Σλ = trace, Πλ = det. Diagonalisable ⇔ GM = AM for every λ. Cayley–Hamilton: p_A(A) = 0. Gram–Schmidt formula and Cauchy–Schwarz.

steps.title: Previous-year-style question
steps.body: Q: Let A = [[1,2],[2,1]]. Find eigenvalues, an orthogonal P with PᵀAP diagonal, and A⁻¹. A: tr 2, det −3 ⇒ λ² − 2λ − 3 = 0 ⇒ λ = 3, −1. Eigenvectors (1,1), (1,−1); normalise: P = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], PᵀAP = diag(3, −1). Cayley–Hamilton: A² − 2A − 3I = 0 ⇒ A⁻¹ = (A − 2I)/3 = (1/3)[[−1,2],[2,−1]].

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body: Why is every field an integral domain? Why is ℤ not a field? Is the zero vector space's basis empty? (Yes, dim {0} = 0.) Can a 3 × 3 real matrix have no real eigenvalue? (No — a real cubic has a real root.)

courses.summary: The ε–δ definition of limits and continuity, differentiability, Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems, Taylor–Maclaurin expansions with L'Hôpital's rule, and successive differentiation with Leibniz's theorem.
outcomes: Learners can prove simple limits with ε–δ
Learners can apply Rolle's and Lagrange's theorems and prove inequalities
Learners can expand functions in Maclaurin series and evaluate indeterminate forms
Learners can find nth derivatives with Leibniz's theorem

scenes.text: An engineer asks how accurately a shaft must be cut so the output stays within 0.01 mm of the target.
That is exactly the ε–δ game: you give me ε, I find a δ.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Limit**: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε
- **Continuity at a**: lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a)
- **Differentiable at a**: f'(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h exists
- Differentiable ⇒ continuous; the converse fails (|x| at 0)
- Discontinuities: removable, jump, infinite, oscillatory (sin(1/x) at 0)

steps.title: Solved: continuity of x sin(1/x)
steps.body:
f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 0.

- |f(x) − 0| ≤ |x| (since |sin| ≤ 1), so take δ = ε ⇒ continuous at 0
- Differentiable at 0? (f(h) − f(0))/h = sin(1/h), which has no limit ⇒ **not differentiable** at 0

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing δ that depends on x (it may depend only on ε and a).
- Assuming continuity implies differentiability.
- Evaluating a limit by plugging in when the expression is undefined at a.
- Forgetting to check left and right limits separately for piecewise functions.

activity.prompt: Classify each function at x = 0.

quiz.q: For lim_{x→2} (5x − 1) = 9, a valid δ is:
quiz.why: We need |(5x − 1) − 9| = 5|x − 2| < ε, which holds when |x − 2| < ε/5, so δ = ε/5 works.

quiz.q: |x| at 0 is:
quiz.why: |x| is continuous at 0, but the left derivative is −1 and the right derivative is +1, so they differ and it is not differentiable there.

quiz.q: Differentiability at a point implies:
quiz.why: If f is differentiable at a point it must be continuous there. The reverse is false, as |x| shows.

quiz.q: sin(1/x) at 0 has a discontinuity of type:
quiz.why: As x → 0, sin(1/x) keeps oscillating between −1 and 1, so no limit exists and it is an oscillatory discontinuity, not a jump or removable one.

quiz.q: x² sin(1/x) (f(0) = 0) has f'(0) =
quiz.why: f'(0) = lim (h² sin(1/h) − 0)/h = lim h sin(1/h), and |h sin(1/h)| ≤ |h| → 0, so f'(0) = 0.

lessons.title: Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems

scenes.text: A car covers 120 km of expressway in 1 hour; the toll booths log entry and exit times.
By Lagrange's MVT, at some instant the speedometer read exactly 120 km/h. Average implies instantaneous.

steps.title: The three theorems
steps.body:
Let f be continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b).

- **Rolle**: if f(a) = f(b), some c ∈ (a, b) has f'(c) = 0
- **Lagrange (MVT)**: some c ∈ (a, b) has f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
- **Cauchy**: for g also such, with g'(x) ≠ 0: (f(b) − f(a))/(g(b) − g(a)) = f'(c)/g'(c)

Consequences: f' = 0 on an interval ⇒ f constant; f' > 0 ⇒ f strictly increasing.

steps.title: Solved: proving an inequality
steps.body:
Show |sin a − sin b| ≤ |a − b|.

- By MVT, sin a − sin b = cos c · (a − b) for some c between a and b
- |cos c| ≤ 1 ⇒ |sin a − sin b| ≤ |a − b| ∎

Similarly, MVT on ln on [1, 1 + x] gives x/(1 + x) < ln(1 + x) < x for x > 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Rolle to |x| on [−1, 1] (not differentiable at 0, and indeed no c works).
- Finding c outside the open interval and accepting it.
- Forgetting to check continuity on the closed interval.
- Thinking c must be unique.

activity.prompt: Find c from Lagrange's MVT for f(x) = x² + 2x on [0, 4].

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem needs f(a):
quiz.why: Rolle's theorem needs f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b). Then f′(c) = 0 for some c.

quiz.q: If f'(x) = 0 on (a, b), then f is:
quiz.why: If f′ = 0 everywhere on (a, b), the MVT gives f(x) − f(y) = f′(c)(x − y) = 0 for any x, y, so f is constant.

quiz.q: MVT c for f(x) = √x on [1, 4]:
Rolle fails for |x| on [−1, 1] because:
quiz.why: Rolle's theorem needs differentiability on the open interval, but |x| has a corner at 0 so f′(0) does not exist, even though f(−1) = f(1).

quiz.q: Cauchy's MVT with g(x) = x reduces to:
quiz.why: With g(x) = x, g′ = 1 and Cauchy's formula f′(c)/g′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/[g(b) − g(a)] becomes the Lagrange mean value theorem.

A few terms of the Maclaurin series, with an error bound from Lagrange's remainder.

steps.title: Expansions
steps.body:
Taylor: f(a + h) = f(a) + hf'(a) + h²f''(a)/2! + … + hⁿ⁻¹f⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾(a)/(n − 1)! + Rₙ, with Lagrange remainder Rₙ = hⁿ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh)/n!, 0 < θ < 1.

- eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …
- sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
- cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …
- ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … (−1 < x ≤ 1)
- (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2! + … (|x| < 1)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying L'Hôpital when the form is not 0/0 or ∞/∞.
- Differentiating the quotient f/g instead of f and g separately.
- Using ln(1 + x) series for x > 1.
- Dropping the factorials in Taylor terms.

quiz.q: Coefficient of x³ in sin x:
quiz.why: The sine series is x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, so the coefficient of x³ is −1/3! = −1/6.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} sin x/x:
quiz.why: The fundamental limit sin x/x → 1 as x → 0 follows from the squeeze theorem on the unit circle, and is also seen by L'Hôpital: cos 0/1 = 1.

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³:
quiz.why: Since sin x = x − x³/6 + …, x − sin x ≈ x³/6, so (x − sin x)/x³ → 1/6.

quiz.q: lim_{x→∞} x/eˣ:
quiz.why: x/eˣ is of the form ∞/∞ and L'Hôpital gives 1/eˣ → 0. The exponential grows faster than any power of x.

quiz.q: Lagrange remainder Rₙ involves:
quiz.why: Lagrange's remainder is Rₙ = hⁿf⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh)/n!, which uses the nth derivative at an intermediate point, not at an end point.

scenes.text: A tutorial sheet asks for the 100th derivative of x²eˣ. Ravi starts differentiating by hand and gives up at the fifth.
Leibniz's theorem does it in one line.

steps.title: Standard nth derivatives
steps.body:
- Dⁿ(e^(ax)) = aⁿ e^(ax)
- Dⁿ sin(ax + b) = aⁿ sin(ax + b + nπ/2); similarly for cos
- Dⁿ (ax + b)⁻¹ = (−1)ⁿ n! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹
- Dⁿ ln(ax + b) = (−1)ⁿ⁻¹ (n − 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ

**Leibniz**: (uv)ₙ = Σ_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) u_{n−r} v_r — choose v as the polynomial so the sum terminates.

steps.title: Solved: x²eˣ
steps.body:
u = eˣ, v = x² (v₁ = 2x, v₂ = 2, v₃ = 0).

- yₙ = eˣ·x² + n·eˣ·2x + C(n,2)·eˣ·2
- yₙ = **eˣ (x² + 2nx + n(n − 1))**
- Check n = 1: eˣ(x² + 2x) ✓

steps.title: Solved: a classic recurrence
steps.body:
If y = sin⁻¹x, show (1 − x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0 and hence (1 − x²)yₙ₊₂ − (2n + 1)xyₙ₊₁ − n²yₙ = 0.

- y₁ = 1/√(1 − x²) ⇒ (1 − x²)y₁² = 1; differentiate: (1 − x²)2y₁y₂ − 2xy₁² = 0 ⇒ (1 − x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0
- Apply Leibniz n times to each product and collect terms ⇒ the stated recurrence ∎

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing the exponential as v (the sum then never terminates).
- Forgetting binomial coefficients C(n, r).
- Sign errors in (−1)ⁿ for reciprocal powers.
- Missing the nπ/2 phase shift for sine and cosine.

questions.q: Lagrange's MVT guarantees a point where the tangent is:

(eˣ − 1)/x is the difference quotient of eˣ at 0, which equals the derivative e⁰ = 1.

questions.why: Rolle's theorem needs f′(c) = 0. For sin x, cos c = 0 on (0, π) gives c = π/2.

questions.q: Assertion: f(x) = x^(2/3) on [−1, 1] satisfies Rolle's theorem. Reason: f(−1) = f(1).
questions.why: The reason is true since f(−1) = f(1) = 1, but f′(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) does not exist at 0, so Rolle's theorem does not apply. The assertion is false.

questions.why: tan x = x + x³/3 + …, so (tan x − x)/x³ → 1/3.

questions.q: y = eˣ sin x. y₂ equals:
questions.why: y₁ = eˣ(sin x + cos x), and differentiating again gives y₂ = eˣ(sin x + cos x + cos x − sin x) = 2eˣ cos x.

questions.q: For f(x) = ln x on [1, e], MVT gives c =
questions.why: MVT: f′(c) = (ln e − ln 1)/(e − 1) = 1/(e − 1). Since f′(c) = 1/c, c = e − 1, which lies in (1, e).

questions.q: Case: Estimate √(1.02) using (1 + x)^(1/2) to two terms beyond 1:

questions.why: (1 + 2x)^(1/x) = exp(ln(1 + 2x)/x), and ln(1 + 2x)/x → 2 as x → 0, so the limit is e².

questions.q: nth derivative of 1/(x² − 1) is:
questions.why: Write 1/(x² − 1) = ½[1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1)]. Since Dⁿ(x − a)⁻¹ = (−1)ⁿ n!/(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹, the stated formula follows.

questions.q: If y = sin⁻¹x, then at x = 0, y₃ equals:
questions.why: From (1 − x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0, the Leibniz recurrence at x = 0 gives yₙ₊₂ = n² yₙ. With y₁(0) = 1, y₃(0) = 1² × 1 = 1.

questions.q: Using MVT, which inequality holds for x > 0?
questions.why: By MVT on ln t over [1, 1 + x], ln(1 + x) = x/c with 1 < c < 1 + x, so x/(1 + x) < ln(1 + x) < x for x > 0.

courses.title: Real Analysis · real numbers, sequences, series, integration
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Completeness and the Archimedean property, convergence of sequences (monotone, Cauchy, Bolzano–Weierstrass), tests for infinite series, and Riemann integration with the fundamental theorem.
outcomes: Learners can find supremum and infimum and use completeness
Learners can prove convergence using ε–N and monotone/Cauchy criteria
Learners can choose and apply series tests
Learners can test Riemann integrability using upper and lower sums

lessons.title: The real numbers: completeness and the Archimedean property

scenes.text: Ancient mathematicians discovered that the diagonal of a unit square is not a ratio of whole numbers.
The rationals have holes; the real numbers fill them. That 'no holes' property is completeness.

steps.title: Supremum, infimum, completeness
steps.body:
- An **upper bound** of S is u with s ≤ u for all s ∈ S; the **supremum** is the least upper bound
- **Completeness axiom**: every non-empty subset of ℝ bounded above has a supremum in ℝ
- ℚ is not complete: {x ∈ ℚ : x² < 2} has no rational supremum
- **Archimedean property**: for any x ∈ ℝ there is n ∈ ℕ with n > x; equivalently, for ε > 0 some 1/n < ε
- **Density**: between any two reals lies a rational (and an irrational)

steps.title: Solved: sup and inf
steps.body:
S = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ} = {0, 1/2, 2/3, …}.

- inf S = **0** (attained at n = 1, so it is the minimum)
- sup S = **1**: every element < 1, and for any ε > 0 choose n > 1/ε so 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε ⇒ nothing smaller than 1 is an upper bound
- 1 ∉ S, so S has no maximum.

steps.title: Solved: √2 is irrational
steps.body:
Suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms.

- 2q² = p² ⇒ p² even ⇒ p even, p = 2k
- 2q² = 4k² ⇒ q² = 2k² ⇒ q even
- Both even contradicts lowest terms ∎

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the supremum must belong to the set.
- Confusing 'bounded' with 'has a maximum'.
- Using completeness for ℚ.
- Writing sup S = ∞ for a set bounded above.

activity.prompt: Match each set with its supremum.

quiz.q: Every non-empty set of reals bounded above has a supremum. This is:
quiz.why: The statement that every non-empty bounded-above set has a least upper bound is the completeness (least upper bound) axiom of the reals. ℚ does not satisfy it.

quiz.q: inf of {1/n : n ∈ ℕ}:
quiz.why: The terms 1/n get arbitrarily close to 0 but never reach it, and every term is positive, so the greatest lower bound is 0.

quiz.q: ℚ fails to be:
quiz.why: ℚ is an ordered field but it is not complete: a bounded set like {q : q² < 2} has no rational supremum, since √2 is a 'hole'.

quiz.q: The Archimedean property says ℕ is:
quiz.why: The Archimedean property says that for any real x there is a natural number n > x, so ℕ has no upper bound in ℝ.

quiz.q: Between two distinct reals there is always:
quiz.why: The rationals are dense in ℝ: between any two distinct real numbers there is a rational (and also an irrational).

scenes.text: Kavya computes √2, √(2 + √2), √(2 + √(2 + √2)) … on her phone; the values creep toward 2.
The sequence is increasing and bounded, so it must converge — and the limit L solves L = √(2 + L).

steps.title: Key theorems
steps.body:
- aₙ → L if ∀ε > 0 ∃N: n ≥ N ⇒ |aₙ − L| < ε
- Limits are unique; convergent sequences are bounded
- **Monotone convergence**: bounded monotone sequences converge (to sup or inf)
- **Cauchy criterion**: (aₙ) converges ⇔ ∀ε ∃N: m, n ≥ N ⇒ |aₘ − aₙ| < ε
- **Bolzano–Weierstrass**: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence
- Sandwich theorem; algebra of limits

steps.title: Solved: a recursive sequence
steps.body:
a₁ = √2, aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ).

- Bounded: if aₙ < 2 then aₙ₊₁ < √4 = 2 (induction)
- Increasing: aₙ₊₁² − aₙ² = 2 + aₙ − aₙ² = (2 − aₙ)(1 + aₙ) > 0
- Converges to L with L = √(2 + L) ⇒ L² − L − 2 = 0 ⇒ **L = 2** (L > 0)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Solving L = g(L) before proving convergence (the equation can have spurious roots).
- Thinking bounded ⇒ convergent ((−1)ⁿ is bounded but diverges).
- Choosing N depending on n.
- Confusing 'Cauchy' with 'consecutive terms get close' (aₙ = √n has aₙ₊₁ − aₙ → 0 but diverges).

statements.why: Beyond N terms are within 1 of L.

statements.s: If aₙ₊₁ − aₙ → 0 then (aₙ) is Cauchy.
Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.
An increasing sequence bounded above converges to its supremum.

quiz.q: lim n/(n + 1):
quiz.why: n/(n + 1) = 1/(1 + 1/n), and as n → ∞, 1/n → 0, so the limit is 1.

quiz.q: (−1)ⁿ has a convergent subsequence because it is:
quiz.why: (−1)ⁿ is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence (for example, the even terms → 1). It is not monotone or Cauchy.

quiz.q: lim (1 + 1/n)ⁿ:
quiz.why: The limit of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n → ∞ is the definition of e.

quiz.q: lim n^(1/n):
A sequence in ℝ converges iff it is:
quiz.why: Because ℝ is complete, a real sequence converges exactly when it is Cauchy. Bounded or monotone alone is not enough (bounded alone, for example).

scenes.text: Half a pizza, then a quarter, then an eighth… Zain realises he'll never exceed one whole pizza.
But 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … (the harmonic series) grows without bound. Tests tell the two kinds apart.

steps.title: The toolbox
steps.body:
- **nth-term test**: if aₙ ↛ 0, Σaₙ diverges (the converse is false)
- **p-series**: Σ1/nᵖ converges ⇔ p > 1; geometric Σrⁿ converges ⇔ |r| < 1
- **Comparison / limit comparison** with a known series
- **Ratio (d'Alembert)**: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|; L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive
- **Root (Cauchy)**: L = lim |aₙ|^(1/n), same rule
- **Leibniz (alternating)**: Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹bₙ converges if bₙ decreases to 0
- Absolute convergence ⇒ convergence; conditional = converges but not absolutely

steps.title: Solved: ratio test
steps.body:
- Σ n/2ⁿ: ratio = (n + 1)/(2n) → 1/2 < 1 ⇒ **converges**
- Σ n!/nⁿ: ratio = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ → 1/e < 1 ⇒ **converges**
- Σ 2ⁿ/n²: ratio → 2 ⇒ **diverges**

steps.title: Solved: comparison and alternating
steps.body:
- Σ 1/(n² + n) = Σ (1/n − 1/(n + 1)) telescopes to **1**
- Σ 1/√(n² + 1): limit comparison with 1/n (ratio → 1) ⇒ **diverges**
- Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n converges (Leibniz) to ln 2, but not absolutely ⇒ **conditionally convergent**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding convergence from aₙ → 0.
- Using the ratio test on p-series (L = 1 always — inconclusive).
- Rearranging a conditionally convergent series and expecting the same sum.
- Forgetting absolute values in the ratio test for alternating terms.

activity.prompt: Does the series converge?

quiz.q: Σ1/nᵖ converges iff:
quiz.why: By the p-series test, Σ1/nᵖ converges when p > 1 and diverges for p ≤ 1.

quiz.q: If lim aₙ = 0, then Σaₙ:
quiz.why: aₙ → 0 is necessary but not sufficient. The harmonic series has terms → 0 yet diverges, while Σ1/n² also has terms → 0 and converges, so it may or may not converge.

quiz.q: Ratio test with L = 1:
quiz.why: If the ratio limit L = 1, the ratio test gives no information; both convergent (Σ1/n²) and divergent (Σ1/n) series give L = 1.

quiz.q: Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n is:
quiz.why: The alternating harmonic series converges by the Leibniz test, but the series of absolute values is the divergent harmonic series, so it is conditionally convergent.

quiz.q: Sum of Σ_{n≥0} (1/3)ⁿ:
quiz.why: This is a geometric series with ratio 1/3, so the sum is 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2.

lessons.title: Riemann integration and the fundamental theorem

scenes.text: A surveyor estimates an irregular plot by laying ever thinner strips over it.
If the over-estimate and under-estimate squeeze together, the area is well defined — that is Riemann integrability.

steps.title: Upper and lower sums
steps.body:
For bounded f on [a, b] and a partition P: U(P, f) = Σ Mᵢ Δxᵢ, L(P, f) = Σ mᵢ Δxᵢ (Mᵢ, mᵢ = sup, inf on each piece).

- f is **Riemann integrable** ⇔ for every ε > 0 there is P with U − L < ε
- Continuous ⇒ integrable; monotone ⇒ integrable; finitely many discontinuities (bounded f) ⇒ integrable
- Dirichlet's function (1 on ℚ, 0 elsewhere) is **not** Riemann integrable: U = 1, L = 0 always
- **FTC**: if F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f, f continuous ⇒ F' = f; and ∫ₐᵇ f = G(b) − G(a) for any antiderivative G

steps.title: Solved: ∫₀¹ x dx from the definition
steps.body:
Uniform partition into n parts, Δx = 1/n.

- U = Σ (i/n)(1/n) = (n + 1)/(2n); L = Σ ((i − 1)/n)(1/n) = (n − 1)/(2n)
- U − L = 1/n → 0 ⇒ integrable
- Both tend to **1/2**

steps.title: Solved: differentiating an integral
steps.body:
d/dx ∫₀^(x²) sin t dt.

- Let F(u) = ∫₀ᵘ sin t dt, so F'(u) = sin u
- By the chain rule: sin(x²) · 2x = **2x sin(x²)**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every bounded function is integrable (Dirichlet's isn't).
- Forgetting the chain-rule factor when the upper limit is a function of x.
- Applying FTC part 1 when f is discontinuous at the point.
- Confusing sup on each subinterval with the function value at the right endpoint (equal only for increasing f).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to show f is Riemann integrable directly.
items: Fix a partition Pₙ of [a, b] into n equal parts
Compute Mᵢ and mᵢ on each subinterval
Write U(Pₙ, f) and L(Pₙ, f) in closed form
Show U − L → 0 as n → ∞
Conclude integrability and identify the common limit

quiz.q: Dirichlet's function on [0, 1] is:
quiz.why: Dirichlet's function is 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals. Every subinterval has both, so upper sum U = 1 and lower sum L = 0 for every partition, so it is not Riemann integrable.

quiz.q: Continuous functions on [a, b] are:
quiz.why: A function continuous on a closed interval [a, b] is uniformly continuous, which makes U − L small, so it is always Riemann integrable.

quiz.q: d/dx ∫₁ˣ eᵗ² dt:
quiz.why: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, d/dx ∫₁ˣ e^(t²) dt = e^(x²), the integrand evaluated at the upper limit.

quiz.q: For f increasing on [0, 1] with n equal parts, U − L equals:
quiz.why: For an increasing f, U − L = Σ[f(xᵢ) − f(xᵢ₋₁)]·(1/n), which telescopes to (f(1) − f(0))/n.

quiz.q: d/dx ∫₀^(3x) cos t dt:
quiz.why: With upper limit 3x, the chain rule gives cos(3x) × d(3x)/dx = 3 cos 3x.

questions.q: sup of (0, 1):
questions.why: The set (0, 1) has upper bounds 1, 1.2, 2 …; the least of them is 1, so sup = 1 even though 1 is not in the set.

questions.q: The harmonic series Σ1/n:
questions.why: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges (the partial sums grow like ln n), even though its terms tend to 0.

questions.q: Every convergent sequence is:
questions.why: Every convergent sequence is bounded, since after some N all terms lie near the limit and only finitely many terms remain outside.
Dividing by n²: (3 + 1/n²)/(1 − 5/n²) → 3.
By the p-series test, 1.01 > 1, so Σ1/n^1.01 converges, though very slowly.

questions.q: A bounded function with finitely many discontinuities on [a, b] is:
questions.why: A bounded function on [a, b] with finitely many discontinuities is Riemann integrable. It need not be continuous or differentiable.

questions.q: Assertion: (√n) is not Cauchy. Reason: √(n + 1) − √n → 0.
options: Both true, reason does not explain assertion
questions.why: Both are true: √(n + 1) − √n = 1/(√(n+1) + √n) → 0, and √n is unbounded so it is not Cauchy. But shrinking consecutive gaps do not imply Cauchy, so the reason does not explain it.

questions.q: Σ nⁿ/n!: by the ratio test it:
questions.why: The ratio of consecutive terms is (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e > 1, so by the ratio test the series diverges (the terms do not even go to 0).

questions.q: inf of {x : x² − 3x + 2 < 0}:
questions.why: x² − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)(x − 2) < 0 exactly when 1 < x < 2, so the set is (1, 2) and its infimum is 1.

questions.q: Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n is:
questions.why: The Leibniz test shows convergence, since 1/√n decreases to 0. The absolute series Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, which diverges, so the convergence is conditional.

questions.q: Case: aₙ = (1 + 2/n)ⁿ. Limit:
questions.why: Using (1 + x/n)ⁿ → eˣ with x = 2, the limit is e².

questions.q: d/dx ∫ₓ^(x²) t dt:
questions.why: By Leibniz's rule, d/dx ∫ₓ^(x²) t dt = x² · 2x − x · 1 = 2x³ − x.
1/(n(n + 2)) = ½(1/n − 1/(n + 2)). The sum telescopes, leaving ½(1 + ½) = 3/4.

questions.q: Root test on Σ (n/(n + 1))^(n²):
questions.why: The nth root of the term is (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)⁻ⁿ → 1/e < 1, so by the root test the series converges.

questions.q: lim_{n→∞} (1/n)Σ_{k=1}^{n} (k/n)² as a Riemann sum equals:
questions.why: The sum (1/n)Σ(k/n)² is a Riemann sum for ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3.

courses.title: Group Theory · groups to the isomorphism theorem
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Group axioms with standard examples, subgroups and cyclic groups, cosets and Lagrange's theorem with number-theory consequences, and normal subgroups, quotient groups and homomorphisms.
outcomes: Learners can verify group axioms and compute element orders
Learners can find subgroups and generators of cyclic groups
Learners can apply Lagrange's theorem and Fermat's little theorem
Learners can use the first isomorphism theorem

scenes.text: It is 10 o'clock; 5 hours later it is 3 o'clock. Neel realises clock arithmetic never leaves the 12 numbers.
Closure, an identity (adding 12), inverses (going back) — the integers mod 12 form a group.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **group** (G, ∗) satisfies:
- Closure: a ∗ b ∈ G
- Associativity: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c)
- Identity e: a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a
- Inverses: a ∗ a⁻¹ = e

Abelian if also a ∗ b = b ∗ a.

Examples: (ℤ, +), (ℚ*, ×), ℤₙ under addition mod n, U(n) = {k : gcd(k, n) = 1} under multiplication mod n, Sₙ (permutations, |Sₙ| = n!), GL(2, ℝ).
Non-examples: (ℕ, +) (no inverses), (ℤ, ×) (2 has no inverse).

steps.title: Solved: order of an element
steps.body:
In U(10) = {1, 3, 7, 9}:

- 3¹ = 3, 3² = 9, 3³ = 27 ≡ 7, 3⁴ = 21 ≡ 1 ⇒ |3| = **4**
- So U(10) = ⟨3⟩ is **cyclic**.
- In U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7}, every element squares to 1 ⇒ not cyclic (it is the Klein four-group).

steps.title: Solved: S₃ is non-abelian
steps.body:
Let σ = (1 2), τ = (1 3) (compose right to left).

- στ: 1 → 3 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2, 2 → 2 → 1 ⇒ (1 3 2)
- τσ: 1 → 2 → 2, 2 → 1 → 3, 3 → 3 → 1 ⇒ (1 2 3)
- στ ≠ τσ ⇒ S₃ is the smallest non-abelian group (order 6)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to check that inverses lie inside the set.
- Assuming all groups are abelian.
- Mixing composition conventions for permutations (state yours).
- Confusing the order of a group with the order of an element.

activity.prompt: Is it a group?

quiz.q: Order of S₄:
quiz.why: The symmetric group S₄ consists of all permutations of 4 objects, so its order is 4! = 24.

quiz.q: Elements of U(12):
quiz.why: U(12) is the set of integers in 1–11 coprime to 12: {1, 5, 7, 11}, a group under multiplication mod 12.

quiz.q: Order of 2 in ℤ₈ (addition):
quiz.why: In ℤ₈, 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 ≡ 0 and no smaller multiple is 0 mod 8, so the order of 2 is 4.

quiz.q: The smallest non-abelian group has order:
quiz.why: Groups of order 1–5 are abelian, and S₃ of order 6 is the smallest non-abelian group.

quiz.q: (ℤ, ×) fails because:
quiz.why: (ℤ, ×) has an identity 1 and is associative and closed, but only 1 and −1 have integer inverses, so it is not a group.

scenes.text: A gear with 12 teeth meshes with one of 8 teeth. Maya asks how often the same teeth meet again.
Orders, gcds and cyclic subgroups answer it — group theory hiding in a gearbox.

steps.title: Subgroup tests and cyclic facts
steps.body:
- **One-step test**: non-empty H ⊆ G is a subgroup iff a, b ∈ H ⇒ ab⁻¹ ∈ H
- **Finite test**: a non-empty finite subset closed under the operation is a subgroup
- A group is **cyclic** if G = ⟨a⟩
- Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic
- In ℤₙ: order of k is n/gcd(k, n); generators are k with gcd(k, n) = 1 (there are φ(n)); for each divisor d of n there is exactly one subgroup of order d

steps.title: Solved: ℤ₁₂
Solved: is H a subgroup?
steps.body:
H = {even integers} in (ℤ, +): a, b even ⇒ a − b even ✓ ⇒ subgroup.
K = {odd integers}: 0 ∉ K ⇒ **not** a subgroup.
Centre Z(G) = {z : zg = gz ∀g} is always a subgroup; Z(S₃) = {e}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking closure but forgetting inverses for infinite subsets.
- Thinking every abelian group is cyclic (U(8) isn't).
- Writing generator count as n − 1.
- Forgetting that the union of two subgroups is usually not a subgroup.

activity.prompt: How many generators does the cyclic group ℤ₃₀ have?

quiz.q: Order of 6 in ℤ₁₅:
quiz.why: The order of a in ℤₙ is n/gcd(a, n). For 6 in ℤ₁₅: 15/gcd(6, 15) = 15/3 = 5.

quiz.q: Number of subgroups of ℤ₁₀:
quiz.why: A cyclic group of order 10 has one subgroup for each divisor of 10: orders 1, 2, 5 and 10, so 4 subgroups.

quiz.q: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is:
quiz.why: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, which follows from the division algorithm.
φ(9) counts numbers up to 9 coprime to 9: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, so φ(9) = 6 (or 9 × (1 − 1/3) = 6).

quiz.q: Centre of an abelian group G is:
quiz.why: In an abelian group every element commutes with every other, so the centre Z(G) is all of G.

scenes.text: Cryptography needs things like 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7 computed instantly.
Lagrange's theorem gives Fermat's little theorem, which makes such powers easy.

steps.title: Cosets
steps.body:
For H ≤ G, the left coset aH = {ah : h ∈ H}.

- Cosets are equal or disjoint, and all have |H| elements ⇒ they partition G
- **Lagrange**: |G| = [G : H] · |H|, so |H| divides |G|
- Corollaries: order of any element divides |G|; a^|G| = e; every group of prime order is cyclic
- **Fermat**: p prime, p ∤ a ⇒ a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) (apply Lagrange to U(p))
- **Euler**: gcd(a, n) = 1 ⇒ a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n)
- The converse of Lagrange fails: A₄ (order 12) has no subgroup of order 6

steps.title: Solved: possible subgroup orders
steps.body: A group of order 15 can only have subgroups of orders **1, 3, 5, 15**. A group of order 7 has no proper non-trivial subgroups, so it is cyclic and generated by any non-identity element.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a subgroup exists for every divisor (true for cyclic groups, false in general).
- Using Fermat when p divides a.
- Mixing left and right cosets in non-abelian groups.
- Forgetting [G : H] counts cosets, not elements.

activity.prompt: Using Euler's theorem, find 7²²² mod 10. (φ(10) = 4)

quiz.q: A group of order 13 is:
quiz.why: A group of prime order p has no proper nontrivial subgroups (Lagrange), so any non-identity element generates it and it is cyclic.

quiz.q: Possible order of an element in a group of order 20:
quiz.why: By Lagrange's theorem, the order of an element divides the group order. Among the options only 5 divides 20.

quiz.q: Index of H = {0, 4, 8} in ℤ₁₂:
quiz.why: H = {0, 4, 8} has 3 elements, so the index in ℤ₁₂ is 12/3 = 4.

quiz.q: 2¹⁰ mod 11:
quiz.why: By Fermat's little theorem, since 11 is prime and 2 is not a multiple of 11, 2¹⁰ ≡ 1 mod 11.

quiz.q: Lagrange's converse fails for:
quiz.why: A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6, so the converse of Lagrange's theorem fails. ℤ₆, ℤ₁₂ and S₃ have subgroups of every order dividing the group order.

scenes.text: Days of the week repeat every 7; to know the weekday, you only need the remainder of the day number mod 7.
That is the quotient ℤ/7ℤ — identifying everything that differs by a multiple of 7.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- N ⊴ G (normal) if gNg⁻¹ = N for all g (equivalently gN = Ng)
- Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal; any subgroup of index 2 is normal
- **Quotient group** G/N: cosets with (aN)(bN) = abN; |G/N| = |G|/|N|
- **Homomorphism** φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b); kernel ker φ = {g : φ(g) = e} is normal
- φ injective ⇔ ker φ = {e}
- **First isomorphism theorem**: G/ker φ ≅ φ(G)

steps.title: Solved: ℤ → ℤₙ
steps.body:
φ(k) = k mod n is a homomorphism of (ℤ, +) onto ℤₙ.

- ker φ = nℤ
- First isomorphism theorem ⇒ **ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ**

steps.title: Solved: determinant
steps.body:
det : GL(n, ℝ) → ℝ* is a homomorphism (det(AB) = det A · det B), onto.

- ker = SL(n, ℝ) (matrices of determinant 1), so SL(n, ℝ) ⊴ GL(n, ℝ)
- **GL(n, ℝ)/SL(n, ℝ) ≅ ℝ***
- In S₃, A₃ = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2)} has index 2 ⇒ normal; the subgroup {e, (1 2)} is not normal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forming G/H when H is not normal (the operation is not well defined).
- Thinking normal means 'commutes with every element' elementwise (it is setwise).
- Forgetting that φ(e) = e and φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹ follow automatically.
- Mapping into the wrong operation (additive vs multiplicative).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to prove G/ker φ ≅ φ(G).
items: Define ψ(g ker φ) = φ(g)
Show ψ is well defined: g ker φ = h ker φ ⇒ φ(g) = φ(h)
Show ψ is a homomorphism using the coset product
Show ψ is injective: kernel of ψ is the identity coset
Show ψ is onto φ(G), hence an isomorphism

quiz.q: A subgroup of index 2 is always:
quiz.why: A subgroup of index 2 has only two left cosets (H and G∖H), which are also the right cosets, so it is normal. It need not be abelian or cyclic.

quiz.q: The kernel of a homomorphism is:
quiz.why: The kernel of any homomorphism is a normal subgroup of the domain, and it need not be trivial.
⟨5⟩ in ℤ₂₀ = {0, 5, 10, 15} has 4 elements, so the quotient has 20/4 = 5 elements.

quiz.q: A homomorphism is injective iff its kernel is:
quiz.why: A homomorphism is one-one exactly when its kernel is trivial, {e}, since φ(a) = φ(b) means ab⁻¹ is in the kernel.

quiz.q: GL(n, ℝ)/SL(n, ℝ) is isomorphic to:
quiz.why: The determinant map GL(n, ℝ) → ℝ* is an onto homomorphism with kernel SL(n, ℝ), so by the first isomorphism theorem the quotient ≅ ℝ*.

questions.q: The identity of (ℤ, +) is:
questions.why: The identity of an additive group is the element with a + e = a. In (ℤ, +) this is 0.

questions.q: |S₃| =
questions.why: S₃ is the group of permutations of three objects, so |S₃| = 3! = 6.

questions.q: A group in which ab = ba always is:
questions.why: A group where ab = ba for all a, b is abelian (commutative). Cyclic groups are abelian but not every abelian group is cyclic.

questions.q: Order of 4 in ℤ₁₀:
questions.why: The order of 4 in ℤ₁₀ is 10/gcd(4, 10) = 10/2 = 5.

questions.q: Number of generators of ℤ₈:
questions.why: The generators of ℤ₈ are the numbers coprime to 8: 1, 3, 5, 7, so there are φ(8) = 4.

questions.q: Every group of prime order is:
questions.why: In a group of prime order, any non-identity element has order dividing the prime and so equal to it by Lagrange, so it generates the group and the group is cyclic.

questions.q: Assertion: U(8) is not cyclic. Reason: Every non-identity element of U(8) has order 2.
questions.why: U(8) = {1, 3, 5, 7}, and 3² = 5² = 7² = 1, so every non-identity element has order 2. A cyclic group of order 4 would need an element of order 4, so U(8) is not cyclic. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: 5³⁸ mod 11:
questions.why: By Fermat 5¹⁰ ≡ 1 mod 11, so 5³⁸ ≡ 5⁸. Then 5² = 25 ≡ 3, 5⁴ ≡ 9, 5⁸ ≡ 81 ≡ 4.

questions.q: Which subgroup of S₃ is normal?
questions.why: A₃ has index 2 in S₃, so it is normal. The subgroups of order 2 are not normal in S₃.

questions.q: Case: φ : ℤ₁₂ → ℤ₄, φ(x) = x mod 4. |ker φ| is:
questions.why: The kernel is {x ∈ ℤ₁₂ : x ≡ 0 mod 4} = {0, 4, 8}, which has 3 elements.

questions.q: Order of the permutation (1 2 3)(4 5) in S₅:
questions.why: The order of a product of disjoint cycles is the lcm of the cycle lengths: lcm(3, 2) = 6.

questions.q: Number of elements of order 5 in ℤ₂₅:
questions.why: A cyclic group ℤ₂₅ has a unique subgroup of order 5, and it has φ(5) = 4 elements of order 5.

questions.q: Number of homomorphisms from ℤ₁₂ to ℤ₁₈:
questions.why: A homomorphism from ℤ₁₂ is fixed by the image of 1, which must have order dividing 12 and 18, so an element of ℤ₁₈ of order dividing gcd(12, 18) = 6. There are 6 such elements, so 6 homomorphisms.

questions.q: A group of order 4 is isomorphic to:
questions.why: Up to isomorphism there are two groups of order 4: cyclic ℤ₄ and the Klein four-group ℤ₂ × ℤ₂. S₃ has order 6.

questions.q: If G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is:
questions.why: If G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian, and so Z(G) = G. This is a standard theorem.

courses.title: Linear Algebra · spaces, maps, eigenvalues, orthogonality
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Vector spaces, bases and dimension, linear transformations and rank–nullity, eigenvalues with Cayley–Hamilton and diagonalisation, and inner product spaces with Gram–Schmidt.
outcomes: Learners can test subspaces, independence and bases
Learners can find kernel, range and verify rank–nullity
Learners can compute eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalise
Learners can orthonormalise with Gram–Schmidt

scenes.text: With red, green and blue lights, Ira can make every colour on her screen.
Three independent directions span the space; adding yellow (= red + green) adds nothing new. That is a basis.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Subspace test**: W ⊆ V non-empty, closed under addition and scalar multiplication (equivalently au + bv ∈ W)
- **Span** S = all linear combinations of S
- **Linearly independent**: c₁v₁ + … + cₖvₖ = 0 ⇒ all cᵢ = 0
- **Basis**: independent and spanning; dimension = number of basis vectors
- In ℝⁿ, n vectors form a basis ⇔ the determinant of the matrix they form is non-zero
- dim(U + W) = dim U + dim W − dim(U ∩ W)

steps.title: Solved: is it a basis of ℝ³?
Solved: dimension of a plane
steps.body:
W = {(x, y, z) : x + y + z = 0}.

- z = −x − y ⇒ (x, y, −x − y) = x(1, 0, −1) + y(0, 1, −1)
- Basis {(1, 0, −1), (0, 1, −1)} ⇒ **dim W = 2**
- W' = {x + y + z = 1} is not a subspace (no zero vector).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to check that 0 is in a candidate subspace.
- Assuming any 3 vectors in ℝ³ form a basis.
- Confusing 'spanning' with 'independent'.
- Thinking the union of subspaces is a subspace.

statements.s: Any set containing the zero vector is dependent.
The set of 2 × 2 real matrices has dimension 4.
{(x, y) : xy = 0} is a subspace of ℝ².
Polynomials of degree ≤ 3 form a space of dimension 4.

quiz.q: Dimension of ℝ⁵:
quiz.why: ℝ⁵ has the standard basis e₁,…,e₅ with 5 vectors, so its dimension is 5.

quiz.q: More than n vectors in ℝⁿ are always:
quiz.why: In ℝⁿ at most n vectors can be linearly independent, so any set with more than n vectors is dependent.

quiz.q: If dim U = 3, dim W = 4 in ℝ⁵ and dim(U + W) = 5, then dim(U ∩ W) =
quiz.why: dim(U ∩ W) = dim U + dim W − dim(U + W) = 3 + 4 − 5 = 2.

quiz.q: A subspace must contain:
quiz.why: A subspace is closed under scalar multiplication, so multiplying any vector by 0 shows that the zero vector must be in it.
Any (a, b) = a(1, 0) + b(0, 1), so these two vectors span all of ℝ².

scenes.text: A torch casts a 3-D object's shadow on a 2-D wall: a linear map ℝ³ → ℝ².
Points along the beam all land on the same spot — they form the kernel. Rank–nullity counts what survives and what is lost.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- T : V → W is **linear** if T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v)
- Kernel ker T = {v : T(v) = 0} (subspace of V); range Im T (subspace of W)
- **Rank–nullity**: dim V = rank T + nullity T
- T injective ⇔ ker T = {0}; for dim V = dim W, injective ⇔ surjective
- Matrix of T: columns are T(basis vectors) written in the target basis
- Change of basis: [T]_B' = P⁻¹[T]_B P (similar matrices)

steps.title: Solved: kernel and range
steps.body:
T(x, y, z) = (x + y, y + z), ℝ³ → ℝ².

- ker: x + y = 0, y + z = 0 ⇒ (x, y, z) = t(1, −1, 1) ⇒ **nullity 1**
- Rank = 3 − 1 = **2** ⇒ T is onto ℝ²
- Matrix: [[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]]

steps.title: Solved: linear or not?
steps.body:
- T(x) = x + 1 on ℝ: T(0) = 1 ≠ 0 ⇒ **not linear**
- D(p) = p' on polynomials of degree ≤ 3: linear; kernel = constants (nullity 1), rank 3 (range = degree ≤ 2) ✓ 1 + 3 = 4

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing images of basis vectors as rows instead of columns.
- Using dim W instead of dim V in rank–nullity.
- Calling an affine map (with a constant term) linear.
- Forgetting that rank of a matrix = rank of its transpose.

activity.prompt: A linear map T : ℝ⁷ → ℝ⁴ is onto. What is the dimension of its kernel?

quiz.q: Rank–nullity states dim V =
quiz.why: The rank–nullity theorem says that for a linear map T on V, dim V = rank T + nullity T.

quiz.q: T linear ⇒ T(0) =
quiz.why: Linearity gives T(0) = T(0·v) = 0·T(v) = 0, the zero vector.

quiz.q: A linear map ℝ³ → ℝ⁵ can be:
quiz.why: The image of ℝ³ has dimension at most 3, but ℝ⁵ has dimension 5, so T can never be onto; it can be one-one (e.g. T(x, y, z) = (x, y, z, 0, 0)).

quiz.q: Nullity of the zero map on ℝ⁴:
quiz.why: The zero map sends every vector to 0, so the kernel is all of ℝ⁴ and the nullity is 4.

quiz.q: Similar matrices have the same:
quiz.why: Similar matrices B = P⁻¹AP have the same characteristic polynomial, so they have the same eigenvalues (and determinant and trace).

scenes.text: Spinning a globe, Aditi notices points on the axis stay put while others move.
Directions a transformation only stretches are its eigenvectors; the stretch factors are eigenvalues.

steps.title: Core results
steps.body:
- Av = λv (v ≠ 0); eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0
- Sum of eigenvalues = trace; product = determinant
- **Cayley–Hamilton**: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation
- A is diagonalisable ⇔ it has n independent eigenvectors; distinct eigenvalues suffice. Then A = PDP⁻¹ and Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹
- Real symmetric matrices: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors (always diagonalisable)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Accepting v = 0 as an eigenvector.
- Thinking repeated eigenvalues prevent diagonalisation always (the identity matrix is diagonal!).
- Sign slips in det(A − λI).
- Forgetting that eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.

activity.prompt: A 3 × 3 matrix has eigenvalues 1, 2 and 4. What is det(A²)?

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of [[2, 0], [0, 3]]:
quiz.why: The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, 2 and 3.

quiz.q: Sum of eigenvalues equals:
quiz.why: The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of the matrix. The product equals the determinant.

quiz.q: If λ is an eigenvalue of A, then λ² is an eigenvalue of:
quiz.why: If Av = λv then A²v = A(λv) = λ²v, so λ² is an eigenvalue of A².

quiz.q: A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is:
quiz.why: If 0 is an eigenvalue then det A = product of eigenvalues = 0, so A is singular (not invertible).

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are:
quiz.why: Real symmetric matrices have only real eigenvalues, by the spectral theorem.

scenes.text: A surveyor has two slanted reference lines and wants perpendicular ones.
Gram–Schmidt removes from each new vector its shadow on the previous ones.

steps.title: Inner product spaces
steps.body:
- ⟨u, v⟩ is linear, symmetric (conjugate-symmetric over ℂ) and positive definite; ‖v‖ = √⟨v, v⟩
- **Cauchy–Schwarz**: |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖; triangle inequality follows
- Orthogonal: ⟨u, v⟩ = 0; orthonormal: also unit length
- **Gram–Schmidt**: u₁ = v₁; uₖ = vₖ − Σⱼ<ₖ (⟨vₖ, uⱼ⟩/⟨uⱼ, uⱼ⟩) uⱼ, then normalise
- Orthogonal matrix: QᵀQ = I (preserves lengths)

steps.title: Solved: projection
steps.body: Projection of b = (3, 4) onto a = (1, 0): (⟨b, a⟩/⟨a, a⟩)a = (3, 0). The error (0, 4) is orthogonal to a — the idea behind least-squares fitting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting projections onto the original vᵢ instead of the new uᵢ.
- Normalising too early and then using the wrong denominator.
- Assuming orthogonal vectors must be unit vectors.
- Forgetting conjugates in complex inner products.

activity.prompt: Order the Gram–Schmidt steps for three vectors.
items: Set u₁ = v₁
Subtract from v₂ its projection on u₁ to get u₂
Subtract from v₃ its projections on u₁ and u₂ to get u₃
Check pairwise inner products are zero
Divide each uᵢ by its norm

quiz.why: The dot product is 1·2 + 2·(−1) = 2 − 2 = 0, so the vectors are orthogonal.

quiz.q: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality:
quiz.why: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality states |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖. The equation with ‖u + v‖ is the case of equality for the triangle inequality, not the general rule.

quiz.q: Orthogonal matrices satisfy:
quiz.why: An orthogonal matrix has orthonormal columns, which is the condition QᵀQ = I.

quiz.q: Orthonormal vectors are automatically:
quiz.why: If c₁e₁ + … + cₙeₙ = 0 for orthonormal vectors, taking the inner product with eᵢ gives cᵢ = 0, so they are linearly independent.

questions.q: Dimension of the space of 3 × 3 real matrices:
questions.why: A 3 × 3 matrix has 9 independent entries, so the space has dimension 9, with the 9 matrix units as a basis.

questions.q: Eigenvalues of an upper triangular matrix are:
questions.why: For a triangular matrix det(A − λI) is the product of (aᵢᵢ − λ), so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.

questions.q: A linear map sends 0 to:
questions.why: Linearity forces T(0) = 0 for any linear map.
The second row is twice the first, so there is only one independent row and the rank is 1.

questions.q: Which set is a subspace of ℝ³?
questions.why: A subspace needs to contain 0 and be closed under addition and scalar multiples. x = 2y is a homogeneous linear condition, so it works; x = 1, x ≥ 0 and xyz = 0 fail.

questions.q: det(A) = 6 for a 3 × 3 A. det(2A):
questions.why: For an n × n matrix, det(kA) = kⁿ det A. For n = 3 and k = 2: 2³ × 6 = 48.

questions.q: Assertion: A matrix with distinct eigenvalues is diagonalisable. Reason: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent.
questions.why: Both are true: eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so n distinct eigenvalues give n independent eigenvectors, a basis. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Nullity of T : ℝ⁴ → ℝ³, T(x, y, z, w) = (x, y, 0):
questions.why: The image is {(x, y, 0)} with dimension 2, so by rank–nullity nullity = 4 − 2 = 2.

questions.q: Eigenvalues of [[0, 1], [1, 0]]:
questions.why: The characteristic equation is λ² − 1 = 0, so the eigenvalues are 1 and −1.

questions.q: Case: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. A¹⁰ has eigenvalues:
questions.why: A is symmetric with eigenvalues 3 and 1 (trace 4, det 3). The eigenvalues of A¹⁰ are 3¹⁰ and 1¹⁰ = 1.

questions.q: Using Cayley–Hamilton for A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] (char. eq. λ² − 5λ − 2 = 0), A² equals:
questions.why: By Cayley–Hamilton, A² − 5A − 2I = 0, so A² = 5A + 2I.

questions.q: Gram–Schmidt on (1, 0), (1, 1) gives second orthogonal vector:
questions.why: Subtract from (1, 1) its projection on (1, 0): (1, 1) − 1·(1, 0) = (0, 1), which is orthogonal to (1, 0).

questions.q: A 4 × 4 matrix A satisfies A² = 0, A ≠ 0. Maximum possible rank of A:
questions.why: A² = 0 means the image lies inside the kernel, so rank ≤ nullity. With rank + nullity = 4, rank ≤ 2.

questions.q: If λ = 2 is an eigenvalue of invertible A, then an eigenvalue of A⁻¹ + 3I is:
questions.why: If Av = 2v then A⁻¹v = ½v, so (A⁻¹ + 3I)v = (½ + 3)v = 3.5v.
The matrix has eigenvalue 1 repeated twice but only one independent eigenvector, so it does not have a full set of eigenvectors and it is not diagonalisable. It is neither symmetric nor orthogonal.

courses.title: Differential Equations · first order to Laplace transforms
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Separable, exact, linear and Bernoulli equations; second-order linear equations with constant coefficients; Cauchy–Euler equations and variation of parameters; and solving initial-value problems with Laplace transforms.
outcomes: Learners can classify and solve first-order ODEs
Learners can find complementary functions and particular integrals
Learners can solve Cauchy–Euler equations and use variation of parameters
Learners can solve IVPs using Laplace transforms

scenes.text: Your chai cools fast at first, then slowly. Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − T_room).
A separable first-order ODE — the solution is an exponential approach to room temperature.

steps.title: Four standard types
steps.body:
- **Separable**: dy/dx = f(x)g(y) ⇒ ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx
- **Linear**: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x); integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx); y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C
- **Exact**: M dx + N dy = 0 with ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x; find F with F_x = M, F_y = N; solution F = C
- **Bernoulli**: dy/dx + Py = Qyⁿ; substitute v = y^(1−n) to make it linear

steps.title: Solved: linear and separable
steps.body:
- dy/dx = xy ⇒ dy/y = x dx ⇒ **y = Ce^(x²/2)**
- dy/dx + y = eˣ: IF = eˣ ⇒ (yeˣ)' = e^(2x) ⇒ yeˣ = e^(2x)/2 + C ⇒ **y = eˣ/2 + Ce^(−x)**

steps.title: Solved: exact and Bernoulli
steps.body:
- (2xy + 3)dx + (x² + 4y)dy = 0: M_y = 2x = N_x ✓. F = x²y + 3x + g(y), F_y = x² + g' = x² + 4y ⇒ g = 2y² ⇒ **x²y + 3x + 2y² = C**
- dy/dx + y = y²: v = 1/y ⇒ dv/dx − v = −1 ⇒ v = 1 + Ceˣ ⇒ **y = 1/(1 + Ceˣ)**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the constant of integration (or adding it in the wrong place).
- Dividing by g(y) and losing equilibrium solutions like y = 0.
- Using IF = e^(∫P) with the equation not in standard form (coefficient of y' must be 1).
- Checking exactness with ∂M/∂x instead of ∂M/∂y.

activity.prompt: Match the equation to its type.

quiz.q: Integrating factor of dy/dx + 2y = x:
quiz.why: For y′ + P y = Q, the integrating factor is e^(∫P dx) = e^(2x) with P = 2.

quiz.q: Exactness condition:
quiz.why: M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, because mixed second partials of the potential function are equal.

quiz.q: Bernoulli with n = 3 uses v =
quiz.why: Bernoulli's equation y′ + Py = Qyⁿ is reduced to a linear equation by v = y^(1−n). For n = 3 that is v = y⁻².

quiz.q: Solution of dy/dx = ky:
quiz.why: Separating variables: dy/y = k dx gives ln y = kx + c, so y = Ce^(kx).

quiz.q: Integrating factor for x dy/dx + y = x³ (standard form first):
quiz.why: In standard form y′ + y/x = x², so P = 1/x and the integrating factor is e^(∫dx/x) = x.

lessons.title: Second-order linear equations with constant coefficients

scenes.text: After a pothole, a good car settles quickly; a worn shock absorber keeps bouncing.
Both obey my'' + by' + ky = 0; the roots of the auxiliary equation decide the behaviour.

steps.title: Complementary function
steps.body:
For ay'' + by' + cy = 0, solve am² + bm + c = 0.

- Real distinct m₁, m₂: y = C₁e^(m₁x) + C₂e^(m₂x)
- Repeated m: y = (C₁ + C₂x)e^(mx)
- Complex α ± iβ: y = e^(αx)(C₁cos βx + C₂sin βx)

General solution of f(D)y = X: y = CF + PI.

steps.title: Particular integral shortcuts
steps.body:
- X = e^(ax): PI = e^(ax)/f(a) if f(a) ≠ 0; if f(a) = 0, PI = x e^(ax)/f'(a) (and so on)
- X = sin ax or cos ax: replace D² by −a²
- X = polynomial: expand 1/f(D) as a power series in D
- X = e^(ax)V(x): shift: 1/f(D) [e^(ax)V] = e^(ax) · 1/f(D + a) V

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing the 'resonance' case f(a) = 0 and dividing by zero.
- Replacing D by −a² instead of D².
- Writing repeated roots as C₁e^(mx) + C₂e^(mx) (only one independent solution).
- Forgetting to add CF to PI.

activity.prompt: Complete the solution of y'' + 2y' + 5y = 0.
activity.text: The auxiliary roots are −1 ± ___i, so y = e^(___x)(C₁cos 2x + C₂sin 2x).

quiz.q: CF of y'' − y = 0:
quiz.why: The auxiliary equation m² − 1 = 0 gives m = ±1, so the complementary function is C₁eˣ + C₂e⁻ˣ.

quiz.q: PI of y'' + 4y = cos x:
quiz.why: For cos x, replace D² by −1: PI = cos x/(D² + 4) = cos x/(−1 + 4) = cos x/3.

quiz.q: Auxiliary roots 3, 3 give:
quiz.why: A repeated auxiliary root 3 gives the solution (C₁ + C₂x)e^(3x).

quiz.q: PI of y'' − 3y' + 2y = e^(3x):
quiz.why: With f(D) = D² − 3D + 2, replacing D by 3 gives f(3) = 9 − 9 + 2 = 2, so PI = e^(3x)/2.

quiz.q: Solutions of y'' + ω²y = 0 are:
quiz.why: y″ + ω²y = 0 has imaginary roots ±iω, giving sin and cos solutions, so they oscillate (simple harmonic motion).

lessons.title: Cauchy–Euler equations and variation of parameters

scenes.text: y'' + y = sec x — the D-operator shortcuts give nothing sensible for sec x.
Variation of parameters works for any continuous right-hand side.

steps.title: Cauchy–Euler
steps.body:
x²y'' + axy' + by = X(x). Substitute x = eᵗ (so xD = θ, x²D² = θ(θ − 1), θ = d/dt) to get constant coefficients. For the homogeneous case try y = xᵐ: m(m − 1) + am + b = 0.

- Distinct roots: y = C₁x^(m₁) + C₂x^(m₂)
- Repeated: y = (C₁ + C₂ ln x)xᵐ

steps.title: Variation of parameters
steps.body:
For y'' + p y' + q y = f(x) with CF y = C₁y₁ + C₂y₂ and Wronskian W = y₁y₂' − y₂y₁':

**yₚ = −y₁ ∫ (y₂ f / W) dx + y₂ ∫ (y₁ f / W) dx**

steps.title: Solved: y'' + y = sec x
steps.body:
y₁ = cos x, y₂ = sin x, W = 1.

- −y₁∫y₂ sec x dx = −cos x ∫ tan x dx = cos x ln|cos x|
- y₂∫y₁ sec x dx = sin x ∫ 1 dx = x sin x
- **y = C₁cos x + C₂sin x + cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying variation of parameters before dividing by the leading coefficient (f must be the right side after the coefficient of y'' is 1).
- Sign errors in the yₚ formula.
- Forgetting ln x in repeated-root Euler solutions.
- Using x = eᵗ but then forgetting to substitute back.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of variation of parameters.
items: Write the equation in standard form y'' + py' + qy = f
Find y₁, y₂ from the homogeneous equation
Compute the Wronskian W
Integrate y₂f/W and y₁f/W
Assemble yₚ = −y₁∫y₂f/W + y₂∫y₁f/W and add the CF

quiz.q: Wronskian of cos x and sin x:
quiz.why: W = cos x·cos x − sin x·(−sin x) = cos²x + sin²x = 1, which is non-zero, so the two are independent.

quiz.q: x²y'' + xy' − y = 0 has solutions:
quiz.why: Put y = xᵐ in the Euler equation: m(m − 1) + m − 1 = m² − 1 = 0, so m = ±1 and solutions are x and 1/x.

quiz.q: Cauchy–Euler substitution:
quiz.why: Substituting x = eᵗ turns a Cauchy–Euler equation into a linear equation with constant coefficients.

quiz.q: Repeated root m = 1 in an Euler equation gives:
quiz.why: With x = eᵗ, a repeated root m gives (C₁ + C₂t)e^(mt) = (C₁ + C₂ ln x)x^m, so for m = 1 it is (C₁ + C₂ ln x)x.

quiz.q: Variation of parameters needs:
quiz.why: Variation of parameters constructs a particular solution from the known complementary-function solutions y₁ and y₂, using the Wronskian.

scenes.text: An electrical engineer studies a circuit switched on at t = 0 with given initial current.
Laplace transforms turn the ODE into algebra, building in the initial conditions automatically.

steps.title: Table and rules
steps.body:
L{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−st) f(t) dt.

- L{1} = 1/s; L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ⁺¹; L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)
- L{sin at} = a/(s² + a²); L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²)
- **Shifting**: L{e^(at)f(t)} = F(s − a)
- **Derivatives**: L{y'} = sY − y(0); L{y''} = s²Y − sy(0) − y'(0)
- Inverse transforms usually by partial fractions

steps.title: Solved: first and second order IVPs
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping initial-condition terms in L{y''}.
- Mixing L{sin at} and L{cos at}.
- Forgetting to shift back when using e^(at) multiplication.
- Partial fraction coefficient errors — always check by recombining.

activity.prompt: Match f(t) with F(s).

quiz.q: L{t²}:
quiz.why: L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ⁺¹, so L{t²} = 2!/s³ = 2/s³.
Integrating by parts, L{y′} = ∫e^(−st)y′ dt = sY − y(0).

quiz.q: Inverse of 1/(s² + 9):
quiz.why: L{sin at} = a/(s² + a²), so with a = 3 we need (1/3) sin 3t to get 1/(s² + 9).

quiz.q: L{e^(2t) cos t}:
quiz.why: L{cos t} = s/(s² + 1). By the first shifting theorem, multiplying by e^(2t) replaces s with s − 2, giving (s − 2)/((s − 2)² + 1).

quiz.q: Inverse of 1/(s(s + 1)):
quiz.why: By partial fractions 1/(s(s + 1)) = 1/s − 1/(s + 1), whose inverse is 1 − e^(−t).

questions.q: Order of y'' + 3y' = x:
questions.why: The order of a differential equation is the order of its highest derivative. Here y″ is the highest, so the order is 2.
L{1} = ∫₀^∞ e^(−st) dt = 1/s for s > 0.

questions.q: y' = 2y has solution:
questions.why: The equation y′ = 2y is separable: dy/y = 2 dx, so y = Ce^(2x).

questions.q: CF of y'' + 9y = 0:
questions.why: The auxiliary equation m² + 9 = 0 gives m = ±3i, so the solution is C₁ cos 3x + C₂ sin 3x.

questions.q: IF of dy/dx − y/x = x:
questions.why: In standard form P = −1/x, so IF = e^(−∫dx/x) = e^(−ln x) = 1/x.

questions.q: Is (3x² + y)dx + (x + 2y)dy = 0 exact?
questions.why: Here M = 3x² + y and N = x + 2y, so ∂M/∂y = 1 = ∂N/∂x, so the equation is exact.

questions.q: Assertion: PI of y'' − 4y = e^(2x) is e^(2x)/0. Reason: f(2) = 0.
questions.why: The reason is true: f(2) = 4 − 4 = 0, so the usual formula e^(2x)/f(2) breaks down and gives division by zero. The assertion is false; the correct PI is x e^(2x)/f′(2) = x e^(2x)/4.

questions.q: General solution of y'' − 4y' + 4y = 0:
questions.why: The auxiliary equation (m − 2)² = 0 has repeated root 2, so y = (C₁ + C₂x)e^(2x).

questions.q: Inverse Laplace of 3/(s − 2):
Case: A tank population obeys dP/dt = 0.1P with P(0) = 100. P at t = 10:
PI of y'' + y = x²:
questions.why: PI = x²/(1 + D²) = (1 − D² + …)x² = x² − 2, since D²x² = 2 and higher terms vanish.

questions.q: Solve by Laplace: y' − y = 1, y(0) = 0.
questions.why: Taking transforms: sY − Y = 1/s, so Y = 1/(s(s − 1)) = 1/(s − 1) − 1/s, and inverting gives y = eᵗ − 1.

questions.q: x²y'' − 3xy' + 4y = 0 has general solution:
questions.why: Put y = xᵐ: m(m − 1) − 3m + 4 = m² − 4m + 4 = (m − 2)² = 0, a repeated root 2, so y = (C₁ + C₂ ln x)x².

questions.q: PI of y'' − 2y' + y = eˣ:
questions.why: Here (D − 1)²y = eˣ, and 1 is a double root, so PI = x²eˣ/2! = x²eˣ/2.

questions.q: Laplace solution of y'' + 4y = 0, y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 2:
questions.why: Transforming: s²Y − s − 2 + 4Y = 0, so Y = (s + 2)/(s² + 4) = s/(s² + 4) + 2/(s² + 4), which inverts to cos 2t + sin 2t.

courses.title: B.Sc Mathematics · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Theorem and formula sheets for all five papers, a solved mixed practice set and a 20-question mock exam.
outcomes: Learners can state key theorems with hypotheses
Learners can recall standard formulas and tests
Learners can solve mixed problems under time pressure

scenes.text: An examiner's favourite question: 'State the theorem precisely.' Half the marks are for the hypotheses.
Write each theorem as: If (conditions) then (conclusion) — and one counterexample when a condition fails.

steps.title: Calculus & analysis
steps.body:
- Rolle: continuous [a, b], differentiable (a, b), f(a) = f(b) ⇒ f'(c) = 0 (fails for |x|)
- MVT: f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
- Completeness; Archimedean; density of ℚ
- Monotone + bounded ⇒ convergent; Cauchy ⇔ convergent; B–W
- Series: nth term, p-series (p > 1), ratio, root, Leibniz
- Continuous ⇒ Riemann integrable; Dirichlet function is not

steps.title: Algebra
steps.body:
- Subgroup one-step test ab⁻¹ ∈ H
- ℤₙ: |k| = n/gcd(k, n); φ(n) generators; one subgroup per divisor
- Lagrange |H| divides |G|; Fermat a^(p−1) ≡ 1; Euler a^φ(n) ≡ 1
- Index 2 ⇒ normal; G/ker φ ≅ Im φ
- Rank–nullity; trace = Σλ, det = Πλ; Cayley–Hamilton; distinct λ ⇒ diagonalisable
- Gram–Schmidt; Cauchy–Schwarz

steps.title: Counterexamples to remember
steps.body:
- |x|: continuous, not differentiable
- (−1)ⁿ: bounded, not convergent
- Σ1/n: terms → 0, diverges
- A₄: no subgroup of order 6
- [[1, 1], [0, 1]]: not diagonalisable

cards.back: Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence
dim V = rank T + nullity T

quiz.q: Which is NOT a hypothesis of Rolle's theorem?
quiz.why: Rolle's theorem needs continuity on [a, b], differentiability on (a, b) and f(a) = f(b). It does not require f′(a) = 0; that is part of the conclusion at some c.

quiz.q: Σ1/n² is:
quiz.why: Σ1/n² is a p-series with p = 2 > 1, so it converges (to π²/6).

quiz.q: A group of order 35 can have an element of order:
quiz.why: By Lagrange's theorem the order of an element must divide 35: possible orders are 1, 5, 7 and 35. Of the options only 7 divides 35.

quiz.q: Rank of a 5 × 3 matrix is at most:
quiz.why: Rank cannot exceed the number of rows or columns, so for 5 × 3 it is at most min(5, 3) = 3.

quiz.q: Monotone bounded sequences:
quiz.why: By the monotone convergence theorem, every monotone bounded sequence converges.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: series expansions and ODEs

scenes.text: Ankit groups ODE questions by the form of their right-hand side.
Each form has one standard trick. He practises recognising the form in five seconds.

steps.title: Expansions and limits
steps.body:
- eˣ, sin x, cos x, ln(1 + x), (1 + x)ⁿ, tan x = x + x³/3 + …
- sin x/x → 1; (1 − cos x)/x² → ½; (1 + a/x)ˣ → eᵃ
- Dⁿe^(ax) = aⁿe^(ax); Dⁿsin(ax + b) = aⁿsin(ax + b + nπ/2); Leibniz (uv)ₙ

steps.title: ODEs
steps.body:
- Linear 1st order: IF = e^(∫P)
- Exact: M_y = N_x; Bernoulli: v = y^(1−n)
- CF: distinct/repeated/complex roots
- PI: e^(ax)/f(a); sin/cos: D² → −a²; resonance: x e^(ax)/f'(a)
- Euler: try xᵐ; variation of parameters with W
- Laplace: L{y'} = sY − y(0), L{y''} = s²Y − sy(0) − y'(0)

steps.title: Recognise the form
steps.body:
- RHS e^(ax) → shortcut
- RHS sec x, tan x, 1/x → variation of parameters
- Coefficients x², x, 1 → Euler
- IVP with given y(0), y'(0) → Laplace is clean

quiz.q: lim (1 + 3/x)ˣ as x → ∞:
quiz.why: (1 + a/x)ˣ → eᵃ as x → ∞. For a = 3 the limit is e³.

quiz.q: PI of y'' + 9y = sin x:
quiz.why: Replace D² by −1 for sin x: PI = sin x/(−1 + 9) = sin x/8.

quiz.q: L{t³}:
quiz.why: L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ⁺¹, so L{t³} = 3!/s⁴ = 6/s⁴.

quiz.q: Dⁿ e^(−x):
quiz.why: Since D e^(ax) = a e^(ax), Dⁿ e^(−x) = (−1)ⁿ e^(−x).

quiz.q: IF of y' + y tan x = sec x:
quiz.why: IF = e^(∫tan x dx) = e^(ln sec x) = sec x.

steps.body:

steps.title: Solved: mixed 1
steps.body:
Show that a group of order 4 is abelian.

- If some element has order 4, G is cyclic ⇒ abelian
- Otherwise every non-identity element has order 2 ⇒ a = a⁻¹ ∀a ⇒ ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba ∎

Test Σ (n + 1)/(n³ + 2).

steps.title: Solved: mixed 3
steps.body:
Diagonalise A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]].

- λ² − 2λ − 3 = 0 ⇒ λ = 3, −1
- v₃ = (1, 1), v₋₁ = (1, −1) (orthogonal — A is symmetric)
- A = PDP⁻¹ with P = [[1, 1], [1, −1]], D = diag(3, −1)

quiz.q: Every group of order 4 is:
quiz.why: Any group of order 4 is either cyclic (ℤ₄) or the Klein four-group, both abelian. A non-abelian group needs order at least 6.
For large n the term behaves like n/n³ = 1/n². By limit comparison with the convergent Σ1/n², the series converges.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of [[1, 2], [2, 1]]:
quiz.why: The characteristic equation (1 − λ)² − 4 = 0 gives 1 − λ = ±2, so λ = −1 or 3. Check: trace 2 = 3 + (−1), det −3 = 3 × (−1).

quiz.q: lim_{x→0} (sin x − x)/x³:
quiz.why: sin x − x ≈ −x³/6, so (sin x − x)/x³ → −1/6.

quiz.q: Solution of y'' = 0:
quiz.why: Integrating y″ = 0 twice gives y′ = C₁ and y = C₁x + C₂, a general straight line.

quiz.q: Order of 9 in ℤ₁₂:
quiz.why: The order of 9 in ℤ₁₂ is 12/gcd(9, 12) = 12/3 = 4.

questions.q: lim_{x→0} tan x/x:
questions.why: tan x/x = (sin x/x)(1/cos x) → 1 × 1 = 1 as x → 0.
This is a geometric series with first term 1 and ratio 1/2, whose sum is 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2.

questions.q: The order of the identity element is:
questions.why: The order of the identity is 1, since e¹ = e and it is the smallest positive power.

questions.q: Dimension of polynomials of degree ≤ 4:
questions.why: Polynomials of degree ≤ 4 have basis {1, x, x², x³, x⁴}, so the dimension is 5.

questions.q: y'' − y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0 gives:
questions.why: The solution is y = Aeˣ + Be⁻ˣ. With y(0) = 1 and y′(0) = 0 we get A = B = 1/2, so y = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2 = cosh x.

questions.q: sup{x ∈ ℚ : x < π}:
questions.why: The rational numbers below π have supremum π in ℝ, but π is irrational, so the set has no supremum within ℚ. The answer is π in the reals.

questions.q: Number of subgroups of ℤ₁₈:
questions.why: ℤ₁₈ is cyclic, so it has one subgroup for each divisor of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, i.e. 6 subgroups.

questions.q: Rank of the identity on ℝ⁴:
questions.why: The identity map on ℝ⁴ is onto, so its image has dimension 4, which is full rank 4.

questions.q: Assertion: Σ sin(n)/n² converges. Reason: |sin(n)/n²| ≤ 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges.
questions.why: Both true: |sin n/n²| ≤ 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges, so by comparison the series converges absolutely. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: MVT c for f(x) = x² on [1, 3]:
questions.why: MVT: f′(c) = (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4, and f′(c) = 2c, so c = 2, which is in (1, 3).

questions.q: 2⁵⁰ mod 7:
PI of y'' + y = cos x:
questions.why: cos x is a solution of the homogeneous equation (resonance), so PI = (x/2) sin x, i.e. x sin x/(2·1).

questions.q: Case: A 3 × 3 matrix has trace 6, det 6 and eigenvalue 1. The other two eigenvalues are:
questions.why: The eigenvalues sum to the trace 6 and multiply to the determinant 6. With one eigenvalue 1, the others sum to 5 and have product 6, so they are 2 and 3.

questions.q: Σ_{n≥1} n/3ⁿ by known result Σnxⁿ = x/(1 − x)²:
Order of (1 2 3 4)(5 6) in S₆:
questions.why: The order of a product of disjoint cycles is the lcm of their lengths: lcm(4, 2) = 4.

questions.q: Laplace inverse of (s + 1)/(s² + 2s + 2):
questions.why: Complete the square: s² + 2s + 2 = (s + 1)² + 1, so (s + 1)/((s + 1)² + 1) is cos t shifted by −1, giving e^(−t) cos t.

questions.q: For T : ℝ³ → ℝ³ with T² = T (projection) of rank 2, its eigenvalues are:
questions.why: A projection T² = T has eigenvalues only 0 or 1. Rank 2 means two eigenvalues are 1 and the third is 0: (1, 1, 0).
Σ1/(n + k) = (1/n)Σ1/(1 + k/n), a Riemann sum for ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x) = ln 2.

questions.q: Number of elements of order 2 in ℤ₂ × ℤ₄:
questions.why: Elements (a, b) of ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ with order 2: (1, 0), (0, 2), (1, 2). That is 3 elements.

questions.q: y = x is one solution of x²y'' − xy' + y = 0. The other is:
questions.why: This is an Euler equation with auxiliary equation m² − 2m + 1 = 0, a repeated root 1. The solutions are x and x ln x.
